Figure 1.44 shows the terminology used to describe the radiographic projections for each anatomical region. In the head, the term rostral is used instead of cranial. In the ribs and extremities, the terms proximal and distal are used instead of the dorsal and ventral. For the extremities, as with the trunk and tail, the terms cranial and caudal are used up to the carpus and tarsus. Then the terminology changes to dorsal and palmar for the carpus, metacarpals and phalanges of the forelimb and dorsal and plantar for the tarsus, metatarsals and phalanges of the hind limbs. Technical artifacts and errors An artifact is defined as any factor that decreases the quality of the radiograph making evaluation and interpretation difficult. The most common artifact seen on veterinary radiographs is blurring of the image caused by patient movement during exposure (fig. 1.45). Proper restraint, either manually or using specific accessories when patient is sedated or anaesthetised, greatly eliminates this artifact. The use of sedation or anaesthesia is highly recommended, especially when examining certain anatomical regions. However, respiratory motion cannot be avoided so the greatest impact of this artifact is seen in chest radiographs. Here we can try to minimise it by reducing the exposure time to the absolute minimum. The main technical errors that can appear in conventional (non-digital) radiographs are: Very dark image: usually due to overexposure (fig. 1.46A). This can be caused by excessively high kilovoltage (kV) or milliamperes- second (mAs), incorrect film development (too long in developer or using it at very high temperature) or incorrect selection of focus-to- film distance. Very light image: usually due to underexposure (fig. 1.46B). This can be due to use of excessively low kV or mAs, incorrect film development (not long enough in developer, deterioration or dilution

of the developer, or too low developer temperature), incorrect choice of film-screen combination or a voltage input failure. Low contrast image (too grey): this is usually caused by the use of a kV that is too high but can also be caused by many other factors such as incorrect development (too high temperature, too long development time, deterioration of chemical solutions), double exposure (repeated X-ray) or the use of expired film. Blurring: This is usually due to patient movement, but there are other reasons for this: selecting an object-to-film distance that is too long, inadequate contact between film and intensifying screen, double exposure or poor centring of the object relative to the beam. Appearance of marked lines on the image: this is usually associated with incorrect grid position, damage to grid lead strips or faults in rollers in automatic film processors. Yellowing of the X-ray: this may be due to inadequate fixing, incomplete washing or when two films come into contact during the fixing process.

Some technical artifacts and error characteristic of digital radiography: When a digital radiograph is overexposed, it will not appear as generalised darkening of the image as occurs in analogue radiographs, but there will be black focal areas that cannot be clarified with computer post-processing tools (fig. 1.47). This artifact can be corrected by lowering the exposure values. When a digital radiograph is underexposed, there will be no lightening of the entire image as occurs in analogue radiographs, but tiny black spots with appear throughout the image and this is what is known as “noise” (fig. 1.48). Increasing exposure values will correct this artifact. The appearance of a radiolucent halo between structures of very different radiographic densities, e.g. between bone and soft tissues (fig. 1.49) or between metal and bone. Observing this halo around

osteosynthesis material such as bone implants (plates, pins or screws) could be mistaken for a sign of material mobility or rejection. This artifact has generally been corrected by many manufacturers, but it may appear or be accentuated when the edge enhancement computer post-processing tool is overused. Use of anti-scatter grids can produce an artifact in which alternating light and dark bands appear on the X-ray, which has been termed a moiré pattern artifact (fig. 1.50). This occurs when the spaces between grid strips coincide with the direction and frequency of the laser beam reading lines in CR systems. Rotating the grid 90° or using a grid that does not match the reading lines resolves this problem. Potter-Bucky grids, which move rapidly when the X-ray is being taken, do not cause this problem. When the data from the phosphor screen in CR systems or the electrical signals in DR are sent to the computer, these data are erased. If this erasure is incomplete, part of the silhouette from the previous exposure may be superimposed on the current image. This is called a ghosting artifact. It usually occurs when very high exposure values have been used in a previous X-ray. In CR images, the appearance of a white line along the laser beam reading direction indicates a lack of reading of that line (fig. 1.51). This is usually caused by dirt accumulation in the CR laser device.

The following data must be included in a radiology report: patient details, date of X-ray, anatomical region examined and the radiographic projections. It is also useful to explain the reason the X-ray was carried out. All abnormalities observed in the image (i.e. radiographic signs) should be described in the report using the correct anatomical and radiological terminology. These abnormal findings may include: Abnormal radiographic density. Abnormal position. Abnormal size. Abnormal contour or shape. Abnormal numbers. Regarding the degree of detail to include in the description, consider the following as a reference point: A radiographic description will be adequate if a professional who does not see the X-ray can quite accurately imagine it after reading or hearing the description. After correlating the radiographic findings with the patient’s clinical data, the report should establish either a final radiological diagnosis or a list of possible differential diagnoses in the order of likelihood from highest to lowest (the most likely presumptive diagnosis will be placed first on the list). The report may also include recommendations for further diagnostic tests that we believe could complement the findings of the X-rays.

Abdomen 2 Normal radiographic anatomy of the abdomen https://goo.by/yQElH Principles of interpretation Radiography of the abdomen is one of the most commonly performed diagnostic tests in small animal veterinary practice. Nowadays, the routine use of ultrasonography has reduced the need for radiographs of the abdomen in many cases. However, it is important to highlight that the diagnostic information provided by both techniques remains complementary. For instance, an ultrasound scan is always performed if there is a clinical suspicion of liver disease, but radiography is more accurate when a possible reduction in liver size needs to be confirmed. Another example of the valuable combination of both techniques can be found in the assessment of the gastrointestinal tract, where ultrasonography has acquired great relevance over the past few years, without minimising the importance of the diagnostic information offered by radiography in this aspect. When taking a radiograph of the abdomen, we should include: The diaphragm. The lumbar spine. The abdominal wall. The pelvic inlet. In large breed dogs, the length of the abdomen may exceed the length of the cassette. This therefore requires taking two radiographs to

examine the whole abdomen: one centred on its cranial part and the other centred on its caudal part. It is necessary to use an anti-scatter grid (either stationary or Potter-Bucky) when the height of the abdomen exceeds 10 cm once the patient has been placed on the cassette or table. This measure will improve the sharpness of the image by reducing the influence of scattered radiation on the radiograph. The radiographic projections that are usually used are the lateral and ventrodorsal projections. On occasions, comparing the images of right lateral and left lateral projections may provide additional information, especially in the case of the gastrointestinal tract. Ventrodorsal radiographs are preferred over dorsoventral ones, since the latter are taken in sternal recumbency and the shadows of the organs therefore appear slightly distorted due to compression. If we want to examine the urethra of a male dog, its course will be better viewed by extending the hind limbs in cranial direction. It is usually possible to identify the liver, spleen, kidneys, bladder, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, abdominal wall and shadow of the diaphragm on a normal radiograph of the abdomen. In male dogs, it is also possible to observe the os penis, the shadow of the prepuce and part of the prostate (fig. 2.1). In normal conditions, it is not possible to identify the pancreas, adrenal glands, gallbladder, ureters, urethra, lymph nodes, blood vessels, ovaries or a non-pregnant uterus. The main differences between the radiographic image of the abdomen in cats and dogs (fig. 2.2) are summarised in table 2.1. The main limiting factors in the interpretation of radiographs of the abdomen are the superimposition of the numerous anatomical structures contained within the peritoneal cavity and the lack of differentiation between many of them, as most of them exhibit similar radiopacity (soft tissue-fluid). The liver, spleen, kidneys, bladder, etc., all have the same radiographic density, the same tone of grey in the image. The walls of the stomach and intestine also have the same radiopacity as the fluid or mucous content that may be present in the lumen of these organs, hindering differentiation on a simple radiograph. The food or gas content of the stomach and gas or faeces in the intestine are more easily identified, precisely because the radiographic density of gas, non-digested or partially digested food and faeces is different from that of the walls and fluid or mucous content of the

gastrointestinal tract, as well as from that of most of the surrounding anatomical structures. Table 2.1. Summary of the main differences in the radiographic appearance of the abdomen between the dog and the cat. Dog Cat Stomach Pyloric antrum to the right of the median line. Pyloric antrum on the median line. A layer of fat is sometimes observed on the wall. Caecum Generally visible in the right mid- abdomen. Not identified. Spleen Visible on lateral and ventrodorsal radiographs. Only visible on ventrodorsal radiographs. Pancreas Not identified. The left lobe is sometimes observed on ventrodorsal radiographs. Adrenal glands Not identified. Calcified adrenal glands with a normal size are sometimes observed as an incidental finding. Os penis Visible. It is not identified as it is minute in size. Abdominal fat More or less homogeneous distribution. Tendency to a greater accumulation of fat in the area of the falcifom ligament (ventral to the liver), surrounding the intestinal mass (which is centred in the mid-abdomen) and in the retroperitoneal space (facilitates the observation of the kidneys).

FIGURE 2.1. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) abdominal radiograph in male dog with labelling of main abdominal structures. The fat that accumulates in the peritoneum interposes between the abdominal organs, facilitating the differentiation of their contours on the radiograph. The radiographic images of very young or very thin adult animals, which have very little abdominal fat, will show a lack of differentiation of the structures. This may be confused with the image of free fluid or peritoneal reaction. However, an excessive amount of abdominal fat significantly increases X-ray scattering, which may lead to a blurry appearance of the image, even in spite of the use of an anti- scatter grid. Advanced diagnostic imaging techniques such as computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging are not often used for the assessment of the abdomen, since the combination of plain or contrast radiography and ultrasonography allows most diagnostic needs to be covered in this anatomical region. Nevertheless, they may be particularly interesting for the evaluation of alterations of the retroperitoneum or blood vessels (e.g. precise diagnosis of portosystemic communications). Both techniques are excellent to examine the pelvic region, as they offer images with great anatomical details of the muscles and bone structures of this area, the rectum, anal

sacs, urethra, vagina and vulval vestibule in females, as well as of the prostate, penis and scrotum in males. Abdominal wall The abdominal wall is formed cranially by the diaphragm and costal wall, ventrally and laterally by the abdominal muscles, dorsally by the sublumbar muscles and caudally by the peritoneum. Radiography allows the detection of alterations in the radiographic density of the wall. The presence of bands of gas lucency is indicative of subcutaneous emphysema, generally associated with penetrating wounds. Lipomas have fat density, while some muscle or skin tumours may appear calcified (fig. 2.3). Areas of calcification that are not associated with masses may also be observed in the wall, for example in patients suffering from Cushing’s syndrome with cutaneous calcinosis.
FIGURE 2.2. Lateral radiographs of the normal abdomen of a dog (a) and of a cat (b).

FIGURE 2.3. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with a calcified mass located in the abdominal wall. It cannot be confused with an intrabdominal mass, since the dorsal margin of the mass can be seen above the lumbar spine (arrows). Radiography is also very useful in the diagnosis of hernias, which may be congenital or the result of trauma (fig. 2.4). Umbilical or inguinal hernias appear as focal distensions of the ventral abdominal wall. Their radiographic density varies in function of the contents of the hernial sac. It is relatively easy to identify the presence of intestinal loops in a hernia, since they appear as structures with a tubular morphology where gas –or faeces in the case of the colon– generally accumulates to a greater or lesser extent. It is also possible to identify the shadow of the bladder if it is distended (fig. 2.5). When the uterus is displaced into the hernial sac, the uterine horns appear as tubular structures with soft- tissue density. These are difficult to differentiate from intestinal loops with fluid or mucous content, unless the uterus is enlarged due to pregnancy or to a pathological dilatation. It is possible to use contrast techniques to confirm the presence of the intestine or bladder in a

hernial sac, but it is usually not necessary as ultrasonography is an excellent complementary technique in those cases and allows a fairly precise examination of the defect in the wall and of the structures contained in the hernia. FIGURE 2.4. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) abdominal radiograph in cat with left lateral abdominal wall hernia due to trauma. The stomach (S), small intestine (SI) and spleen (Sp) appear herniated.

FIGURE 2.5. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a cat with an inguinal hernia containing the bladder and segments of the small intestine and colon. Two lines of fracture (arrows) can be observed in the bony pelvis. The diaphragm is a musculotendinous sheet that separates the thoracic and abdominal cavities. In normal conditions it is not possible to identify the diaphragm on a plain radiograph, since the liver lies adjacent to it and has the same radiographic density. However, the characteristic morphology of the diaphragm, which is divided into two dorsal crura and a ventral dome, allows us to distinguish its shadow on radiograph. The shadow of the diaphragm will vary according to the chosen radiographic projection (fig. 2.6). The radiographic image of a diaphragmatic hernia varies in function of the size and location of the defect or rupture in the diaphragm. The most characteristic radiographic sign is the identification of abdominal anatomical structures in the thoracic cavity. A stomach or intestine with gas, food or faeces is easier to identify, while organs with soft-tissue density, such as the liver or spleen, may appear less differentiated (fig. 2.7). In some cases, the abdominal cavity may appear partially empty

of its contents (fig. 2.8). If an associated pleural effusion appears, this may mask the images of the abdominal organs displaced into the thorax. When the defect in the diaphragm is small, it is more difficult to diagnose as there may be no evident radiological signs, for instance, when only a part of the liver protrudes through the defect. Ultrasonography is sometimes useful to provide complementary information, although small diaphragmatic hernias are also difficult to diagnose with this technique. Perineal hernias (fig. 2.9) occur more frequently in males and may contain the prostate and bladder. Although a positive-contrast cystogram may be performed to confirm the presence of the bladder in the hernial sac, ultrasonography allows the easy identification of all the structures contained in it. Peritoneal cavity and retroperitoneal space The peritoneum is a serous membrane essentially composed of connective tissue, which delimits the peritoneal space. The retroperitoneum is the anatomical space located between the dorsal parietal peritoneum and the vertebrae and paraspinal muscles; the kidneys, adrenal glands, ureters, blood vessels and lymph nodes lie in it. In dogs, abdominal fat essentially accumulates in the mesentery and greater omentum, which are spaces formed by folds of peritoneum. In cats, on the other hand, more fat is accumulated in the falciform ligament (ventral to the liver) and retroperitoneal space than in the mesentery. In obese cats, the small intestinal loops may appear clumped in the centre of the abdomen due to a more peripheral accumulation of intraperitoneal fat (fig. 2.10). Pneumoperitoneum It is defined as the presence of free gas in the peritoneal cavity. The most frequent cause is iatrogenic, due to an accumulation of air after a laparotomy, which may remain up to one month in this anatomical space and is progressively absorbed. The pathological causes of pneumoperitoneum are penetrating wounds and the perforation or rupture of abdominal organs containing gas (stomach and intestine).

The upright lateral view has traditionally been considered the most suitable to demonstrate the presence of free gas in the abdomen, especially when the quantities of gas are low, but recent studies have shown that the left lateral view is equally as sensitive for the detection of mild pneumoperitoneum. The left lateral image is preferred because in the right it is easy to confuse the free gas with gastric fundus gas. The patient should be kept in lateral recumbency for at least 2 minutes before taking the radiograph. This will allow the gas to rise and collect in the upper part of the abdomen and make it easier to identify.

FIGURE 2.6. Right lateral (a), left lateral (b), ventrodorsal (c) and dorsoventral (d) radiographs of the thorax, in which it is possible to see the normal appearance of the diaphragmatic shadow. Right crus of the diaphragm: rc. Left crus of the diaphragm: lc. Diaphragmatic dome: dd. In the right lateral projection, the right crus of the diaphragm is located cranial to the left crus, while in the left lateral projection it is the left crus that has the most cranial position. The two crura of the diaphragm can be differentiated radiographically because the caudal vena cava (CVC) blends with the right crus, while the fundus (F) always appears immediately caudal to the left crus. On the ventrodorsal view, the diaphragmatic shadow may appear as three

convex images (the two crura in caudal position and the dome in cranial position), although they are not always easy to identify on radiographs. On the ventrodorsal view, the diaphragmatic shadow always appears as a single convex image (arrows). FIGURE 2.7. Right lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) radiographs of the thorax and ventrodorsal radiograph (c) of the abdomen of a dog with a diaphragmatic hernia of traumatic origin. Several abdominal structures, the stomach (S) being one of them, are located in the thoracic cavity. FIGURE 2.8. Right lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the abdomen and thorax of a young dog with a diaphragmatic hernia of congenital origin. It is possible to identify intestinal loops with gas content in the thorax, while the abdomen appears partially empty.

The radiographic signs of pneumoperitoneum depend on the amount of accumulated gas in the cavity. When gas accumulates in large amounts, a general reduction of abdominal radiopacity and a greater definition of the contour of the organs due to the accumulation of gas between them are observed (fig. 2.11). On the other hand, it may be difficult to identify small amounts of free gas, since they are usually mistaken for gas contained in the digestive tract. If gas accumulates between the liver and the diaphragm, the latter can be observed as a thin line of soft-tissue opacity limited cranially by the lung and caudally by free peritoneal gas (fig. 2.12). The observation of this radiological finding confirms the diagnosis of pneumoperitoneum. FIGURE 2.9. Lateral radiograph of the caudal abdomen and perineal region of a male dog with a perineal hernia. It is not possible to visualise the shadow of the bladder in the caudal area of the abdomen, as it is located in the hernial sac together with the prostate and part of the rectum.

FIGURE 2.10. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of an obese cat. Cats accumulate more fat in the falciform ligament (ventral to the liver, marked with a white asterisk) and in the retroperitoneal space (marked with black asterisks) than in the mesentery. In obese cats, the intestinal loops appear clumped in the centre of the abdomen due to the greater accumulation of fat in the peripheral areas.

FIGURE 2.11. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with a pneumoperitoneum. There is a large amount of intra-abdominal free gas. It is located between the organs, which facilitates the observation of their outline and causes a general reduction of radiopacity of the abdomen. This way, it is possible to identify the liver lobes (asterisks) and the diaphragm (arrows) and to view the external aspect of the gastric and intestinal wall clearly, especially in the segments containing gas, since the soft-tissue opacity of the wall contrasts with the gas lucency on both sides (tip of the arrow).

FIGURE 2.12. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with a pneumoperitoneum. The amount of intra-abdominal free gas is moderate. When it is located between the diaphragm and the liver, it is possible to identify the diaphragm (arrow), since it contrasts with the gas located cranial and caudal to it, which confirms the pneumoperitoneum. Free fluid It may be exudate, transudate, blood, urine, bile or lymph. The most common causes of accumulation of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity are: Congestive heart failure. Hepatic alterations. Trauma. Renal disease. Hypoproteinaemia.

Peritonitis. Abdominal neoplasia. The most frequent causes of accumulation of free fluid in the retroperitoneal space are: Acute kidney injury (the amount of fluid is usually minimal and accumulates next to the affected kidney or kidneys). Extravasation of urine of traumatic origin. Haemorrhage associated to trauma. Coagulopathies. Vessel rupture. Rupture of highly vascularised retroperitoneal masses. The radiographic signs of ascites depend on the amount of accumulated fluid in the peritoneal cavity. In general, increased soft- tissue opacity may be observed in the abdomen due to the accumulation of fluid between the organs. This accumulation of liquid causes a decrease or loss of the differentiation of the contour of the organs. Radiologically, this is termed loss of serous definition or loss of serosal detail. This may be the only evident sign when the amount of liquid is low. If this is very large, the abdomen will have practically homogeneous soft-tissue opacity, and only the gas, food or faeces contained in the stomach and intestine will be discernible (fig. 2.13). It may be accompanied by more or less marked abdominal distension, depending on the amount of accumulated fluid.

FIGURE 2.13. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of two cats (a and c) and of a dog (b) with different degrees of ascites. In image (a), it is possible to observe a loss of detail of the intestinal loops in the central and ventral area of the abdomen (delimited by the rectangle), due to the presence of a small amount of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. Image (b) corresponds to a dog with moderate ascites, which causes increased soft-tissue opacity of the abdomen with a loss of detail of the outline of most of the abdominal structures. In image (c), the abdomen has a practically homogeneous soft-tissue radiopacity, indicative of severe ascites. It is only possible to identify the gas, food and faeces in the gastrointestinal tract. The presence of free fluid in the retroperitoneal space increases radiopacity in this anatomical cavity, together with a loss of detail of the structures contained in it (fig. 2.14). Ultrasonography is more useful than radiography to detect small amounts of free fluid in the retroperitoneum and also allows the collection of samples under ultrasound guidance. Peritonitis and retroperitonitis

Inflammation of the peritoneum causes a loss of detail of the outline of the abdominal structures that is similar to that caused by free fluid. In fact, ascites and peritonitis cannot be differentiated on a radiograph. In the case of focal peritonitis, the poorly defined structures (loss of serosal detail) will only be evident in the affected area of the abdomen. The image would therefore be very similar to that caused by the presence of small amounts of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. If peritonitis is generalised, the image will be very similar to that caused by a large amount of free peritoneal fluid, although it is not usually accompanied by abdominal distension (fig. 2.15). However, it is important to bear in mind that peritonitis is often associated with ascites, in which case there will be two causes leading to the same radiographic image (fig. 2.16). Ultrasonography allows us to clearly distinguish between free fluid, which appears anechoic and improves the identification of the contour of the structures it surrounds, and peritonitis, which is characterised by increased echogenicity of the mesentery (fig. 2.17). A common cause of focal peritonitis is pancreatitis. A normal pancreas cannot be identified on radiographs, although in obese cats it may be possible to identify its left lobe as an area of soft-tissue density located between the fundus of the stomach, the spleen and the left kidney (fig. 2.18). When pancreatitis is associated with peritonitis, an irregular increase of soft-tissue opacity in the medial or cranial area of the abdomen may be observed on radiographs (fig. 2.19). The descending duodenum may appear curved and displaced in ventral and lateral direction (fig. 2.20). Pancreatitis is sometimes associated with secondary paralytic ileus, which causes generalised and moderate dilatation of the small intestine.

The most frequent causes of retroperitonitis are the penetration of foreign bodies, penetrating wounds, the extension of local infections (e.g. pyelonephritis) and iatrogenic lesions of the urethra. The most common radiographic finding is increased radiopacity in the retroperitoneal area, with a displacement of the adjacent structures if associated masses appear (e.g. abscess). The appearance of gas in this area may be due to retroperitonitis caused by penetrating wounds or gas-producing anaerobic bacteria (fig. 2.21), but it can also appear in cases of severe pneumomediastinum, due to passage of gas from the mediastinum to the retroperitoneal space (fig. 2.22). In chronic

cases, signs of spondylitis may appear in lumbar vertebrae, which are characterised by the appearance of bony overgrowths in the ventral margin of the affected vertebral bodies. Although ultrasonography is useful to detect accumulated fluid, abscesses, alterations of the renal parenchyma, etc., the information it provides is sometimes limited due to the location and size of the lesions. In these cases, the use of computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging becomes necessary, as they offer detailed anatomical information of the area and both are very sensitive for the detection of most of the pathological alterations that may be found at this level. Peritoneal carcinomatosis The neoplastic infiltration of the peritoneum is termed peritoneal carcinomatosis. This may have a very similar image to that of peritonitis and therefore to that of free intra-abdominal fluid. In addition, carcinomatosis often causes ascites. In the ultrasound examination, it is possible to observe thickening and irregular margins of the mesentery and, on occasions, focal hypo-echoic lesions in it. Masses An abdominal mass appears as a consequence of the increase in size of one or various intra-abdominal structures. This increase in size may be due to pathological causes (neoplasia, hyperplasia, haematoma, abscess, granuloma or cyst, essentially), but also occurs in some physiological processes such as pregnancy, or in iatrogenic diseases such as splenomegaly associated with the administration of barbiturates.

FIGURE 2.19. Enlarged image of the cranial abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a dog with peritonitis secondary to pancreatitis. The area of speckled radiopaque spots indicated by the arrows is due to focal peritonitis. Radiographically, it is not possible to distinguish between peritonitis caused by pancreatitis and other potential causes of inflammation or neoplastic infiltrations (carcinomatosis) of the peritoneum.

FIGURE 2.20. Lateral contrast radiograph (barium) of the abdomen of a dog with pancreatitis. The presence of the contrast medium in the duodenum shows its displacement and ventral curvature, caused by the inflammatory process of the pancreas. The central area of the abdomen shows a loss of differentiation of the structures due to the peritonitis associated with the process. Although it is not usually possible to determine with certainty the origin of an abdominal mass based only on plain radiographs, its location in the cavity (table 2.2) and the displacement of other abdominal structures it causes may be of great help when establishing a differential diagnosis. For example, a hepatic mass causes a caudal and dorsal displacement of the stomach (fig. 2.23), while a splenic mass usually appears located in the central and ventral area of the abdomen, generally on the left side, and may displace the caecum and the colon in dorsal direction and the small intestine in dorsal and caudal direction (fig. 2.24). Taking radiographs in the two orthogonal

projections, lateral and ventrodorsal, provides more complete information in this aspect. Abdominal masses usually have soft-tissue opacity, although lipomas appear as fat opacity masses. Exceptionally, gas may be identified in an abdominal mass when there are areas of necrosis or when it is related to the digestive tract. FIGURE 2.21. The visibility of a mass on a radiograph depends on its size and on the degree of definition of its margins, which may be significantly reduced when free fluid is present or if the patient also suffers from peritonitis or carcinomatosis, or is very thin. If the margins of a mass cannot be clearly seen in the image, but there is an evident abnormal displacement of the adjacent anatomical structures, we will use the term “mass effect” (fig. 2.25). Depending on their size, retroperitoneal masses may displace adjacent abdominal structures in ventral direction (fig. 2.26). They may have a renal, adrenal, muscular, lymphatic or vascular origin, essentially. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging allow us to precisely define the borders of the mass and determine whether the adjacent structures are affected (fig. 2.27). The adrenal glands can only be identified on a radiograph if they are enlarged or calcified. An adrenal origin should be suspected when a mass (with soft-tissue density or partially calcified) is identified craniomedial to a kidney (fig. 2.28). The radiographic finding of a calcified adrenal mass in patients with Cushing’s syndrome is very indicative of a neoplasm. However, it should be borne in mind that in cats, the adrenal glands may be calcified with no pathological significance. Ultrasonography will allow a more precise assessment of the peritoneal and retroperitoneal masses and in many cases, will enable ultrasound-guided cytology or biopsy.

This finding is due to the presence of a small-sized mass in the central area of the splenic tail.

Liver, spleen and lymph nodes Liver On lateral radiographs, the liver occupies a triangular area between the diaphragm and the ventral abdominal wall. Its caudoventral border has an angular shape and does not generally extend beyond the costal arch, or only very slightly. This caudal border is sometimes masked by

the splenic shadow. The longitudinal axis of the stomach on this view should be, in normal conditions, perpendicular to the spine or parallel to the ribs. On ventrodorsal radiographs, the liver occupies almost the whole concavity of the diaphragm. Its caudal border appears delimited by the cranial duodenal flexure, the cranial pole of the right kidney and the lesser curvature of the stomach. The left lobes appear superimposed on the fundus on this view (fig. 2.29). Radiographically, we can detect changes in the size, outline, location and radiographic density of the liver. A recent publication described a radiographic liver size evaluation method, measuring the area occupied by the liver shadow in digital images (RLA: radiographic liver area) and how this correlates with the patient's T11 body area (fig. 2.30) and body weight. The normal reference values for these ratios are: RLA to T11 = 32.7 ± 6.2 and RLA to body weight = 7.0 ± 1.4. When the liver increases in size in a generalised manner, the stomach is displaced caudally. The caudoventral border may appear round and is located farther away from the costal arch (fig. 2.31). If the increase in size is localised, these signs may not be as obvious on the radiograph. The radiographic image of liver masses depend on their size and location in the organ, but if they are large, they occupy the most cranial part of the abdominal cavity and significantly displace the stomach caudally and dorsally (fig. 2.32).

FIGURE 2.27. Lateral radiograph (a) and magnetic resonance image in the sagittal, dorsal and transverse (b) planes of the abdomen in a dog with a retroperitoneal tumour. A heterogeneous increase in radiopacity in the retroperitoneal area with ventral displacement of the colon may be observed on the radiograph. The MRI scan allows a clear view of the limits and morphology of the mass, which is especially useful when it comes to planning a surgical treatment. Radiography is a fairly precise tool to detect a reduction of the size of the liver (microhepatia). The axis of the stomach appears displaced cranially and the distance between the margin of the diaphragmatic dome and caudal hepatic border (fig. 2.33). Doubts about the size of the liver may sometimes arise with ultrasonography, but this technique provides much more information about alterations of the liver parenchyma and margins, which is why both methods are used in a complementary manner to diagnose a reduction of the size of this organ.

The fact that it is located cranial to the renal shadows indicates that it is of adrenal origin, although masses of other origins (e.g. glandular) may also appear in this location.

Gallbladder sludge or calcified gallbladder stones are often identified on plain radiographs and are in many cases a casual finding (fig. 2.34). If the calcified areas have a linear pattern, the most probable diagnosis is that of calcification of the biliary tract (fig. 2.35), which is sometimes an incidental finding in small breed dogs. Abscesses, haematomas, cysts and tumours may also appear partially calcified in this organ. In

addition, the presence of gas may be detected in the liver parenchyma or in the gallbladder and biliary tract. This may be due to an infection caused by anaerobes or, in diabetic patients, by microorganisms that ferment glucose, giving rise to the formation of carbon dioxide. If the morphology of the gas opacity areas is linear, this suggests involvement of the biliary tract (neumobilia), if it is oval, of the gallbladder, and if it is irregular, this is more suggestive of the presence of an abscess or of a tumour with a necrotic centre in the parenchyma. In any case, both calcifications and the presence of gas in this organ can be assessed and confirmed by means of ultrasonography. FIGURE 2.31. Spleen The spleen is an organ with a relatively variable size and location, especially in dogs. The head of the spleen has a more stable position in the left craniodorsal area of the abdomen, thanks to the gastrosplenic ligament. On ventrodorsal radiographs, it appears as a shadow with a triangular morphology superimposed on the last ribs of the left side (fig. 2.36), and it is visible both in dogs and cats. The position of the tail of the spleen, by contrast, may considerably vary. On lateral radiographs, the canine spleen usually appears as a triangular or oval shadow in the mid to ventral abdomen. The feline spleen is proportionally smaller than the canine spleen. Its distal end is generally not identified in the lateral view while its proximal

end may be visualised in some cases dorsally and caudally to the fundus of the stomach. In the ventrodorsal projection, the head of the feline spleen appears similar to the canine spleen, i.e. a triangular shadow superimposed on the most caudal ribs in the left hemithorax. Sometimes in ventrodorsal views, a normal splenic tail can be seen adjacent to the left abdominal wall (fig. 2.37). FIGURE 2.35. Enlarged images of two lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the cranial abdomen of a dog with calcification of the bile ducts. This finding may be incidental in small breeds.

FIGURE 2.36. Ventrodorsal radiograph of the abdomen of a healthy dog. The shadow of the head of the spleen (arrows) has a triangular morphology on this view and is located in the left cranial abdomen, superimposed on the most caudal ribs of the same side. The length of the splenic shadow in dogs will vary on lateral radiographs depending on the position of the tail of the spleen. If the latter is almost completely located in the cranial part of the mid- abdomen, the shadow will be relatively short; if it is in an oblique position in the mid-abdomen, the shadow will be longer; and if it is

located along the left side of the animal, the shadow will then be very long on the radiograph (fig. 2.38). We should not confuse a longer shadow of the spleen with splenomegaly. Splenomegaly is assessed in a subjective manner but is always accompanied by an enlargement (fig. 2.39) and in many cases rounded borders of the organ. It should be borne in mind that healthy German Shepherd dogs have a larger spleen than other breeds of a similar size. With lateral views, a clear visualisation of the distal extremity of the spleen is considered indicative of splenomegaly in cats (fig. 2.40). In the case of a splenic torsion, the organ usually appears very enlarged, with rounded margins and an abnormal position in the abdomen. The image of splenic masses varies in function of their size and location (fig. 2.41). If there is a haemorrhage, the tumour margins may appear totally or partially masked, although the displacement of the adjacent viscera will be an evident sign of its presence in the abdominal cavity. FIGURE 2.38. Lateral radiographs of the abdomens of three healthy dogs showing different positions of the tail of the spleen. In image (a), the shadow is short because the tail of the spleen (S) is located in the cranial abdomen. In image (b), the shadow is slightly longer because the tail of the spleen is located obliquely in the mid-abdomen. Changes in the radiographic density of the spleen are rare. The organ may show areas of calcification associated with dystrophic calcification of neoplasms, abscesses, granulomas or haematomas. A recently published report described 3 cases of emphysematous splenitis secondary to Clostridium spp. infection, all in Golden Retrievers. With such a small number of patients, no conclusions can be drawn as to whether or not there is a predisposition in this breed. This is a rare pathology in human medicine, only described in severe forms of sepsis produced by anaerobic pathogens. In dogs, radiography shows a focal or multifocal coalescing gas pattern in the splenic region, which may be accompanied by signs of loss of serosal detail and pneumoperitoneum. Other causes of gas accumulation in the splenic parenchyma include abscesses or neoplasms infected by gas- producing bacteria and gas embolism secondary to splenic torsion or infarction. These are also uncommon.

Lymph nodes Abdominal lymph nodes are only identified on radiographs when they are enlarged or calcified. The more retroperitoneal fat a patient has, the easier it will be to observe them. The medial iliac (sublumbar) lymph nodes are the easiest to identify on radiographs of the abdomen when they are enlarged. They are located ventral to the lumbar vertebrae L6 and L7. If the enlargement is very pronounced, their silhouette can extend more cranially (fig. 2.42) and produce conspicuous displacement of the descending colon and rectum ventrally (fig. 2.43). The enlargement may be due to lymphadenitis, hyperplasia or neoplasia. A tumoral infiltration of these lymph nodes may be primary (e.g. lymphoma) or metastatic (e.g. in the case of localised tumours in the caudal area of the abdomen or in the pelvis). Urinary system Conventional radiography is a very important diagnostic technique in the study of diseases of the urinary system, although it has now been replaced to a great extent by ultrasonography, since this latter allows a direct assessment of the internal architecture of the kidneys and bladder. However, contrast radiographic techniques still are the standard method of choice to examine the ureters and urethra. Kidneys A plain radiograph allows the observation of alterations in the number, size, outline, position and radiographic density of the kidneys, but it does not offer any information about their internal architecture. That is why the diagnostic imaging technique of choice to assess the kidneys

is ultrasonography, since this technique does offer detailed information about the normal internal structure and its possible alterations. The contrast technique used to examine the kidneys and ureters is excretory urography. It involves the intravenous administration of a positive contrast medium that is selectively excreted by the kidneys. With this technique it is possible to obtain a certain amount of information about the internal structure of the kidney (although not as complete as that offered by ultrasonography), and functional information based on the qualitative assessment of the degree of filtration of the contrast agent through the renal parenchyma. FIGURE 2.42. Enlarged image of the caudal abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a dog with sublumbar lymphadenopathies. Its outline cannot be seen properly due to the presence of surrounding retroperitoneal fat.

FIGURE 2.43. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with very large sublumbar lymphadenopathies due to a lymphoma. The “mass effect” is located ventral to L5-L7 and causes the ventral displacement of the descending colon. The kidneys are located in the retroperitoneal space. On lateral radiographs, they appear located in the craniodorsal area of the abdomen and partially superimposed, while on ventrodorsal radiographs they are not superimposed on one another but on other structures, which masks the shadow of one or the two kidneys, particularly in dogs. The greater the amount of retroperitoneal fat an animal has, the more defined the renal shadows will be in the image. Cats accumulate more fat in this anatomical location, which significantly improves the visualisation of the kidneys. The anatomical location of the right kidney is more cranial than that of the left one, which allows their differentiation on lateral radiographs. The evaluation of the size of the renal shadows is based on the comparison of their length with that of the vertebral body of the L2

vertebra. In healthy animals, the maximum length of the renal shadows should be comprised between 2.5 and 3.5 times the length of L2 in dogs (fig. 2.44), and between 2.4 and 3 times its length in cats (fig. 2.45), although lower ranges have been published in older cats with no clinical symptoms of kidney disease (2.1 to 3.2 in non-neutered cats and 1.9 to 2.6 in neutered cats.) An increase in the size of the renal shadows may be due to very different diseases. A decrease in the size of the kidneys in young animals is usually caused by congenital diseases such as renal dysplasia or hypoplasia, while in adult animals it is usually attributed to chronic renal diseases at an advanced or terminal stage. The relative assessment of the kidneys, that is to say, comparing the size, shape and outline of a kidney with those of the other, may be more useful in practice than evaluating the actual size of each kidney. If the two renal shadows appear enlarged, the differential diagnosis will include renal lymphoma (fig. 2.46), bilateral hydronephrosis, polycystic kidney disease, bilateral perinephric cyst (fig. 2.47) and bilateral neoplasia. If the two kidneys appear decreased in size, the most probable cause is chronic interstitial nephritis (fig. 2.48). When one of the shadows maintains a normal size and the other one is enlarged, this suggests neoplasia, renal trauma, unilateral perinephric cyst or unilateral hydornephrosis. Finally, if the shadow of a kidney is enlarged and the other one is reduced, the most probable cause is chronic interstitial nephritis in a kidney with compensatory hypertrophy of the other one (fig. 2.49).

The most common causes of changes in the contour of the kidneys are: polycystic renal disease, neoplasia, abscess, simple cysts, haematoma, cortical infarction or chronic renal disease at an advanced stage (fig. 2.50). As a general reference for normality, the length of the renal shadows in cats should be between 2.4 and 3 times the L2 length, although lower ranges have been published in older cats (2.1 to 3.2 in non-neutered cats and 1.9 to 2.6 in neutered cats). Measuring the length of the renal shadow in the ventrodorsal view is considered more accurate as in lateral decubitus the kidneys may acquire a certain degree of obliquity.

FIGURE 2.47. Lateral (a) and (b) ventrodorsal radiographs of the abdomen of a cat with bilateral perinephric cysts (perinephric pseudocysts). This disease is very uncommon and mainly affects older cats. It is characterised by an accumulation of a large amount of fluid (urine, transudate, lymph, or blood) that totally or partially surrounds one or the two kidneys. In this case, it gives rise to the appearance of large masses in the region of the kidneys. It is uncommon to detect significant anomalies in the position of the kidneys. When they appear displaced from their normal position, this is generally due to an increase in the size or displacement of the structures that are adjacent to the kidneys, although they may also have an abnormal location due to congenital alterations (renal ectopy) or to trauma causing their avulsion. Calcification of the renal parenchyma due to the presence of calculi (fig. 2.51) or to dystrophic calcification is frequent, especially in older animals. Not all calculi are observed as mineral opacities. Those composed of ammonium urate and cystin have a similar radiopacity to that of soft tissues and fluids, which is why they are usually qualified as radiolucent in plain radiography. Ultrasonography allows the detection of all types of calculi, although if they are small it will be difficult or impossible to distinguish them from calcifications in the renal parenchyma. Excretory urography may offer more precise information in this sense, especially if it is evaluated by means of computed tomography. Dystrophic calcification alone does not usually have any pathological significance, although it sometimes coincides with the appearance of other signs of chronic kidney disease in the patient.

In some healthy cats, it is possible to identify the normal renal pelvis due to the presence of fat in this area, which contrasts with the soft- tissue opacity of the surrounding parenchyma. Negative-contrast or

double-constrat cystography also allows the identification of the presence of gas in the kidneys as a consequence of vesicoureteral reflux. The non-iatrogenic presence of gas in the kidney may suggest the presence of anaerobic bacteria that produce gas. Patients with chronic renal failure may show secondary signs on plain radiographs, such as dystrophic calcification of the folds of the gastric wall or osteopaenia caused by secondary renal hyperparathryroidism, which essentially affects the maxilla and mandible (see chapter 6). Excretory urography Compared with plain radiography, excretory urography provides additional morphological information as well as qualitative information about renal function. Taking into account the information that other imaging techniques can provide, it would currently be recommended to perform excretory urography in cases of urinary incontinence, uroabdomen (suspicion of rupture of the kidney, bladder or ureter), or to investigate haematuria or locate the kidneys in the presence of a retroperitoneal mass. It would be contraindicated in patients suffering from anuria, dehydration and allergy to iodine. Excretory urography is not an appropriate technique to specifically examine the bladder, since the contrast medium mixes with urine in this organ and, in addition, an adequate degree of bladder distension is not usually achieved. However, it may be used as an alternative technique to conventional cystography when it is impossible to catheterise the patient. The intravenous administration of hyperosmotic iodinated contrast media (e.g. diatrizoate or meglumine amidotrizoate) may cause adverse reactions in some patients, although the incidence is low. Nausea and vomiting are the most frequent adverse effects, while systemic hypotension and acute kidney injury induced by the contrast agent are possible, although less probable, complications. There is a risk of anaphylaxis but it is very uncommon. However, the necessary medication to treat it should always be available before starting the procedure and the intravenous catheter should be maintained until the end in case administration of emergency medication is required.

It is recommended to obtain a signed informed consent from the pet’s owner every time a contrast technique is performed. The risk of adverse effects is reduced with the use of low osmolarity, non-ionic iodinated contrast media, such as iohexol or iopamidol, although their much higher cost limits their indication to those patients that have previously been diagnosed with renal disease. The preparation of the patient prior to an intravenous urogram is very important. The animal should be kept on an empty stomach for 12–24 hours, a mild laxative should be administered and an enema should be performed 2 hours before starting the procedure. This will avoid the loss of information due to superimposition of food or faeces on the renal shadows. If a urinalysis or urine culture is necessary, the sample should be collected before administering the contrast agent, since this may affect the results and inhibit the growth of some bacteria. It is very convenient to perform urography with the animal under sedation or anaesthesia. This a procedure requires obtaining numerous radiographs in a short time, and the intervals given in the protocol have to be respected, which will be easier if we do not have to restrain the patient manually. Anaesthesia also somewhat reduces the incidence of vomiting and nausea associated with the administration of contrast media. Before administering the contrast medium, lateral and ventrodorsal radiographs should be taken to evaluate the appropriate preparation of the patient (absence of food in the stomach and of faeces in the colon), adjust the exposure values and rule out any evident alterations that would exclude the need to perform a contrast technique. It should be borne in mind that small renal calculi can be detected on a plain radiograph and, in contrast, can be masked by the contrast media. If the objective is to assess the entry of the ureters into the bladder with precision, it is highly recommended to perform a pneumocystogram before the intravenous administration of the iodinated contrast medium. In order to do so, the bladder should previously be emptied from urine and, next, gas should be introduced (air, carbon dioxide or nitrous oxide) until it is adequately distended. This way, the gas contained in the bladder will clearly contrast with the distal end of the ureters when these are filled the with positive contrast

agent during the urography procedure. Oblique lateral radiographs will help to differentiate a ureter from the other. Although two methods for intravenous administration of the iodinated contrast agent are usually described, slow infusion and bolus administration, it is more common to use the latter, with a dose of 600 to 800 mg of iodine per kg of live weight (mg l/kg). Box 2.1 summarises the protocol to take radiographs. The phases into which a urography procedure is divided (fig. 2.52) are: 1.Vascular phase: the renal arteries become radiopaque 5–7 seconds after the start of contrast medium injection, which is why it will only be observed on a radiograph if this is taken at the same time as the contrast medium bolus is injected. 2.Nephrogram: the renal parenchyma becomes opaque 10–20 seconds after the start of contrast medium injection, which is when maximum opacification is reached. Opacity will then progressively decline in healthy animals. 3.Pyelogram: the renal pelvis and ureters become radiopaque. Their visualisation starts 1–2 minutes after the start of contrast medium injection. In normal conditions, the pelvis has a curvilinear shape and is less than 2 mm long. In some dogs and in the majority of cats, normal pelvic diverticuli, measuring less than 1 mm, can be identified. Given the ureteral peristalsis, which pumps the urine forward, often only an opacified part of the ureter appears in each radiograph. 4.Cystogram: opacification of the bladder. If air has previously been injected in the bladder to improve the visualisation of the openings of the ureters, the iodinated contrast material will progressively mix with the negative contrast material. If this does not allow an appropriate evaluation of the ureters, it will be useful to empty the bladder and introduce additional negative contrast medium during the course of the study. The excretion of the contrast medium depends on the degree of glomerular filtration. A delay in the excretion of the contrast medium may be indicative of renal failure, but it is not a precise method for its evaluation. The nephrographic phase should gradually disappear throughout the procedure, although up to 25 % of dogs with no kidney

disease may still have a detectable nephrogram up to 2 hours after the contrast medium injection. Some of the abnormal patterns (fig. 2.53) that may be observed on excretory urograms are: Lack of renal opacification: insufficient dose of contrast medium, severe renal disease, renal aplasia or atrophy, avulsion or obstruction of the renal artery, extreme hydronephrosis, severe neoplasia. Heterogeneous renal opacification: cysts, abscesses, haematomas, neoplasia, infactus, nephritis, pyelonephritis. Normal initial opacification, which then persists or increases: severe renal disease, acute renal obstruction, systemic hypotension or acute renal injury caused by the contrast. Dilatation of the pelvis and/or ureters. Abnormal location of the end of the ureters. Filling defects: calculi or blood clots. Computed tomography optimises the information that can be obtained from excretory urography, since it prevents the loss of information due to superimposition of structures. The dose of contrast medium may be reduced to 400 mg l/kg (important for patients with kidney disease) and allows a more precise calculation of the degree of glomerular filtration. Percutaneous pyelography Percutaneous pyelography may be used as an alternative to excretory urography. This technique involves the direct administration of a contrast medium in the renal pelvis by means of an ultrasound-guided puncture, thus avoiding the adverse effects of intravenous administration. The contrast medium is not diluted and its excretion does not depend on renal function. The main indication of this procedure is the assessment of a ureteral obstruction. The most important potential risk of this test is the possibility of causing haemorrhage in the kidney. It may also cause extravasation of the

contrast medium to the peritoneal space, which has no clinical significance, but makes the interpretation of the images difficult. Once the ultrasound-guided puncture has been performed, 1–2 ml of urine first have to be aspirated so as to slowly introduce the same volume of contrast medium, under ultrasound or fluoroscopic control. BOX 2.1. Excretory urography protocol Before the urography procedure 12-24 hours before: fasting and mild laxative. 2 hours before: enema to empty the colon. Plain L and VD radiographs. Injection of air into the bladder (if the ureters are to be assessed). Administration of the contrast medium 600-800 mg l/kg in an intravenous bolus. Sequence of radiographs 10-20 seconds: VD. 1-2 minutes: VD. 5 minutes: VD and L (+ oblique is the ureters are to be assessed). 20 minutes*: VD and L (+ oblique is the ureters are to be assessed). 40 minutes: VD and L to assess the bladder. Additional radiographs may be necessary if no conclusive results have been obtained. * The ureters are best seen between 5 and 20 minutes after the administration of the contrast medium and additional radiographs may therefore be taken during this interval to evaluate their image more precisely.

Ureters

Normal ureters are not usually identified on a plain radiograph. However, the excellent contrast resolution offered by digital radiography allows, in some cases, the partial visualisation of one or the two ureters in animals with a large amount of retroperitoneal fat (fig. 2.54). FIGURE 2.53. Abnormal patterns on excretory urograms. (a) Absence of pyelogram in the right kidney 10 minutes after the contrast medium injection, indicative of a marked delay in glomerular filtration. (b) The contrast agent improves the visualisation of the alteration in the outline of both kidneys, the decrease in size of the left kidney and the mild proximal dilatation of the left ureter and moderate dilatation of the right one. (c) Mild dilatation of the renal pelvis and moderate dilatation of the proximal part of the right ureter, which could be due to pyelonephritis or to an obstructive condition of the ureter.

FIGURE 2.54. Enlarged image of a lateral radiograph showing the retroperitoneal region of the abdomen of a healthy dog. The large amount of retroperitoneal fat allows the visualisation in this case of one of the ureters (arrow). This finding is more frequent on digital radiographs, thanks to the greater contrast resolution they have when compared with conventional radiographs. Ultrasonography is of limited use for the examination of the ureters, as it is very complicated to identify their whole course owing to their small diameter and the presence of gas. Visualising the ureteral jet that causes the entry of urine into the bladder, which can be identified with B-mode or Doppler ultrasonography, helps to assess ureteral permeability and locate the vesicoureteral junction. Conventional excretory urography is the technique of choice to evaluate these structures, due to its low cost and high availability. However, a urographic contrast study using computed tomography is excellent to diagnose any ureteral alteration, since it avoids the loss of information due to the superimposition of structures (it does not require the previous emptying of the colon by means of laxatives and an enema) and images with great spatial resolution of small regions can be obtained. The disadvantages of computed tomography are the low availability of equipment and the high cost of the study.

Excretory urography allows the evaluation of the location, diameter, permeability and integrity of the ureters. With this technique, it is possible to observe tubular structures with a diameter of 2–3 mm, which extend from the renal sinus to the vesical trigone. It is usual not to be able to visualise the whole course of the ureter in one single image due to peristalsis (fig. 2.55). The area of opening of the ureters is better observed if gas is injected into the bladder immediately before the urogram, since the gas that is introduced in the bladder contrasts better with the ureters when they are subsequently filled with a positive contrast agent. Oblique lateral views are very useful to differentiate one ureter from the other with certainty in the image (fig. 2.56). On a plain radiograph it is possible to detect mineral density structures compatible with radiopaque calculi in the area of the ureters (fig. 2.57). However, excretory urography will be necessary to confirm the diagnosis, as we may confuse these structures with calcifications of other tissues or with foreign bodies with mineral density on a plain radiograph. Exceptionally, it may be possible to identify a ureteral dilatation on plain radiographs, in animals with a large amount of retroperitoneal fat (fig. 2.58), although excretory urography is usually required to establish this diagnosis. The dilatation of the ureters makes their ultrasound examination easier, although it may be complicated to follow their whole course. Ureteral dilatations may have a congenital (megaureter) or acquired (hydroureter) origin. Ureteral obstructions, which may be caused by calculi, clots, stenosis or masses, cause dilatation anterior to the site of obstruction (fig. 2.59). When a ureter is accidentally ligated during an ovariohysterectomy, it rapidly dilates and permanent distension, urinary stasis and a tendency to suffer from recurrent infections may occur. Pyelonephritis may also cause dilatation of the proximal part of the ureter, although it is usually mild in comparison with the dilatation caused by obstructions.

FIGURE 2.55. Normal excretory urograms in lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) projection of a healthy dog. On the lateral view (a), the complete course of the right ureter is visualised, while the central area of the left ureter is not opaque in this image due to peristalsis. The previous introduction of gas into the bladder facilitates the visualisation of the opening of the ureters into the area of the vesical trigone. An ectopic ureter is a congenital anomaly, which affects dogs more frequently than cats, especially females. The clinical sign shown by affected animals is urinary incontinence, although it does not always occur in males. The caudal end of one or the two ureters does not open into the normal anatomical location, the vesicular trigone (caudodorsal area of the bladder), but into a different location, which is usually the neck of the bladder or urethra (fig. 2.1) (see video 2.1), and less frequently, the vagina, uterus or rectum. Ectopic ureters may have a normal diameter or be dilated and have a relatively tortuous course (fig. 2.61). In some cases, an ectopic ureter enters the area of the vesicular trigone but then has an intraparietal course and opens into an abnormal location, generally the urethra, which can cause confusing images on an excretory urogram, especially if the ureter is not dilated. This intraparietal course, in which the ectopic ureters usually “leave the bladder out”, is more frequent in dogs than in cats. Fluoroscopy and

ultrasonography may sometimes help to establish a diagnosis. When the excretory urogram is not conclusive, it should be complemented with a retrograde urethrogram in males and retrograde vaginourethrogram in females. FIGURE 2.56. This image was obtained in right lateral projection, so that the ureter with a more ventral location is the right one (white arrow) and the ureter in a more dorsal position is the left one (black arrow).

A small foreign body with mineral density (stone) can be observed in the intestine as an incidental finding. Ureteroceles are focal cystic dilatations of the submucosa of the ureters and usually form at their distal end, at the vesicoureteral junction or close to it. They may sometimes project towards the lumen of the bladder or urethra. They appear more frequently in ectopic ureters. The excretory urogram shows a focal dilatation with accumulation of contrast where they are located. Ureteral tumours (fig. 2.62) are uncommon and appear as areas of filling defect on the urogram, accompanied by dilatation anterior to the obstructed site when they cause obstruction. Some bladder tumours may extend to the ureter. When rupture of a ureter occurs, generally due to trauma, signs of the presence of free fluid may be observed in the retroperitoneal space on plain radiographs and extravasation of the contrast to the

peritoneum on the excretory urogram, although the exact site of rupture may be difficult to find. A perirenal or paraureteral urinoma, which consists in a retroperitoneal fibrous sac where extravasated urine accumulates (fig. 2.63), may occasionally form as a consequence of the rupture. Bladder Plain radiography allows the observation of the size, shape, location and radiographic density of the bladder, but does not provide any information about its internal structure. The bladder wall and urine have the same radiopacity on radiographs and therefore cannot be differentiated in normal conditions. That is why, as for the assessment of the kidneys, the technique of choice for the study of the bladder is ultrasonography, since it offers detailed information of the bladder wall and content. Cystography is the contrast technique used to complement the diagnostic information provided by plain radiography. The diagnostic superiority of ultrasonography over cystography is indisputable, but not all veterinary clinics have an ultrasound scanner or enough experience to make a correct ultrasound diagnosis. That is why cystography is still used in those cases for the diagnosis of calculi, inflammations, masses and trauma. It the bladder is ruptured, cystography can provide more precise information than ultrasonography, since ultrasound findings may be uncertain, while the extravasation of the contrast medium to the peritoneal cavity always confirms the diagnosis. Cystography involves the introduction of a contrast medium (positive, negative or both) in the bladder through a flexible catheter. In order to obtain optimum results, it is important to empty the bladder from urine prior to introducing the contrast material. Sedation or anaesthesia of the patient will facilitate the procedure. Positive-contrast cystography Iodinated contrast media, generally diluted at 10 %, are used in doses of 6–12 ml/kg. It is the technique of choice to evaluate anomalous positions of the bladder or a possible rupture of the wall. On the other hand, it may mask small irregularities of the bladder mucosa as well as some abnormal intraluminal contents.

Negative-contrast cystography (pneumocystography) A negative contrast medium, generally air, is used. When performing this technique, there is a minimal risk of causing gas embolism, which may even lead to the death of the animal. This risk is higher in cats than in dogs and may be reduced by using carbon dioxide or nitrous oxide instead of air, due to the greater solubility of these two substances. Doses of 6–12 ml/kg may be used, or gas may simply be introduced, checking the degree of distension of the bladder by palpation. This is the cheapest and most simple method, but it is the least sensible of the three techniques to detect alterations of the mucosa and small defects in the bladder wall. Double-contrast cystography First, a small amount of positive contrast medium is introduced (1–5 ml in dogs and 0.5–1 ml in cats) and then, the bladder is distended with a negative contrast medium. This way, a thin layer of positive contrast material will clearly define the internal margin of the wall. This technique is ideal to examine alterations of the mucosa and the presence of radiolucent calculi in the bladder. Pathological alterations On a plain radiograph, the size and the position of the shadow of the bladder vary in function of the amount of urine it contains. The animals that have not urinated for many hours, whether due to pathological causes or not, may have a very distended bladder, which should not be mistaken for an abdominal mass (fig. 2.64). A scarcely distended bladder will be more difficult to identify, especially when it is superimposed with the intestine or when the animal has very little retroperitoneal fat. The neck of the bladder may appear located cranial to the pubis or in an intrapelvic position in healthy dogs, especially when the bladder is not very distended. However, the position of the bladder is always intra- abdominal in cats. The alteration of the bladder that is most often diagnosed by means of radiography is lithiasis. Radiopaque calculi (fig. 2.65) are identified on plain radiographs, although they may be masked by other

superimposed structures if very small (fig. 2.66). Ultrasonography is required for the diagnosis of radiolucent calculi (generally with ammonium acid urate or cystine) or, alternatively, double-contrast cystography (fig. 2.67). This is because these calculi may be masked by the contrast if positive-contrast cystography is used, particularly if small and few in number. Radiolucent calculi may have a very similar image to that produced by clots or gas bubbles on a double-contrast cystogram. On the other hand, they are easily identified by means of ultrasonography. Alterations of the radiographic density of the bladder wall may also be detected on plain radiographs. The appearance of calcified areas in the wall is usually due to its dystrophic calcification (fig. 2.68), which is generally associated with chronic inflammatory processes or neoplasms. The presence of gas in the bladder lumen is usually iatrogenic, when gas is introduced voluntarily or involuntarily when catheterising the patient (fig. 2.69). In case of emphysematous cystitis, the gas may have an intraparietal (fig. 2.70) or intraluminal location. This type of cystitis is more frequent in diabetic patients, in which the formation of gas is due to microorganisms causing the fermentation of glucose.

The information provided by cystography as regards the thickness of the bladder wall is more limited than that offered by ultrasonography. Double-contrast cystography allows the differentiation of small irregularities of the wall that would otherwise go unnoticed if a positive contrast medium or gas alone were used (fig. 2.71). If the irregularities of the wall are more marked, for example in the case of tumours or polypoid cystitis, or if the thickness of the wall is significantly increased, even homogeneously, the three techniques provide useful information. However, double-contrast cystography is always the most recommended method for this type of evaluation. Generalised cystitis is usually caused by a relatively homogeneous increase in the thickness of the bladder wall (fig. 2.72), although the thickening is sometimes more marked in the cranioventral area of the

bladder. Tumours, on the other hand, usually cause a more focal and irregular increase in thickness (fig. 2.73), although it may be similar to that caused by localised or polypoid cystitis, or to the image produced by the presence of clots adhered to the bladder wall. Most bladder tumours form in the bladder trigone and usually cause some degree of ureteral or urethral obstruction as they grow. Ultrasonography allows a better definition of the extension of this type of lesions as well as the collection of samples for cytology or biopsies. FIGURE 2.68. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a young dog with dystrophic calcification of the bladder wall.

FIGURE 2.70. Enlarged image of the caudal abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a dog with emphysematous cystitis. Areas of gas opacity distributed throughout the bladder wall can be observed. Emphysematous cystitis is more frequent in diabetic patients.

FIGURE 2.71. Enlarged image of a double-contrast cystogram showing the caudal abdomen of a dog. Small areas of accumulation of positive contrast material may be observed in the cranioventral region of the bladder, in addition to a slight deformation of the bladder wall at the same location. These findings are indicative of localised cystitis, although they may also be caused by a tumour (second possible diagnosis). If bladder rupture is suspected, either as a consequence of trauma or due to iatrogenic causes, positive-contrast cystography should be chosen (fig. 2.74), even ahead of ultrasonography. The contra17st medium used should be very diluted, as it is irritating for the peritoneum. Although ionic iodinated contrast media may be used for other types of assessments, if a rupture is suspected it is better to choose nonionic iodinated contrast media. Indeed, although all the iodinated contrast agents are absorbed in the peritoneum, ionic contrast agents may worsen a possible bleeding if the lesion is recent. The extravasation of the contrast medium may sometimes not be observed immediately and may appear after 5–10 minutes. The test should therefore not be considered negative until this time has passed. Pneumocystography is not recommended to confirm a bladder rupture,

since if this latter is small, the extravasation of the gas to the peritoneum will be slow and may be mistaken for gas contained in the gastrointestinal tract. Positive-contrast cystography is also more useful than double- contrast cystography to detect anomalous positions of the bladder, for example when it is displaced into a hernial sac or in the case of intrapelvic bladders. In cases of urinary incontinence due to an incompetence of the urethral sphincter mechanism, the animal is able to void its bladder normally, but leaks urine when at rest or during sleep. This anomaly may have a congenital origin in females, which may have a shorter urethra than normal or a bladder with an intrapelvic location (fig. 2.75). Although they are not very frequent, some anomalies of the urachus may be diagnosed by means of cystography, such as patent urachus (fig. 2.76), patent urachal ligament and urachal diverticula, these latter being more frequent in cats. The animals that suffer from this anomaly of the urachus usually have recurrent bacterial cystitis. Urethra A normal urethra is not identified on plain radiographs and ultrasonography is often not useful either for its evaluation. The technique of choice is therefore urethrography. Iodinated contrast media are used and the patient must previously be sedated or anaesthetised.
