This image is compatible with generalised cystitis, although it may also be caused by a tumour (second possible diagnosis, although it is unlikely since the tumours that affect the entire bladder wall usually have irregular margins).

FIGURE 2.73. Enlarged image of a double-contrast cystogram showing the caudal abdomen of a dog, in which a focal thickening of the ventral wall of the bladder can be observed. A thin layer of positive contrast medium clearly delimits the internal margin of the lesion (white arrows). The outer margin is indicated with black arrows. This image is compatible with a bladder neoplasm (other possible diagnoses include localised cystitis and, with much less probability, adhered blood clot). Fluoroscopy is an excellent technique to provide more accurate diagnostic information when performing an urethrography, allowing real-time visualisation of the dynamic bladder filling processes. The male urethra is divided into 3 segments: prostatic urethra, membranous urethra and penile or spongy urethra. Together, the prostatic and membranous sections make up the pelvic part of the urethra. The prostatic urethra is completely surrounded by prostatic tissue in dogs, and only dorsolaterally covered in cats. The membranous urethra is covered by cavernous tissue and the urethral muscle. The penile urethra extends from the ischial arch to the tip of

the penis and is mostly encased by the erectile tissues of this organ. The female urethra is shorter and wider and entirely pelvic in location. In the cat, the bladder has an intra-abdominal position, so the urethra has a prepelvic segment, proximal to its pelvic segment. FIGURE 2.74. Lateral positive-contrast urogram showing the abdomen of a dog. Extravasation of the contrast medium to the peritoneal cavity can be observed, which confirms a bladder rupture.

FIGURE 2.75. Enlarged image of the caudal abdomen of a dog after an excretory urogram and positive-contrast cystogram, in which it can be seen that the bladder has an intrapelvic location. This anomaly is a frequent cause of urinary incontinence in young females.

FIGURE 2.76. Lateral positive-contrast cystogram of the abdomen of a cat. The bladder has an ellipsoidal morphology and still has a tube that connects it with the umbilical area (arrow). This image is compatible with patent urachus. Retrograde urethrography is performed in male animals by inserting a flexible catheter, filled with contrast material (to prevent entry of air bubbles) into the penile urethra (fig. 2.77) (see video 2.2). Tongue forceps can be used to hold the catheter in position and prevent leakage. Next, a small volume of contrast medium (1 ml/kg in dogs and 2–4 ml in total in cats) is introduced without exerting too much pressure, since there is a risk of rupturing the urethra. If fluoroscopy is used, the end of the catheter can be placed in the neck of the bladder to be withdrawn later, at the same time as the contrast medium is injected; this way, the whole course of the urethra is filled and can be visualised in real time on the monitor. The normal urethra has a larger diameter in the pelvis than in the perineal and penile areas. It is normal

to observe an area of narrowing at the level of the ichial arch, which should not be mistaken for pathological stenosis. In females, the urethra is not usually directly catheterised, since the presence of the catheter in the lumen may mask lesions. A retrograde vaginourethrogram under anaesthesia is therefore performed in these patients. A Foley catheter is placed, with its end cut and filled with contrast material, in the vaginal vestibule. The balloon is inflated and the lips of the vulva are closed with forceps, to avoid leakage of the contrast medium at the moment of its injection. As in males, a dose of 1 ml/kg is used. The contrast medium fills the bladder and the urethra at the same time. This procedure is usually performed as a complementary technique to urography when an ectopic ureter is suspected. Anterograde urethrography is also used for those cases in which the urethra cannot be catheterised. The animal is previously anaesthetised and an iodinated contrast agent is introduced in the bladder by means of bladder puncture or intravenous urography. Next, the bladder is manually compressed to allow the passage of the contrast medium to the urethra at the same time as the radiograph is taken. Plain radiography allows the detection of radiopaque calculi in the course of the urethra (fig. 2.78). Calculi are most commonly found in males around the ischial arch and at the base of the os penis, because these are areas of natural narrowing. In male cats, calculi or blockages are usually located in the penile urethra, although their radiopacity is often insufficient for them to be detected on a radiograph. Urethral lithiasis is much less frequent in female dogs and cats. In urethrography, calculi will produce images of filling defects in the contrast column (fig. 2.79), which are easily misinterpreted as gas bubbles introduced as a result of catheterisation. The os penis sometimes has a separate centre of ossification at its distal end, which should not be confused with a urethral calculus.

On a urethrogram, the normal urethra has a tubular morphology and smooth margins. Irregular margins suggest neoplasia or severe inflammation of the urethra (fig. 2.80). Urethral tumours are more frequent in female dogs than in males or cats of both sexes. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging (fig. 2.81) allow a detailed study of the lesion and its possible extension to adjacent tissues or structures. Stenosis appears as permanent focal narrowings of the urethral diameter. Although they may be associated with tumours or severe inflammation, in many cases they are due to inflammation caused iatrogenically by repeated catheterisation (fig. 2.82) (see video 2.3). Real urethral strictures can be confused with inadequate urethral distension or urethral spasms. Real strictures remain unchanged in repeated images and may be accompanied by focal irregularity of the urethral wall, as well as luminal dilatation proximal to the stricture point.

Urethral ruptures can cause urine to leak into the peritoneal cavity, the pelvic cavity or the peri-penile tissues, depending on the location of the rupture or perforation. This is confirmed if extravasation of the contrast medium is noted when conducting the urethrography. Urethral rupture should be suspected in patients with a hip fracture and dysuria or anuria (fig. 2.83). An iatrogenic origin is also common, after repeated catheterisation, especially in patients with recurrent urethral obstructions (fig. 2.84), or in cases of erosion of the wall due to severe inflammation or neoplasia. Urethral ruptures can provoke fistulas that communicate with the lumen of nearby organs, such as the vagina or the rectum (fig. 2.85). In young animals, urethral fistulas are usually due to congenital defects.

Genital system Genital system of the female The normal genital system of a female is not identified on a plain radiograph, with the exception of the uterus during the second half of gestation. Ultrasonography is the technique of choice to assess a normal uterus and ovaries, as well as to identify any pathological changes in these structures. However, the number of foetuses and the relationship between the diameter of the foetal head and that of the pelvic canal in term pregnancies are assessed by means of plain radiography, since ultrasonography does not provide precise information in those cases. Retrograde vaginourethrography, which has

previously been described (see Urethra section), allows the radiological examination of the morphology of the vagina and vaginal vestibule. The normal pregnant uterus can be identified on a plain radiograph from day 30 of pregnancy in the dog and between days 25 and 35 in the cat (fig. 2.86), but it will not be possible to differentiate this image from that produced by a pathological distension of the uterus until bone mineralisation can be detected, that is to say at day 45 of pregnancy in the dog and between days 36 and 45 in the cat. It is necessary to bear in mind that these data refer to the days of pregnancy, which do not necessarily coincide with the days that have passed since the time of breeding in the dog, since sperm may remain viable in the uterus up to 7 days before fertilisation. This means that an absence of foetal bone mineralisation on day 45 post-breeding does not necessarily imply a negative pregnancy diagnosis. However, ultrasonography is much more precise to diagnose a pregnancy, since it is possible to identify the embryonic vesicles from days 18 to 20 of pregnancy in the dog and 15 to 17 in the cat, although it is recommended to confirm the diagnosis a few days later (from day 23), when the heartbeat can be observed. Ultrasound examinations may however be less precise than radiographs when it comes to counting the number of foetuses. In order to carry out this assessment, it is recommended to take lateral and ventrodorsal radiographs of the abdomen at the end of pregnancy. In order to improve the precision of the diagnosis, the number of heads and that of spines should be counted on both projections, since the superimposition of the foetuses with each other and with other structures may lead to diagnostic errors, especially when there are many of them (fig. 2.87). Ultrasonography does not enable a precise assessment of the relationship between the size of the foetus and the diameter of the pelvic canal. This measurement should be made using radiography (fig. 2.88). If the cranial diameter of the foetus clearly exceeds the width of the canal on the radiograph, this is considered as an evident sign of dystocia. This usually occurs when the size of the male is much greater than that of the female, especially in pregnancies of one or two foetuses, or in brachycephalic breeds, in which the size of the skull is proportionally greater and the morphology of the maternal pelvis is flatter. Other causes of dystocia observable by means of radiography include morphological alterations of the bony pelvis (fractures of

traumatic origin, which can cause a more or less marked narrowing of the pelvic canal, are the most common) or poor foetal position at the time of birth. Radiography allows the observation of the normal uterus after birth, due to its increased size until day 12 postpartum in the dog and day 6 postpartum in the cat. It will also be useful to detect any retained foetuses once the birth is over. FIGURE 2.86. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a cat on day 30 of pregnancy. The dilated uterus appears cranial to the bladder, displacing the colon in dorsal direction and the small intestine in cranial direction. As the bones of the foetuses are not mineralised yet, this image may be confused with dilatation of the uterus due to pathological causes. A fracture of the ischion can also be identified.

FIGURE 2.87. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the abdomen of a dog on day 60 of pregnancy with five foetuses. Radiography is the most precise technique to count the number of foetuses, although the radiographs must be taken on the last days of pregnancy so as to minimise the damage that radiation may cause to the foetuses (the risk is higher during the first third of pregnancy, during the period of organogenesis).

FIGURE 2.88. Ventrodorsal abdominal radiograph of female dog at day 62 of pregnancy. With a ventrodorsal radiograph, the cranial diameter (28.71 mm) can be compared with the width of the pelvic canal (39.15 mm) to prevent possible dystocia due to excessive foetal size. Although ultrasound examinations are much more appropriate to assess a possible foetal death, some signs suggesting this diagnosis may be detected on the radiograph:

Presence of gas in the foetus or in the lumen of the pregnant uterus (fig. 2.89). Anomalous position of the mineralised foetal structures. Evident signs of delay in foetal growth (fig. 2.90). Those cases of endometrial hyperplasia and endometritis that are not accompanied by a great accumulation of fluid in the lumen of the uterus are easily identified on an ultrasound scan, but are not usually detectable on a plain radiograph. However, marked dilatations of the uterus, generally due to pyometra and, on a less frequent basis, to hydrometra, mucometra or haematometra, are easily identified on radiographs. They appear as tubular structures with soft tissue opacity, in many cases with a tortuous course, which occupy the central and caudal part of the abdomen (fig. 2.91). In some cases, the dilatation only affects one or two uterine horns, so the changes may only be observed in one of the sides of the abdomen on ventrodorsal radiographs. FIGURE 2.89. Enlarged images of the abdomen on lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of a bitch on day 64 of pregnancy with two foetuses. Intrafoetal and intrauterine gas may be observed and are both indicative of foetal death. The foetal abdominal wall (arrows) may be identified as there is gas on both sides of it.

FIGURE 2.90. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a bitch on day 50 of pregnancy with seven foetuses. The foetus shown in the rectangle is smaller and the degree of mineralisation is lower compared with other foetuses. This finding may be due to foetal death, although it should be confirmed by means of an ultrasound examination. Uterine stump abscesses or granulomas, which may appear as a complication of an ovariohysterectomy, are not usually detected on radiographs, unless they reach a size that is sufficiently large to produce a clear “mass effect” between the bladder and the colon. Uterine neoplasms are very uncommon and cannot normally be differentiated from masses of another origin on radiographs of the abdomen. Ovarian neoplasms also have a low incidence in small animals. These latter may be uni- or bilateral and are sometimes accompanied by free peritoneal fluid and carcinomatosis, which may mask the image of the mass or masses on the radiograph. They are located caudal to the kidneys and may displace these latter in cranial direction and the intestine in ventral direction if they reach a large size (fig. 2.92). Some ovarian tumours (teratomas and teratocarcinomas) may appear calcified. When a vaginourethrogram is performed, it is important to keep the end of the Foley catheter in the vaginal vestibule and not to introduce it in the vagina, as a vaginal rupture may occur when inflating the

balloon. The normal vagina has a spindle-shaped morphology and it is common to see a small amount of contrast medium passing to the body of the uterus during oestrus. The vestibulovaginal junction appears as an area of narrowing between the vagina and the vestibule (fig. 2.93). Vaginal masses (neoplasms, polyps, abscesses, haematomas, infiltration secondary to a urethral tumour) may create filling defects on the vaginogram. Vaginal hypertrophy, more common in brachycephalic breeds, and tumours can cause marked irregularity in the margins of the vagina (fig. 2.94). Ectopic ureters that open into the vagina may be filled with contrast medium during a retrograde vaginourethrography study, although it is recommended to combine this technique with excretory urography for a more precise evaluation of this anomaly. FIGURE 2.91. Lateral radiographs of the abdomen of four bitches (a-d) and a cat (e) with pyometra. The dilated uterus gives rise to the appearance of more or less folded or tortuous tubular shadows of soft-tissue opacity, which occupy a great part of the middle and caudal abdomen. Vestibulovaginal stenosis is the abnormal narrowing of the vestibulovaginal junction (fig. 2.95), which may be asymptomatic or predispose affected females to recurrent urinary and genital infections.

Although it has traditionally been considered that if the height of the vestibulovaginal junction is lower than a third of the height of the vagina on lateral radiographs, this is indicative of stenosis, some research studies suggest that this finding may be incidental in healthy animals. Genital system of the male Ultrasonography is the technique of choice to examine the prostate and testicles. The information provided by a radiograph is much more limited. In dogs, the prostate is located immediately caudal to the neck of the bladder. Its normal position is intrapelvic, so its shadow is usually completely or partially masked by the bony pelvis on radiographs of the abdomen. In cats, the prostate has a more caudal anatomical position than in dogs and its size is very small, which is why it is not identified on radiographs. In addition, prostatic diseases are extremely rare in cats, so we will only refer to dogs from this point on.

The triangle of fat that accumulates between the caudoventral margin of the bladder and the cranioventral margin of the prostate, which is visible on lateral radiographs, helps to identify the image of this gland on the radiograph (fig. 2.96). The normal prostate is sometimes slightly displaced in cranial direction, especially if the bladder is very distended, which facilitates its evaluation. It is considered that the height of the prostatic shadow in non-neutered healthy males does not exceed 70 % of the distance between the promontory of the sacrum and the pubis on lateral radiographs. In some breeds, such as the Scottish Terrier, the normal prostate may exceed this limit. Retrograde urethrography enables the evaluation of the image of the prostatic urethra and sometimes provides additional information on the prostatic parenchyma. In a healthy dog, the prostatic urethra has a more or less homogeneous diameter and smooth margins. It is sometimes possible to observe the passage of contrast medium to the normal prostatic parenchyma, when the prostatic ducts are partially filled. The most frequent cause of an increase in the size of the prostate is benign hyperplasia, which is very common in non-neutered males from 5 years of age. Prostatitis, prostatic abscesses and neoplasms may also cause a more or less marked increase in the size of the gland (fig. 2.97). In some cases, prostate enlargement is accompanied by the cranial displacement of the gland towards the abdomen. If the increase in size is marked, this usually causes compression or dorsal displacement of the rectum, which may be the only evident radiological sign of prostatomegaly if the gland maintains its intrapelvic position (fig. 2.98). When the height of the shadow exceeds 90 % of the distance between the promontory of the sacrum and the pubis, this finding is considered indicative of a mass-type lesion (tumour, abscess, large- sized cyst). If the increase in size is significant, a mass in the caudal abdomen that displaces the adjacent structures in cranial and dorsal direction (fig. 2.99) will appear on the radiograph. When the diameter of the urethra is very reduced as a consequence of a prostatic disease, the bladder may appear very distended. In the case of prostatic neoplasms, the outline of the gland may be irregular or appear poorly defined in the image, even if there is sufficient fat surrounding it. As associated findings, it is possible to observe images indicative of an increase in the size of the sublumbar

lymph nodes (“mass effect” located ventral to L5-L6-L7) and lesions in the closest bony structures, which suggest metastasis. Bone metastases from prostatic tumours usually appear as proliferative lesions in the ventral margin of the lumbar vertebrae and, in a less frequent manner, in the margin of the sacrum, wings of the ilium and femur. At more advanced stages, they may metastasise to the lungs and other long bones. The appearance of areas of calcification in the prostatic parenchyma is very suggestive of neoplasia (fig. 2.100), although they may also appear in severe chronic prostatitis. Paraprostatic cysts can reach a large size and are identified on plain radiographs as soft-tissue opacity masses located in the caudal area of the abdomen. Calcification of the wall is sometimes observed. An ultrasound scan or alternatively a cystogram will allow the differentiation of the bladder from masses with an origin located in other abdominal organs (fig. 2.101). Neutered dogs show prostatic atrophy secondary to orchiectomy, so the identification of the shadow of the prostate on radiographs will be difficult. The same may occur in patients with Sertoli-cell testicular tumour or in those that receive oestrogen therapy. If the prostatic shadow is large and the urethra appears displaced within it, this finding will be indicative of the presence of a mass-type lesion in the parenchyma of the gland, while if the image of the prostatic urethra shows a marked narrowing or irregularity in its margins (fig. 2.102), this will indicate aggressive disease of the prostate or urethra. The contrast medium may extravasate into cavitary lesions of the prostatic parenchyma that are communicated with the urethra (fig. 2.103). If the morphology of these lesions is very irregular, this is considered compatible with neoplasia.

Stomach Although plain radiography and contrast radiography have traditionally been considered the techniques of choice for the asessment of the stomach and intestine, the now almost daily use of ultrasonography as a diagnostic tool perfectly complements the information provided by plain radiographs and drastically reduces the need to perform other contrast techniques to examine the gastrointestinal tract in small animals. The stomach is divided into a cardiac part, a fundus, a body and a pyloric part (pyloric antrum and canal). In the dog, the body of the stomach has a central position and the pyloric antrum is located in the right side. In the cat, the stomach is located mainly in the left side, with the pyloric antrum on the median line. The image of the stomach depends on its content (fig. 2.105) and on the radiographic projection used. When the patient has not eaten for

some time, the stomach usually contains a variable amount of gas and fluid/mucus. In healthy dogs and cats, the stomach with no food usually appears cranial to the last pair of ribs, although it may also extend slightly beyond them, occupying approximately two intercostal spaces. When it contains food, this latter appears as radiopaque material with a granular aspect, and the size of the stomach may double or triple in normal conditions. On lateral radiographs, the axis of the stomach lies perpendicular to the spine, parallel to the ribs or at an intermediate point between these two positions. One of the most important factors that affect the image of the stomach is the position of the patient when taking the radiograph. The relationship between the position of the stomach and its radiographic image is an important concept that should be borne in mind to interpret radiographs correctly and identify certain gastric lesions. The variation in the image of the stomach is due to changes in the distribution of the fluid and gas that can be found in its lumen: the fluid content is deposited on the inclined area as a result of gravity and the gas is displaced towards the uppermost area of the lumen of the stomach (fig. 2.106). It is important to know how to make the most of the displacements of fluid and gas in the stomach to visualise some of its parts with more clarity (fig. 2.107). It is not possible to appropriately evaluate the thickness of the wall or its folds by means of plain radiography, since the wall and the gastric fluid/mucous content have the same radiographic density and cannot be distinguished in the image (that is to say, we can think that a wall is thickened, when in fact what we see is the image of the wall plus the fluid in the lumen (fig. 2.108). Different contrast techniques may be used to assess the stomach: Conventional gastrography with barium sulphate. Gastrography with iodinated contrast media. Pneumogastrography. Double-contrast gastrography. Gastric emptying studies using food mixed with barium or with radiopaque markers.

Peristalsis and gastric emptying can be observed in real time using fluoroscopy and a positive contrast medium. Before performing a contrast study of the stomach, the patient must not eat for 12 to 24 hours. The study should start by taking plain radiographs to confirm the need to carry out the examination with a contrast medium, ensure the correct preparation of the patient and adjust the exposure values. If sedation of the animal is necessary, acepromazine or ketamine may be used, since those drugs almost do not affect gastric motility. Gastrography using barium sulphate To perform a conventional gastrogram using barium sulphate, this latter is administered in a liquid preparation, preferably at a concentration of 30 % and at doses of 7–15 ml/kg (7–8 ml/kg in large breed dogs and 10–15 ml/kg in small breed dogs and cats). Although it is easier to administer the contrast medium by oral route using a syringe, this method involves some risk of aspirating the contrast medium, which could lead to the development of aspiration pneumonia (fig. 2.109). As an alternative, it is possible to administer the contrast material through an orogastric tube. Nowadays, this technique is almost only used to carry out gastric emptying studies. Gastric emptying is a complex phenomenon, which depends on various factors, such as the type of contrast medium used, the volume administered and the use of certain drugs. The greater the volume of intraluminal content, the faster the stomach will empty; it is therefore important to use the standard dose of the contrast medium. In normal conditions, gastric emptying usually starts in the first 15 minutes after the administration of barium, although in nervous animals it may be delayed until 30–45 minutes. The stomach usually completely empties in 1 to 4 hours in the dog. Minimal significance should be given to abnormally fast gastric emptying. On the other hand, a delay in gastric emptying is more significant. If the administered dose of barium is low, a delay in gastric emptying may be observed, which may lead to a false diagnosis of pyloric obstruction. If the administered dose is high, gastric emptying may be faster than normal.

FIGURE 2.105. Enlarged images of the stomach on lateral radiographs of five healthy dogs. Depending on the gas content, the shadow of the stomach will be more or less clearly defined in the image. It is easier to identify the limits of the shadow of the stomach when it contains gas (a) or food, either partially digested (b) or undigested (c). On the other hand, when it contains a small amount of fluid/mucus and gas (d) or only fluid/mucus (e), the shadow appears poorly defined and is difficult to differentiate from the soft-tissue opacity structures that surround it.

The fluid content fills the fundus and the rest of the body of the stomach. If they are completely empty, the fundus and body may appear as homogeneous soft-tissue density shadows.

FIGURE 2.107. Enlarged image of the cranial abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a dog with a radiolucent foreign body in the pyloric antrum. When taking a left lateral radiograph, the gas is displaced to the antrum and surrounds the object (arrow), which allows its identification in the image.

FIGURE 2.108. Enlarged image of the cranial abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a dog, in which prominent gastric folds are observed. This radiological finding may appear in cases of gastritis, but this diagnosis should never be confirmed only by means of radiography, since the presence of fluid or mucus between the folds of a normal gastric wall may create the same image. An ultrasound scan must be performed for a precise assessment of the thickness of the gastric wall. Some gastric emptying studies have been performed using food mixed with barium, but this is not considered useful since the range of normality for the empyting time is very wide (from 7 to 15 hours). Radiopaque barium-impregnated polyethylene spheres (BIPS) have also been used mixed with food. The number and size of the spheres,

the type and amount of food with which they are mixed and the amount of time without eating should be strictly adjusted to a standardised protocol, or else the results will be difficult to interpret. A disadvantage of this technique is that the time of examination may be very long (up to 10 hours), so it is not used in practice. Positive-contrast gastrography using iodinated contrast media Positive-contrast gastrography using iodinated contrast media is recommended only when a rupture or perforation of the stomach (or the intestine) is suspected. These contrast media are diluted in the gastrointestinal tract, so the quality of the contrast study is lower in comparison with that of the studies performed with barium, but they will be absorbed in the peritoneal cavity if they extravasate. Their use is contraindicated in dehydrated patients. Although hyperosmotic iodinated contrast media can be used at doses of 7 ml/kg, low- osmolarity nonionic iodinated contrast media such as iohexol and iopamidol, which can be administered diluted at 33 % in doses of 8 ml/kg, are more recommended. Negative-contrast gastrography Negative-contrast gastrography is performed by introducing air (20 ml/kg) in the stomach through a gastric tube. It is essential that the animal does not eat for 12–24 hours prior to the study so as to avoid the presence of food in the stomach at the time of examination. It is a relatively simple technique, which can improve the visualisation of certain radiolucent foreign bodies and intraparietal masses. However, it is hardly ever used nowadays, firstly, because double-contrast gastrography would provide more information in these cases and secondly, because the combination of plain radiography and ultrasonography frequently allows the establishment of these diagnoses without the need to sedate the patient or administer contrast media. Double-contrast gastrography

Double-contrast gastrography would be the most appropriate contrast technique to evaluate the mucosa and folds of the stomach, although we should bear in mind that an ultrasound examination is preferable, since it provides direct information about the thickness, differentiation of the layers and peristalsis of the stomach wall. In order to perform a double-contrast gastrogram, non-diluted liquid barium sulphate (3–5 ml/kg) is administered first by means of an orogastric tube, followed by air (10–20 ml/kg or simply the sufficient amount to achieve an appropriate distension of the organ). This technique limits the study to the stomach since it is does not allow a correct assessment of gastric emptying or of the intestine. FIGURE 2.109. Lateral radiograph of the thorax and cranial abdomen of a dog with barium aspiration in the airways after its administration by oral route with a syringe. The aspiration of a small or moderate amount of barium is usually well tolerated by the patient, although its reabsorption through the lymphatic system may last

months or years, and it may remain visible on radiographs of the thorax during this period of time. Pathological alterations The most common indication for a plain radiograph of the stomach is the suspicion of a foreign body. It is easy to visualise objects with a higher radiopacity than that of soft tissues and fluids (radiopaque foreign bodies), as there is a clear difference between these and the wall of the stomach and fluid or mucous content in its lumen (fig. 2.110). Diagnostic interpretation may be more difficult when these objects are surrounded by food, which has a heterogeneous opacity that may be confused with that of other objects, especially if these are small. When foreign bodies have a similar radiopacity to that of soft tissues or fluids (radiolucent foreign bodies), their radiographic identification is much more complicated. Indeed, if they are surrounded by fluid or mucus, or adjacent to the gastric wall, it will often be impossible to distinguish them on plain radiographs (fig. 2.111), unless they have a characteristic morphology (e.g. some types of balls) (fig. 2.112). Contrast techniques may help to confirm the presence of an object in the stomach, but it is worth trying to identify it by means of an ultrasound examination, although it will provide a limited amount of information when the foreign body is surrounded by gas. If gastrography is used, foreign bodies are usually easier to diagnose when a small amount of barium is administered, or with double-contrast gastrography instead of barium gastrography with the standard dose, since the administration of a large volume of positive contrast agent may lead to the object being masked in the image. The aspect of foreign bodies on a contrast radiograph of the stomach depends on their characteristics. Some objects such as balls, wood, fruit stones, plastic, etc., produce well-defined and delimited filling defects. On the other hand, objects with an absorbent surface such as fabrics or sponges may not initially create a filling defect image, as they absorb the contrast medium and are better visualised when most of the contrast material has passed from the stomach to the duodenum (fig. 101).

(b) Plastic objects with different radiopacities: a linear object with low opacity in the area of the body of the stomach (arrow) and several flat fragments with high radiopacity in the antrum. (c) Plastic object (chew toy). (d) Wire. (e) Ball. Another diagnosis that is usually made by means of radiographic studies is pyloric obstruction, which can be acute or chronic. An acute obstruction may be due to a gastric volvulus or to the presence of foreign bodies. Chronic pyloric obstruction is generally due to a narrowing of the orifice of the pylorus, caused by diseases that affect the wall or block the orifice, such as hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, pyloric spasm, inflammation, fibrosis, neoplasia or hypertrophy of the mucosa of the antrum. On a plain radiograph, obstructive diseases of the pylorus may be visualised as a stomach increased in size, depending on the severity and duration of the obstruction. An accumulation of mineral opacity material located proximal to a point of gastrointestinal obstruction (stomach or intestine), which has been termed “gravel sign”, is sometimes observed (fig. 2.114). This sign usually appears associated with chronic digestive obstructions. FIGURE 2.111. Enlarged images of the cranial abdomen on lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of a dog with a radiolucent foreign body in the stomach. On the lateral view, the object (a piece of fabric) may be mistaken for normal gastric content, although on the ventrodorsal projection, the presence of

parallel bands of gas density in the fundus (arrow) suggests the presence of a foreign body. FIGURE 2.112. Enlarged image of the abdomen on a ventrodorsal radiograph of a dog with a ball (arrows) in the body of the stomach. The ball has a very similar radiopacity to that of the gastric wall and fluid/mucous content, but its characteristic round edge allows its identification in the image. FIGURE 2.113. Enlarged images of the cranial abdomen on lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of a dog, 75 minutes after the administration of barium. An accumulation of the contrast material can be observed mainly in the stomach (S) and proximal duodenum (PD), due to the presence of a foreign body that retains a great part of the contrast agent (plastic grid).

In contrast studies, the main finding in cases of pyloric obstructions is delayed gastric emptying. A delayed gastric emptying should be considered significant when only a small amount of contrast material has passed to the duodenum after several hours. The retention of most of the barium in the stomach 3 to 4 hours after its administration is indicative of an obstructive pyloric disease. A pyloric spasm may occur when the contrast study is performed if the animal is nervous. That is why it is useful to keep the animal in a quiet place for 30 minutes and repeat the radiograph after this period of time. A sedative or spasmolytic drug may also be administered. If the passage of the barium to the duodenum is delayed more than one hour even though the animal has been kept in a quiet place and has been administered a spasmolytic drug, the possibility of a pyloric dysfunction should be considered (2.115). Gastric dilatation and torsion or volvulus are diagnosed by means of plain radiography. Acute dilatation of the stomach may be due to a complex variety of causes. The stomach will maintain its normal position and anatomical relationships, but will appear increased in size and filled mainly with gas in the image (fig. 2.116). The dilatation of the stomach may be caused by an obstruction of the pyloric canal or by atony of the gastric wall, but it may also appear due to aerophagy. Acute dilatation may or not be followed by a gastric torsion. Gastric torsion or volvulus can be differentiated from simple acute dilatation because the stomach is rotated. The radiographic image of the stomach varies depending on the type and degree of rotation, on the one hand, and on the degree of distension, on the other (fig. 105). As the stomach dilates, the greater curvature turns in ventral direction and to the right, and is located along the ventral abdominal wall. The pylorus is displaced in dorsal and cranial direction and to the left. Rotation in the opposite direction is uncommon. In case of doubt, taking radiographs in the four standard radiographic projections (right lateral, left lateral, ventrodorsal and dorsoventral) may provide more precise information (fig. 2.118). Apart from the distension and displacement of the stomach, a typical radiographic finding in case of torsion is the image of compartments, or “double bubble” sign. This image is created by bands of soft -tissue density projected through the stomach lumen, which is filled with gas

(they appear because the stomach folds in on itself and the folded wall is projected towards its lumen and is thus outlined by the intraluminal gas that surrounds it). Gastric torsion can also affect the image of other organs, such as the spleen, which may appear enlarged and displaced from its normal position. Radiographic signs of reflex paralytic ileus, dilatation of the oesophagus due to an obstruction at the level of the gastroesophageal junction and pulmonary hypovolaemia and microcardia may also be visualised. At the initial stages of gastric perforation, the findings on a plain radiograph may be difficult to interpret. Depending on the size of the perforation or rupture, a variable amount of stomach content will pass to the peritoneal cavity. This causes an initially focal peritonitis, which is easily detected with an ultrasound scan, but can be more difficult to detect on radiographs. The most significant radiological finding is the detection of free gas in the peritoneal cavity. When the amount of gas is small, the sign that is easiest to recognise is the visualisation of the diaphragm when gas accumulates between this structure and the liver (fig. 2.119) (see Peritoneal cavity and retroperitoneal space). It may be difficult to identify the area of perforation or rupture of the gastric wall with an ultrasound examination, which is why in almost all the cases in which a gastric perforation is suspected, the use of positive-contrast gastrography with iodinated contrast media will be recommended, since these latter are absorbed in the peritoneum if they are extravasated, while barium is not. Barium extravasation into the peritoneal cavity is a serious complication that requires urgent treatment, if possible within 2 hours. A thorough lavage of the peritoneal cavity, with copious irrigation and wiping up of any barium traces with gauze or sponge is required. It may, however, be difficult to remove all barium residues from the cavity. An omentectomy is recommended, if deemed necessary. Patients should be monitored for the following two weeks, as mortality rates are higher during this time.

FIGURE 2.114. Enlarged image of the cranial abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a dog with a persistent accumulation of radiopaque material (“gravel sign”) in the pyloric antrum (arrow). This finding may be indicative of an obstructive process, in this case in the pylorus.

FIGURE 2.115. Enlarged image of the cranial abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a dog after receiving a standard dose of barium 70 minutes before the radiograph was taken. Limited passage of contrast material to the duodenum one hour after the administration of barium is indicative of pyloric dysfunction.

FIGURE 2.116. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with severe gastric dilatation. No signs of rotation of the stomach are observed. FIGURE 2.117. Lateral radiographs of the abdomen of four dogs with gastric torsion (gastric volvulus). (a) Marked dilatation of the stomach with 180-degree

rotation. A soft-tissue density band is projected through the lumen filled with gas, creating an image of compartments or “double bubble” sign (arrows in images a, b and c). (b) Similar image to the previous one, although in this case the radiopacity of the stomach is greater because it contains fluid and gas. (c) Marked gastric dilatation with a rotation of less than 180º, the stomach essentially contains gas. (d) Extreme gastric dilatation with mainly fluid content and a moderate amount of gas, which makes the identification of the rotation of the stomach difficult. Although an ultrasound scan should always be performed in case of suspicion of a gastric neoplasm, radiography can also provide useful information, especially if no ultrasound scanner is available or we do not have enough experience to establish a precise ultrasound diagnosis. The radiographic image of a gastric neoplasm may vary depending on its size, shape and location. On a plain radiograph, it may be possible or not to observe a more or less evident “mass effect”. In contrast studies, the main radiographic finding is the visualisation of a mass-type lesion that is projected towards to the lumen of the stomach, thus creating an image of filling defect on the gastrogram (fig. 2.120). Small masses may be completely masked when a relatively large amount of barium is used. Diffuses diseases of the stomach include those producing inflammation, hypertrophy or atrophy of the wall. These processes generally do not cause any evident alteration in the radiographic image of the stomach and ultrasonography or endoscopy are more useful diagnostic techniques. We should insist on the fact that an image with prominent gastric folds does not necessarily indicate inflammation of the wall, since the same image may be observed in a healthy animal due to the presence of fluid or mucus between the folds of the stomach. In uraemic gastritis, calcification of the gastric mucosa, which is sometimes radiographically identified, may occur (fig. 2.121).

FIGURE 2.118. Enlarged images of the cranial abdomen on right lateral (a), left lateral (b), ventrodorsal (c) and dorsoventral (d) radiographs of a dog with gastric torsion. On the lateral views, the pyloric antrum (PA) is located dorsal and the fundus (F) ventral, and on the ventrodorsal and dorsoventral views the pyloric antrum is located on the left and the fundus on the right, as opposed to what occurs in normal conditions. In a healthy dog, the gas is displaced to the fundus and the fluid content to the pyloric antrum on right lateral views, while on left lateral views the gas accumulates in the antrum and the fluids do so in the fundus. The opposite occurs in this patient due to gastric rotation. In a similar way, when the stomach has a normal position, the gas accumulates in the antrum and part of the body of the stomach and the fluids are displaced towards the fundus on ventrodorsal views, while on dorsoventral views, the gas would be located in the fundus and the fluids in part of the body of the stomach and antrum. In this patient, these relationships are inverted due to the torsion.

FIGURE 2.119. Enlarged image of the cranial abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a dog with gastric perforation. The amount of free peritoneal gas is small and this essentially accumulates in the area ventral to the stomach (black arrow), which may be mistaken for an accumulation of fat. The identification of the diaphragm (white arrow), which is possible due to the presence of a minimal amount of gas between the diaphragm and the liver, confirms the diagnosis of pneumoperitoneum. A gastrogram with iodinated contrast media is necessary to confirm that this gas comes from the stomach.

FIGURE 2.120. Enlarged images of the cranial abdomen on lateral radiographs, before (a) and after (b) the administration of barium (lower dose than the standard one so as not to mask the lesion) to a dog with a gastric neoplasm. The mass creates a filling defect in the pyloric antrum. (c) Ultrasound image of the mass. FIGURE 2.121. Enlarged image in lateral projection of the cranial abdomen of a dog with calcification of the gastric mucosa in the area of the pyloric antrum (arrow). This finding often appears associated to uraemic gastritis.

Small intestine Plain radiographs allow the assessment of the outline, size, position, shape and radiopacity of the intestine, but contrast studies or ultrasound scans are required to examine the alterations of the wall, as well as peristalsis or abnormal transit times. Various references for the normal diameter of the small intestine in dogs have been published (fig. 2.122): It should not exceed twice the width of a rib. It should not exceed the height of the central part of the body of L2. The ratio between the maximum diameter of the small intestine and the minimum height of the body of L5 should not exceed 1.6. In cats, the small intestine diameter should not exceed 12 mm or twice the L2 vertebral height (fig. 2.123). The width of the duodenum may slightly exceed these limits in normal conditions, since its diameter is slightly greater than that of the jejunum and ileum. It is not possible to appropriately evaluate the thickness of the intestinal wall on a plain radiograph, as we may mistake it for the wall plus intraluminal fluid/mucus (fig. 2.124), which may lead to an incorrect diagnosis of increased thickness (fig. 2.125). The real thickness of the intestinal wall is best observed directly by means of ultrasonography.
FIGURE 2.122. References of the normal diameter of the small intestine on lateral radiographs of the abdomen in the dog: it should not exceed the width of a rib (a); it

should not exceed the height of the central part of the body of L2 (b); the ratio between the maximum diameter of the small intestine (A) and the minimum height of the body of L5 (B) should not exceed 1.6 (c). Nowadays, the administration of a contrast medium will be necessary to evaluate the intestines only on a few occasions. It is recommended to prepare the animal prior to the contrast study (no food for 24 hours and administration of an enema 2 to 4 hours before the test). Barium sulphate in suspension (in the form of micropulverised or liquid preparations) is the contrast medium of choice in most cases. A dose of 6–12 ml/kg at a concentration of 20 % in dogs and 12–16 ml/kg in cats is recommended. The administration of an inappropriate dose is one of the most common cases of non-diagnostic contrast studies. Lateral and ventrodorsal radiographs are taken every 10 to 30 minutes, depending on the speed of transit of the contrast medium, until this latter reaches the colon. It is convenient to take a radiograph 24 hours later to rule out any abnormal retentions of the contrast material in the small intestine. The normal transit time varies from 2 to 4 hours in dogs and is approximately 1 hour in cats. Iodinated contrast media are usually used when a perforation is suspected or when a faster transit time is required. Hyperosmotic contrast agents attract fluids towards the lumen of the intestine, are diluted and progress faster than barium, but offer images with a poorer diagnostic quality (fig. 2.126) and may cause transient dehydration of the patient. They are administered in doses of 2–3 ml/kg in dogs and 2 ml/kg in cats. Low-osmolarity iodinated contrast agents, such as iohexol or iopamidol, also progress faster through the intestine, but attract fewer fluids to the lumen. The diagnostic quality of the study is therefore improved (although it cannot be compared to that of barium studies) and their use is more recommended in very sick animals. They may be diluted at 1:2 in water and 10 ml/kg of the mixture may be administered both in dogs and cats.

FIGURE 2.123. References for normal small intestine diameters in lateral abdominal radiograph in the cat: measuring less than 12 mm in the image or does not exceed 2 times the caudal or cranial height of L2.

FIGURE 2.124. Diagram representing the radiographic image of the small intestine depending on its intraluminal content. It is not possible to evaluate the thickness of the intestinal wall on a radiograph, since the fluid/mucous content has the same radiopacity and cannot be differentiated from the wall, thus creating a false appearance of increased thickness of the wall. The use of barium-impregnated polyethylene spheres to detect alterations of the intestinal transit has also been described. They are presented in two sizes: 1.5 mm and 5 mm of diameter. The smaller ones have a similar intestinal transit time to that of food, while the

larger ones are designed to remain trapped in the area immediately anterior to an obstructive lesion. The lack of passage of luminal content through the intestinal tract is termed ileus, and is radiographically characterised by an image of intestinal dilatation. Different patterns of intestinal dilatation may be observed: Mild focal dilatation: 1 to 3 affected loops and luminal distension of 1.5 to 2 times the normal diameter (fig. 2.127). Severe focal dilatation: 1 to 3 affected loops and luminal distension greater than twice the normal diameter (fig. 2.128). Mild generalised dilatation: great number of affected loops and luminal distension of 1.5 to 2 times the normal diameter (fig. 2.129). Severe generalised dilatation: great number of affected loops and luminal distension greater than twice the normal diameter (fig. 2.130). An ileus may be mechanical, when it is due to a physical obstruction of the lumen of the intestine, or functional (paralytic ileus), when the peristaltic contractions of the intestine stop due to vascular or neuromuscular anomalies in the intestinal wall. In a mechanical ileus, the physical obstruction of the intestinal lumen may be complete or partial. The most common causes of obstruction are large foreign bodies, intussusceptions and intestinal masses. A lesion that is extrinsic to the intestine may also cause a mechanical obstruction by external compression of an intestinal loop; adherences due to previous surgeries, hernias of the abdominal wall and, occasionally, masses that originated in other abdominal organs are included in the category. The most indicative radiographic sign of mechanical obstruction is the dilatation of the intestinal loops anterior to the obstruction. The degree of dilatation of the loops is variable. The more complete an obstruction is, and the longer it lasts, the greater the degree of dilatation of the loops will be (fig. 2.131). The more distal (along the small intestine) the obstruction is, and the more complete, the greater the number of dilated loops there will be. Thus, partial obstructions create less evident alterations on plain radiographs (fig. 2.132),

especially if they are recent or if they are located in proximal segments of the small intestine. The “gravel sign” may appear due to an accumulation of granular material at a site anterior to a point of obstruction. When the obstruction is complete, the segment of small intestine that is distal to the point of obstruction is usually empty. FIGURE 2.125. Very enlarged image of the central area of the abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a healthy dog. The intestinal segments that have a small amount of gas or a large amount of fluid/mucus in the lumen (arrow) have a false appearance of “thickened intestinal wall” on the radiograph. An ultrasound scan, on the other hand, does allow the examination of the real thickness of the wall.

FIGURE 2.126. Ventrodorsal radiograph of the abdomen of a dog 45 minutes after the administration of an iodinated contrast medium by oral route. These contrast media are diluted with the fluid content of the small intestine and progress through it faster than barium. They are therefore only used when a perforation is suspected or when there is a real interest in a faster transit, although a good detailed image of the intestinal mucosa is not obtained.

FIGURE 2.127. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the abdomen of a dog with a mild (1.5 to 2 times the normal diameter) focal intestinal dilatation (1 to 3 dilated loops). This pattern is indicative of a partial obstruction or of a recent complete obstruction in proximal segments of the small intestine. FIGURE 2.128. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the abdomen of a dog with a severe (more than twice the normal diameter) focal intestinal dilatation (1 to 3 dilated loops). This pattern is indicative of a complete obstruction in proximal segments of the small intestine, recent complete obstruction in any segment of the intestine, or chronic partial obstruction. As a reference to assess a possible obstruction, it is considered that a value above 1.6 times the ratio between the diameter of the intestine and the minimum height of the body of the L5 vertebra is indicative of an intestinal obstruction in dogs. When the clinical and radiographic findings are indicative of a mechanical obstruction of the intestine, it is recommended to carry out

an ultrasound study of the abdomen, since it will often allow the determination of the cause of the obstruction. If the ultrasound scan is not conclusive and the suspicion is maintained, a contrast study or an exploratory laparotomy will then be indicated. In a functional ileus, the peristaltic contractions of the intestine stop due to vascular or neuromuscular anomalies and the lumen dilates, although it is still permeable. A functional ileus may be secondary to different processes, such as peritonitis, pancreatitis, a recent abdominal surgery, severe viral enteritis and diseases of the autonomic nervous system, among others (fig. 2.133). FIGURE 2.129. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a cat with mild (1.5 to 2 times the normal diameter) generalised intestinal dilatation (elevated number of dilated loops). This pattern is indicative of a partial or recent complete obstruction in distal segments of the small intestine or functional ileus.

FIGURE 2.130. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with severe (more than twice the normal diameter) generalised intestinal dilatation (elevated number of dilated loops). This pattern is indicative of a complete or chronic partial obstruction in distal segments of the small intestine.
FIGURE 2.131. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with a complete obstruction of the small intestine after several days of evolution.

FIGURE 2.132. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the abdomen of a dog with a chronic partial obstruction in distal segments of the small intestine. It is often not possible to differentiate intestinal dilatation caused by a functional ileus from that caused by a mechanical ileus on plain radiographs. The affected length of the intestine may provide some information in this sense, since localised dilatations are more likely to be due to mechanical causes while generalised dilatations are more likely to be caused by a functional ileus, although it is not always the case. In fact, moderate to severe chronic mechanical obstructions may lead to a functional ileus. Radiopaque foreign bodies are easily recognised on plain radiographs (fig. 2.134). On the other hand, those objects with a similar radiopacity to that of fluid/mucus and soft tissues (radiolucent) may not be identified on plain radiographs, although intestinal dilatation will be observed depending on the degree of mechanical obstruction they cause. Ultrasound examinations or contrast studies may offer a more precise diagnosis in this aspect. If the foreign body is fenestrated or absorbent, barium may go through it or be retained, thus causing a mottled or linear pattern of opacification (fig. 2.135). If it is not fenestrated or absorbent, the object may stop the transit of barium (fig. 2.136) or create a filling defect in the contrast column.
FIGURE 2.133. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a cat with a functional ileus secondary to a peritonitis.

FIGURE 2.134. Lateral radiographs of the abdomen of two dogs with radiopaque foreign bodies in the small intestine. (a) Remnants of plastic tubes. (b) Crushed ball. Signs of intestinal obstruction are observed in both cases. Linear foreign bodies (e.g. shoelaces, threads, etc.) create a relatively characteristic radiographic image. Part of the object often remains in the stomach (or even in the oesophagus or mouth) while the rest is located in the small intestine. This latter appears pleated in the image, with focal retention of small amounts of gas (gas pockets) between the folds (fig. 2.137). The image of intestinal pleating may be more evident in the contrast study (fig. 2.138) and is also observed by means of ultrasonography. Invaginations or intussusceptions usually cause severe intestinal dilatation, although in most patients it is not possible to differentiate an invagination from other causes of mechanical obstruction (fig. 2.139) only with plain radiography. The ultrasound diagnosis of an invagination is relatively easy and in most cases, radiographic contrast studies are excluded, as the image may vary in function of the degree of permeability of the intussusceptum (invaginated part of the intestine), and of the space between the intussusceptum and the intussuscipiens (part of the intestine containing the invaginated part). The masses that originate on the intestinal wall include tumours, polyps or granulomatous infiltrates. The development of an obstructive intestinal pattern due to these lesions depends on their size, of whether they grow towards the lumen of the intestine or outside it (fig. 2.140). With time, most of them, which initially do not cause any obstruction, evolve and cause a partial and then complete obstruction. They are usually detected clinically in the phase of partial obstruction, with mild to severe focal distension. These lesions are better identified if an ultrasound scan is performed or, alternatively, a contrast study, in which an image of a filling defect or luminal narrowing associated or not with multiple marks in the barium column (“apple core” appearance) may appear.

FIGURE 2.135. Enlarged radiographic image of a peach stone with remnants of barium in its structure. FIGURE 2.136. Lateral abdominal radiograph of a dog with a complete obstruction caused by a foreign body, 30 minutes after the administration of barium. The object causes a sudden interruption of the contrast column.

FIGURE 2.137. Lateral abdominal radiograph of a dog with a linear foreign body in the small intestine. The folded intestinal wall causes the retention of gas between the folds (gas pockets, arrows). Bladder lithiasis is also observed. FIGURE 2.138. Lateral abdominal radiograph of a dog, with a linear foreign body in the small intestine, 45 minutes after the administration of barium. The folded

intestinal wall causes a “string of pearls” appearance. This type of image may also be found in the duodenum of healthy cats due to peristaltic waves (see chapter Most common diagnostic errors). Diffuse infiltrative diseases of the intestinal wall (intestinal inflammatory disease, inflammation of infectious origin and some types of neoplasia) may cause an abnormal gas density pattern with or without intestinal dilatation, although radiography will often not reveal any significant findings. An ultrasound examination is much more appropriate to evaluate this type of disease. Large intestine Plain and contrast radiographs have traditionally been used to evaluate the diseases of the large intestine. Nowadays, endoscopy has replaced contrast radiography of the colon to a large extent, especially when a flexible endoscope, which can reach the transverse colon, ascending colon and caecum, is available. Ultrasonography also provides useful diagnostic information, in particular regarding alterations of the wall, excluding the rectum due to its intrapelvic location. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging may have a great interest for the examination of rectal diseases, since they offer images with excellent anatomical detail of the whole pelvic region. The large intestine is easily identified on plain radiographs because it usually contains faeces and gas, which have a radiographic density that contrasts with the surrounding structures. The colon has a similar shape to that of a question mark (fig. 2.141). The canine caecum is semicircular (“C” or spiral shape), is compartmented and usually contains a certain amount of intraluminal gas. This gas and its characteristic shape make the caecum easy to recognise in the right middle abdomen on most plain radiographs (fig. 2.142). The feline caecum is a short diverticulum, with no compartments, which rarely contains gas, so it is not usually identified on radiographs.
FIGURE 2.139. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with an invagination in the small intestine. A pattern of severe focal intestinal dilatation may be observed.

FIGURE 2.140. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with a small-intestinal neoplasm (arrows). The diameter of the normal colon varies depending on the amount of faeces it contains and on the defecation habits of each individual. As a general rule, the normal colonic diameter should not exceed the length of L7 in dogs, while in cats, the maximum diameter of the colon should not exceed 2.2 times the diameter of the small intestine, 2.8 times the height of the cranial end of the body of L2 or 1.3 times the length of the body of L5. These measures are nonetheless indicative. Any slight increase in the diameter should always be correlated with the rest of the patient's clinical data. The position of the midportion of the descending colon can vary in the caudal left abdomen. In some dogs, it is positioned along or even slightly right to the median axis, depending on the amount of content in the bowel, the amount and distribution of intra-abdominal fat and the degree of bladder distension.

Some dogs may have a longer length than usual, which is called “redundant colon”. This is considered an anatomical variation without any clinical significance. A more exhaustive assessment of the large intestine requires a contrast study using barium sulphate in suspension (barium enema), gas (pneumocolon) or a combination of both (double-contrast enema). The most commonly used technique is barium enema. Nowadays, a barium enema would be indicated in the following cases: When a narrowing of the lumen hinders the passage of an endoscope. If the limitations of the endoscope itself do not allow a complete examination of the colon and caecum. When a parietal or extraparietal lesion is suspected and the mucosa has a normal aspect in the endoscopic examination. The animal that is going to undergo a contrast enema must not eat for 24 to 36 hours and should be administered laxatives by oral route and hot water enemas prior to the study. Plain radiographs will be taken before administering the contrast agent to adjust the exposure values and confirm that the patient has been properly prepared.
FIGURE 2.141. Ventrodorsal radiograph of the abdomen of a healthy dog. The large intestine has the shape of a question mark on this view.

FIGURE 2.142. Ventrodorsal radiograph of the abdomen of a healthy dog. The caecum (arrows) often appears as a curved tubular structure filled with gas in the right cranial abdomen on radiographs. We should not confuse this image with an abnormal dilatation of the small intestine. After anaesthetising the patient, barium is administered at room temperature through a catheter with an inflatable balloon, which is placed in the distal part of the rectum to avoid leakage of the contrast agent. Doses of 7 to 15 ml/kg of barium sulphate in suspension at a

concentration of 20 % are usually used. If a perforation of the colon is suspected, barium should be replaced by an iodinated contrast medium, preferably of low osmolarity, at a concentration of 15 to 20 %, although the amount of detail of the mucosa will be significantly reduced. The persistence of faecal material in the colon and rectum is termed faecal retention (fig. 2.143). If there is an accumulation of a great amount of faeces that acquire a very high radiopacity due to the continuous absorption of water from the content of the colon, we are dealing with a case of faecal impaction (fig. 2.144). A chronic impaction may cause a generalised increase of the size of the colon. The presence of foreign bodies in the large intestine has a limited significance, since they rarely cause problems if they have not caused any when progressing through the small intestine (fig. 2.145). However, importance should be given to those that are sharp and may seriously damage the wall. Inflammatory processes do not usually cause any radiographic alterations. They can usually be properly evaluated by means of ultrasonography, with the exception of the rectum due to its intrapelvic location. In case of severe colitis (fig. 2.146), contrast studies may show irregularity and localised or generalised ulceration of the mucosa, narrowing of the lumen, thickening of the folds of the wall, diverticula and adherences. Localised dilatations of the colon are usually due to faecal impactions (fig. 2.147.) or mechanical obstructions, caused for example by caecocolic or ileocolic intussusceptions, narrowing of the pelvic canal due to fractures, tumours of the colon or foreign bodies. The colon may be generally dilated due to an excess of faecal content. If the dilatation is associated with hypomotility of the wall, it is then called megacolon. The most common causes of megacolon include chronic constipation and alterations of nutritional, metabolic, neurological or mechanical origin (foreign bodies, anorectal anomalies, perineal hernias, intrapelvic masses, etc.). Idiopathic megacolon, which is more frequent in cats (fig. 2.148), has also been described. To distinguish permanent and irreversible megacolon in cats from colon dilation due to excess faecal content, the colon diameter:L5 length ratio can be used. A ratio over 1.5 is considered suggestive of megacolon.

A localised narrowing of the lumen of the large intestine can be due to a spasm or stenosis caused by a neoplasm, chronic inflammation or scar tissue. As opposed to stenosis, a spasm is transient and is usually caused by an incorrect technique when performing the barium enema. Most cases of stenosis are caused by neoplasms (fig. 2.149), although adenomas, ulcerative colitis and eosinophilic colitis may show similar radiographic findings. FIGURE 2.143. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a cat with faecal retention due to constipation.

FIGURE 2.144. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a dog with faecal impaction. The large intestine appears very dilated (it occupies a great part of the abdomen) and filled with faecal material with a high radiopacity. Colorectal diverticula are not very frequent and usual- ly appear in senior male dogs with prostatic alteration and chronic constipation, or associated with perineal hernias. A localised accumulation of faeces may be observed on plain radiographs, while in contrast studies the contrast medium accumulates in a structure with a saccular morphology and smooth margin (fig. 2.150). Vaginorectal, urethrorectal and rectocutaneous fistulas, which may have a congenital or acquired origin, have been described. If this type of lesions is suspected, it is recommended to perform the positive- contrast enema with iodinated contrast agents, which may show the communication between the colon and the vagina, urethra or skin. Colonic torsion is a serious but uncommon disease in small animals. It causes ischaemia and necrosis of the affected intestinal segment, which lead to sepsis, circulatory shock and, ultimately, the death of the patient. The clinical signs are non-specific and, often, not

representative of the degree of torsion. The plain radiograph can show marked focal segmental distension of the colon, significant focal narrowing and/or displacement of cecum or descending colon, generally with mild or no small intestine distension. These findings are inconclusive so a barium enema is recommended when colonic torsion is suspected. This would usually show focal narrowing of the affected colon segment and longitudinal striations of the wall that course in a helical pattern, which is considered a very indicative sign of colon torsion. It is important to remember that displacement of the cecum or descending colon may be incidental findings in the plain radiograph without pathological significance. Such findings must be correlated with the clinical history, other additional findings in the plain radiographs and, above all, with barium enema results in order to grant them clinical significance. The spontaneous appearance of gas in the colonic wall has been described, which is called pneumatosis coli. It is characterised by the visualisation of thin bands of gas opacity in the colonic wall (submucosal or subserosal emphysema). This may be an incidental finding, but it has also been associated with various pathological situations, some serious such as intestinal infarction. Possible causes should always be investigated. It can lead to a secondary pneumoperitoneum. Congenital anomalies of the large intestine are uncommon in dogs and cats. Anal perforation (fig. 2.151), atresia of the rectum, atresia of the colon, fistulas, diverticula, duplication of the large intestine or rectum, and a short colon and rectum with the caecum in the left hemiabdomen have been described.
