Neck and thorax 3 Normal radiographic anatomy of the neck and thorax https://goo.by/SoZuL Principles of interpretation Neck Except in the case of the cervical spine, which is reviewed in Chapter 5, radiographs of the neck provide a limited amount of information on the anatomical structures that form this part of the body. In normal conditions, it is possible identify the pharynx, larynx, cervical trachea, soft palate, epiglottis and hyoid bone. The other soft tissues (oesophagus, blood vessels, lymph nodes, muscles, salivary glands and thyroid and parathyroid glands) are not identified in normal radiographic images. The presence of a very small amount of air in the lumen of the cervical oesophagus is usually an incidental finding associated with aerophagia, although the persistence of this finding in repeated studies may be due to pathological alterations. The partial calcification of the cartilages of the larynx is very common and usually takes place at 2–3 years of age. Lateral radiographs are most appropriate for the examination of soft tissues in the neck, since most of the identifiable structures are superimposed with the cervical spine on ventrodorsal and dorsoventral radiographs. However, it will sometimes be necessary to take two orthogonal radiographs, for example when a foreign body is identified on the lateral projection, since its exact location cannot be confirmed in any other way. Other diagnostic techniques may provide much more information about this anatomical region. Ultrasound scans may be very useful for

the assessment of the thyroid and parathyroid glands, larynx, salivary glands and masses in general, and they also allow the collection of samples for cytology or biopsy. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are excellent for the examination of this region, although MRI is somewhat better than tomography due to its better definition of soft tissues. While offering real-time radiographic images with somewhat decreased anatomical detail, fluoroscopy does not provide any morphological information comparable to that provided by other diagnostic imaging techniques. Nevertheless, it has a significant advantage over them when assessing swallowing alterations, as it enables the direct visualisation of the passage of food from the mouth to the oropharynx and then to the esophagus. Thorax Radiographs of the thorax are essential for the diagnosis of most of the diseases that affect this region. Although radiographic findings are often sufficient to establish a fairly precise diagnosis, the combination of radiography with other diagnostic imaging techniques, such as ultrasonography or computed tomography, guarantees in most cases an accurate diagnosis of the patient with a thoracic condition. The main limiting factors in the interpretation of radiographs of the thorax are: The loss of information due to the superimposition of structures. The wide variety of anatomical conformations and physiological changes that affect the image of the thorax. The similarity between physiological and pathological images in some cases. The same appearance that very different diseases have on radiographs. In dogs, the cardiac silhouette and the shadows of the mediastinum and diaphragm may greatly vary depending on the conformation of

the thorax. Three types of conformation are basically identified (fig. 3.1): Deep, narrow chest (e.g. Greyhound, Doberman, Collie). Intermediate (e.g. German Shepherd, Labrador, Poodle). Wide and shallow chest (e.g. Bulldog, Dachshund, Basset Hound). The conformation of the thorax is quite constant in cats and is similar to the intermediate conformation in dogs. The thoracic vertebrae, thoracic inlet, sternum and shadow of the diaphragm should be included when taking a radiograph of the thorax. Apart from these structures, the trachea, mediastinum, aorta, caudal vena cava, cardiac silhouette and lung fields may also be visualised in the image. It is recommended to follow a systemic order of assessment and, whenever possible, to carefully examine each of these elements in two orthogonal views, which should include a lateral view and a dorsoventral or ventrodorsal view.

FIGURE 3.1. Normal images in lateral projection of the thorax of three dogs with different thoracic conformations: narrow and deep thorax (a), intermediate conformation (b) and wide and shallow thorax (c). In image (a), several degenerative signs are observed due the advanced age of the animal: pleural calcifications, calcification of the bronchial walls, bony bridges between the sternebrae, calcification of the costochondral junctions and spondylosis deformans in some thoracic vertebrae. In image (c), several parallel bands of soft-tissue density created by folds of skin appear superimposed with the shadow of the liver and cardiac silhouette. Depending on the reason why the radiographic study is carried out, the projections should be chosen taking the following criteria into account:

Assessment of the cardiac silhouette: the right lateral and dorsoventral projections are used, since they provide a more real image of the silhouette. In the left lateral projection, the silhouette appears more rounded (fig. 3.2); in the ventrodorsal view, the heart is positioned farther away from the cassette than in the dorsoventral view, causing the silhouette to appear slightly magnified (fig. 3.3). Assessment of the lungs: lateral (generally right) and ventrodorsal projections are used. In order to correctly assess the lung parenchyma, it is better if this is filled with as much air as possible (there will be a greater contrast with the structures that have different radiographic densities), so we will preferably take a ventrodorsal radiograph, as the capacity of distension of the lungs is greater when the animal is placed in dorsal recumbency than in sternal recumbency. Assessment of pulmonary metastases: the two lateral projections, right and left, are used. When placing the animal in lateral recumbency, the lung that is lower (closer to the cassette) is partially collapsed, as its expansion capacity is limited. On the other hand, the other lung is normally filled with air. If soft-tissue density nodules appear in the lung parenchyma, these would be easier to differentiate in a fully distended lung than in a slightly collapsed lung. That is why the presence of metastases is assessed with a right lateral radiograph, which offers a better image of the left lung, and a left lateral radiograph, which allows a better examination of the right lung. When suspicious images appear on these projections, it is recommended to complete the study with a ventrodorsal radiograph. If the animal presents with severe dyspnoea, taking standard radiographs may lead to significant respiratory distress. In these cases, it would be recommendable to take radiographs with the animal standing, although not all machines allow the placement of the X-ray tube in horizontal position so as to take this type of radiographs. If this cannot be done, the dorsoventral projection should be chosen ahead of the ventrodorsal and lateral ones, as there is a smaller risk of respiratory distress for the animal.

Oblique radiographs centred on the lesion may be useful to evaluate lesions of the thoracic wall, e.g. rib tumours. FIGURE 3.2. Right (a) and left (b) lateral projections of the chest of a healthy dog. The shape of the cardiac silhouette is more rounded on the left lateral X-ray, which could lead to a misdiagnosis of cardiomegaly.

FIGURE 3.3. Dorsoventral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) projections of the chest of a healthy dog. The shape of the cardiac silhouette changes from one projection to another. It appears magnified in the ventrodorsal view because the patient is in dorsal recumbency, and this means that the distance from the heart to the cassette/detector is longer. It is very important to pay maximum attention to the technical quality of radiographs of the thoracic wall. The use of incorrect exposure values, improper patient positioning, poor developing technique or incorrect digital post-processing can greatly affect the interpretation of the images. Generally, a high kilovoltage and low milliamperage should be used so as to reduce the time of exposure and minimise the influence of respiratory movements on the images. If exposure values are too low (resulting in underexposed X-rays), the image will appear lighter than expected in analog radiography, while noise artifacts may appear in digital radiography. On the other hand, if the exposure values used are too high (resulting in overexposed radiography), the entire image will appear darker in analog radiography, and black focal areas will be noticeable in digital radiography, as explained in Chapter 1. In both cases the image of the lung will be particularly affected and these variations may even be mistaken for pathological alterations. Generally, the use of an anti-scatter grid (either stationary or Potter- Bucky) is necessary when the thickness of the thorax, once placed on the cassette, exceeds 10 cm. However, high-quality direct digital detector panels can provide excellent images of the thorax and other anatomical regions with a thickness greater than 10 cm without the need for a grid. This allows for a large reduction in milliamperage per second, which in turn significantly reduces the amount of scatter radiation produced. Although it is difficult in practice, chest radiographs should ideally be taken at maximum inspiration. The greater the amount of air in the lungs, the easier it will be to identify small lesions in these organs radiographically. If the X-ray is taken during exhalation, the cardiac silhouette will appear larger and may come into contact with or overlap with the shadow of the diaphragm, and the lungs will exhibit higher radiographic density.

As regards the position of the patient, special attention should be paid to the position of the forelimbs, which must be correctly extended so they are not superimposed with the cranial part of the thoracic cavity. In addition, when a radiograph is taken in lateral recumbency, the median plane of the thorax is usually inclined on the cassette rather than being parallel to it, due to the relatively triangular morphology of this anatomical region. A radiolucent wedge should therefore be placed under the sternum in order to correct the position. When observing a lateral radiograph, we will know that the thorax was correctly placed when the costochondral junctions of both sides appear practically at the same level. If they appear widely separated in the image, this finding will indicate that the median plane is not parallel to the X-ray table, affecting the image of the cardiac silhouette and the trachea. As a result, the cardiac silhouette appears more supported on the sternum and the trachea appears falsely elevated (fig. 3.4). It is quite important not to mix up these findings caused by an incorrect positioning with real pathological alterations. The rotation of the thorax at the time of taking a dorsoventral or ventrodorsal radiograph will be identified in the images by the lack of superimposition of the sternum and thoracic spine, and will particularly affect the cardiac silhouette, which will appear falsely deformed (fig. 3.5). Digital radiographs offer a better contrast resolution than conventional radiographs, which translates into a better definition of some structures, especially in the thorax, such as the pulmonary vessels or the walls of larger bronchi. Lungs appear less radiolucent than in analog radiographs, which may lead to an incorrect diagnosis of a pathological increase in lung opacity. In comparison with dogs, the thorax of cats has a more triangular morphology, the cardiac silhouette is of a smaller craniocaudal diameter (2 intercostal spaces compared to 2.5 to 3.5 intercostal spaces in dogs) and the dorsocaudal margin of the caudal lung lobes may appear slightly separated from the spine in lateral projections in healthy animals. This latter finding would raise suspicion of mild pleural effusion in the case of dogs (fig. 3.6). In young animals, it is possible to identify the shadow of the thymus until approximately 6 months of age. After that, the shadow cannot be differentiated from the rest of the structures contained in the cranial

mediastinal space. Due to the typical organomegaly observed in young animals, the cardiac silhouette may also appear larger in comparison with adult animals. Degenerative changes can frequently be observed in older animals, such as spondylosis deformans in the thoracic vertebrae, formation of bony bridges between the sternebrae, calcification of the costochondral junctions, calcification of the tracheal rings and bronchial walls, formation of pulmonary osteomas, calcified pleural plaques, thickening of the pleura and a diffuse interstitial lung pattern associated with fibrosis. In older cats, the heart tends to lie more on the sternum due to an elongation of the aorta, which may increase the curvature of the aortic arch and cause a marked undulation of the descending aorta. The superimposition of subcutaneous fat in obese animals may significantly worsen the quality of the images of the thorax and especially affects the assessment of the lungs. The mediastinum and cardiac silhouette may also appear enlarged in obese patients and the lung margin may be slightly separated from the thoracic wall, which could be confused with a mild pleural effusion. The combination of radiography and echocardiography offers very complete information about the diseases that affect the heart and great vessels. Non-cardiac thoracic ultrasonography is also useful to obtain complementary information in cases of pleural or mediastinal effusion, assess thoracic masses that are not surrounded by air, pulmonary consolidation and diaphragmatic hernias, and collect samples or perform thoracic drainage under ultrasound guidance. Fluoroscopy allows real-time evaluation of peristalsis of the oesophagus and of the passage of food or contrast medium through it. It is very useful for the diagnosis of tracheal, bronchial or laryngeal collapse, diaphragmatic paralysis and sliding hiatal hernias. this also allows samples to be collected for cytology and biopsy of thoracic lesions not detectable by ultrasound, as well as angiography studies. Some state-of-the-art X-ray machines come with the option of dynamic digital radiography (DDR), which is based on the rapid acquisition of radiographic series. This technique may serve as an alternative to fluoroscopy in some cases, especially when the examination time is relatively short, as DDR may result in a significant increase in exposure compared to fluoroscopy. Reducing the

exposure dose and, therefore, the resolution of dynamic radiographic images to the minimum required may make this an appropriate alternative for some dynamic radiological studies in veterinary medicine. Among advanced imaging techniques, computed tomography is generally more appropriate to examine the thorax than magnetic resonance imaging. A computed tomography examination can be performed in a few seconds, which allows the use of techniques of apnoeic anaesthesia to avoid the influence of respiratory movements on the images. Conversely, several minutes are usually necessary for an examination with conventional magnetic resonance imaging equipment. Such prolonged apnoea cannot be maintained and the artefacts due to respiratory and cardiac movements significantly affect the quality of chest images. Computed tomography is particularly indicated for the assessment of pneumothoraces or persistent and recurrent pleural effusions, localised lesions in the mediastinum, tracheal collapse and bronchial obstruction. It is also useful for the detection of pulmonary metastases and lymphadenopathies, thomboembolism, pulmonary torsion, infiltrative interstitial lung disease, as well as to differentiate between consolidation and atelectasis and assess thoracic masses in general. Magnetic resonance may also be of interest for the pre-surgical examination of the thoracic wall and pleural and mediastinal masses, essentially.

Compared with that of a dog, the thorax of a cat has a more triangular morphology, the cardiac silhouette has a smaller craniocaudal diameter (2 intercostal spaces) and the caudodorsal margin of the caudal pulmonary lobes may appear slightly separated from the spine in normal conditions (arrows). This latter finding would make us suspect a mild pleural effusion in the case of dogs. Thoracic wall The thoracic wall is formed by the thoracic spine (see chapter 5), the sternum, the diaphragm (see chapter 2), the ribs, costal cartilages and intercostal spaces.

Ribs In normal conditions, the ribs are symmetrical, have a homogeneous density and smooth borders. The space between them must be regular. However, congenital anomalies, hypoplasia or aplasia, which are uni- or bilateral, are often seen in the thirteenth pair of ribs. The C7 and L1 vertebrae may also have rudimentary ribs when they are transitional. In the first weeks of life, costal cartilages cannot be identified on radiographs as they have soft-tissue opacity. They become apparent as they start calcifying. In older cats, segments of the costal cartilages may appear markedly calcified, thus having an appearance of ruptures. In older dogs and cats, calcifications with an irregular morphology may be observed in the costochondral junctions, and these may even be mistaken for intrathoracic lesions. In chondrodystrophic breeds, especially in the Teckel and Basset Hounds, the ribs have a peculiar curvature, which may create a similar image to that of a mild pleural effusion on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal radiographs (fig. 3.7). There may be a generalised increase of the intercostal space in conditions that cause an excessive expansion of the thorax, for example, in severe cases of pleural effusion, pneumothorax or emphysema.

FIGURE 3.7. Right lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) projections of the chest of a Basset Hound with no significant abnormalities in the thoracic image. The left lung is less distended due to atelectasis brought about by prolonged left lateral recumbency. In image (a) the arrows indicate the relatively high position of the costochondral joints in this breed. In the dorsoventral projection, the peculiar morphology of the ribs results in (b) the visualisation of soft tissue density bands (arrows) in the lateral areas of the chest, which could be mistaken for pleural effusion. Rib fractures are more or less easily identified depending on their location and the degree of displacement of the fragments (fig. 3.8). When dealing with thoracic trauma, a thorough examination of each pair of ribs is advised and should be performed on two orthogonal radiographs whenever possible. The early detection of rib fractures after a trauma is considered to be indicative of possible lung trauma, although the radiographic image of a contusion in the lung may be undetectable until 6 hours after the trauma occurred. A patient with a rib fracture may present with paradoxical motion of the affected region of the thorax: outward motion during expiration and inward motion during inspiration. Fractures are usually transverse and generally affect more than one rib. They are often associated with a pneumothorax or subcutaneous emphysema. Although their most frequent cause is thoracic trauma, pathological fractures may appear secondary to a neoplasm or to conditions that cause severe osteopenia (e.g. secondary renal hyperparathyroidism). They may also be caused by sustained or repetitive stress in cases of feline asthma, chronic bronchial disease or lobular emphysema. Old fractures may appear as incidental findings on chest radiographs. The most frequent primary neoplasms of the ribs are osteosarcomas and chondrosarcomas. Their image is usually that of a mixed aggressive bone lesion, which is both osteolytic and osteoproliferative, with marked inflammation of soft tissues. They may cause a displacement of the adjacent ribs and a secondary involvement of these. They usually originate what is termed the extrapleural sign, which refers to a focal displacement of the pleura and lung to the inside of the thorax caused by masses in the thoracic wall, either of costal or soft-tissue origin (it is an adaptation of the general term “mass effect”). Many rib tumours are diagnosed at an

advanced stage because their growth is greater towards the inside of the thorax than towards the outside. They are sometimes associated with pleural effusion (fig. 3.9), which may make the radiographic detection of the primary lesion more difficult. In cases of multiple myeloma, ribs and bone metastases in this location may have a multiple osteolytic pattern. Benign neoplasms (osteomas, chondromas and osteochondromatosis) are uncommon and usually appear as osteoproliferative, non-aggressive lesions. FIGURE 3.8. Enlarged images of the thorax on a dorsoventral radiograph of a dog (a) and on a lateral radiograph of a cat (b), both with rib fractures. The degree of displacement of the fragments is minimal in both cases, so they may go unnoticed in a quick examination of the radiographs, especially in image (b) (indicated by arrows). That is why a careful examination of each pair of ribs is recommended in case of thoracic trauma and should be performed on two orthogonal radiographs whenever possible.

On occasions, we may find soft-tissue tumours that affect the ribs in a secondary manner (e.g. mesotheliomas) and have a similar image to that of primary tumours. In both cases, the differential diagnosis should include osteomyelitis. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging allow a very accurate assessment of any mass affecting the costal wall, the extension of the lesion and the degree of infiltration in adjacent tissues, although computed tomography is preferred to examine the lung when there is a suspicion of metastasis. Sternum Variations in its size, morphology or in the number of sternebrae that have no clinical significance are frequently observed. Cats often have a ventral displacement of the xyphoid process, which sometimes causes pain. In geriatric animals, it is usual to find bony overgrowths that originate from the ends of the sternebrae and tend to form bridges between each other (fig. 3.10). It is considered to be a degenerative sign associated with age and with no clinical significance. Fractures of the sternebrae are usually incidental findings and rarely cause clinical signs. A poor alignment of the sternum may also be observed, but it should only be considered significant if it is accompanied by inflammation of soft tissues, pleural effusion or associated clinical signs.

FIGURE 3.9. Lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) radiographs and computed tomography image of a dog with a primary neoplasm on the seventh left rib. An aggressive osteoproliferative and osteolytic bone lesion is observed, as well as signs of severe pleural effusion in the left hemithorax. In image (b), signs of pleural effusion can be observed in the right hemithorax, while in image (c), obtained several days later, the degree of effusion is moderate. It is uncommon to find neoplasms affecting the sternum. They usually appear as aggressive osteolytic and osteoproliferative lesions and marked inflammation of the adjacent soft tissues. Osteomyelitis may have a similar aspect and is usually caused by penetration of foreign bodies or bites in this region. Pectus excavatum is a congenital deformity of the sternum, which causes it to have a more or less marked abnormal dorsal curvature (fig. 3.11). The ribs appear deformed and the heart and mediastinum are displaced dorsally, and to one side of the thoracic cavity on some occasions. It does not usually cause any clinical symptoms, but it may make breathing more difficult when the deformity is marked. Although it affects both cats and dogs, it is more common in brachycephalic dog breeds. It is sometimes associated with other congenital deformities such as peritoneopericardial hernia, tracheal hypoplasia or defects of the ventricular septum. Pharynx, larynx and trachea Pharynx and larynx The pharynx is a musculomembranous sac that belongs to the digestive and respiratory system. Its cranial part is connected with the mouth and nasal cavity, while its caudal end communicates with the oesophagus and the larynx. This latter connects the pharynx with the trachea. Figure 3.12 shows the radiologically identifiable structures of the pharynx, larynx and trachea. The larynx contains air and is surrounded by cartilages, which are radiographically identified as soft-tissue opacities. Calcification of these cartilages is a common finding of no clinical significance, which improves visualisation on X-rays.

Radiological examination of the pharynx and larynx is indicated in patients with suspected upper airway obstruction, nausea, ptyalism, dysphagia, dysphonia, palpable mass in the cranial area of the neck or presence of fistulous tracts in the area. Radiography provides only limited information on the alterations that may occur in the pharynx and larynx, although it can be useful for locating foreign bodies or identifying neoplasms, inflammatory polyps, cysts, stenosis, abscesses, inflammation and functional alterations. Fluoroscopy is preferable for the diagnosis of functional disorders of the pharynx as it provides real-time radiographic images allowing direct visualisation of the passage of the food bolus from the mouth to the oropharynx and from the oropharynx to the oesophagus. Ultrasound could help to more easily diagnose functional disorders of the larynx, such as laryngeal paralysis. FIGURE 3.10. Enlarged image of the sternal region on a lateral radiograph of an older dog. It is possible to observe bony overgrowths, which tend to connect the ends of the sternebrae, and calcifications with an irregular morphology in the costochondral junctions. Both findings do not have any clinical significance.

FIGURE 3.11. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of a cat with pectus excavatum. This is a congenital alteration in which the sternum appears deformed and curved in dorsal direction towards the thoracic cavity. Foreign bodies can be easily identified if their radiopacity is higher than that of soft tissues (fig. 3.13), or if they are surrounded by gas in the pharyngeal or laryngeal lumen. Sharp objects may puncture the wall and cause the formation of abscesses in adjacent areas and/or the appearance of gas in the surrounding soft tissues (fig. 3.14).

FIGURE 3.12. Radiographic anatomy of the pharynx and larynx of a dog as visualised in the lateral projection. FIGURE 3.13. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the neck of a dog with a metallic foreign body (nail) in the larynx. It is essential to obtain two orthogonal radiographs to determine the exact location of the object. The identification microchip is shown with an arrow in both images.

Pharyngeal and laryngeal masses are generally of neoplastic or inflammatory origin, but benign laryngeal cysts have also been described in dogs and cats. Nasopharyngeal polyps are common in cats (fig. 3.15), often associated with otitis media. Mass-like lesions (space-occupying lesions) are also common in tissues adjacent to the pharynx or larynx, which may cause displacement or obliteration of the lumen, as occurs in the case of retropharyngeal lymphadenopathy (fig. 3.16) and thyroid tumours (fig. 3.17). Pharyngeal and cricopharyngeal dysphagias may have a congenital origin, especially in Spaniel breeds, or be acquired, generally in older animals, in which they may appear as a sequela of diseases of the central nervous system or neuromuscular diseases. They usually do not cause any significant alterations on radiographs and would require a real-time fluoroscopic study of the patient’s swallowing movements (see video 3.1), in which food mixed with barium is administered to the patient, in order to be diagnosed. In cases of dysphagia, it is possible to observe nasal reflux of barium, its accumulation in the pharynx, a failure in the relaxation of the cricopharyngeal sphincter, aspiration of barium into the larynx and pharynx or uncoordinated movements of the pharyngeal muscle. It is important to take chest X-rays when dysphagia is suspected, since it is very common for these patients to suffer from aspiration pneumonia. The incidence and clinical relevance of pharyngeal collapse have recently been studied in small animals, the etiology of which is not yet well defined, although it is most likely multifactorial. Pharyngeal collapse may be partial or total and may result from a dorsal displacement of the soft palate, a ventral deviation of the dorsal pharyngeal wall, or a combination of both. Most patients with pharyngeal collapse have concomitant respiratory diseases, such as tracheal collapse, mainstem bronchial collapse or brachycephalic syndrome. It has been reported that dogs with brachycephalic syndrome (especially English Bulldog, French Bulldog and Pug) are more predisposed to pharyngeal collapse. This may be due to the progressive development of pharyngeal muscle abnormalities as a

result of sustained increase in upper airway resistance in these patients. Conventional X-rays may reveal narrowing of the nasopharynx lumen, but as this is a dynamic process that is not sustained over time, a cervical X-ray may not provide useful diagnostic information if the time at which the static image is captured does not coincide with the time at which the lumen is narrowed. Therefore, the most appropriate radiological technique to confirm the diagnosis of pharyngeal collapse is fluoroscopy, although dynamic digital radiography serve as an alternative (see video 3.2). Dynamic radiography of a dog with pharyngeal collapse Laryngeal collapse may appear as a single pathology or may be associated with laryngeal paralysis, nasal or nasopharyngeal obstruction or trauma. Chronic upper airway obstruction can lead to laryngeal collapse due to fatigue and progressive cartilage degeneration. Although the neck X-ray does not provide useful information in patients with laryngeal paralysis, a chest X-ray should be included in the diagnostic protocol of these patients, as secondary aspiration pneumonia is common before and after surgical treatment. In cases of brachycephalic syndrome, which is characterised by several anomalies in the upper airways in brachycephalic dog and cat breeds, an anomalous image of the soft palate may be observed in

this region. The soft palate may appear fairly elongated (extending beyond the epiglottis) or thickened due to oedema (fig. 3.18). The affected animals sometimes have laryngeal collapse, but it usually occurs in laterolateral direction and is therefore difficult to identify on lateral radiographs, unless it is very severe. Tracheal hypoplasia also commonly appears in these patients. In cases of retroversion of the epiglottis, caused by its excessive mobility, the epiglottis may have a more vertical position than normal. Trachea The trachea is a semi-rigid tubular structure that connects the larynx with the bronchi. The carina can be identified in its distal part. On lateral radiographs, it appears as a more radiolucent circular or oval area that is located at the level of the 4th or 5th intercostal space. The tracheal rings have a “C” shape and are dorsally connected by the tracheal muscle and connective tissue. In order to examine the complete trachea, it is necessary to take a radiograph that includes its cervical and thoracic parts (fig. 3.19). In medium or large-sized dogs, it will be necessary to take two radiographs, one of the neck and another of the thorax, to carry out this assessment. On plain radiographs, the internal aspect of the tracheal wall is easily observed because it contrasts with the intraluminal air. On the other hand, in normal conditions, the external aspect of the wall is difficult to differentiate from the structures of the neck or from the mediastinum that surrounds it. In general, lateral radiographs are more useful, since the trachea is superimposed with the cervical and thoracic spine on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal radiographs. A craniocaudal tangential radiograph of the trachea may be taken to visualise the tracheal lumen at the level of the thoracic inlet, but it is difficult to place the patient correctly and it rarely provides significant additional information. In cats and dog breeds with an intermediate conformation, the thoracic trachea forms an acute angle with the spine. This angle is greater in dogs with a narrow and deep thoracic conformation, while in those with a wide and shallow thorax, the course of the trachea is almost parallel to the vertebrae.

The diameter of the trachea is assessed by dividing its value by the height of the thoracic inlet, which is measured on a lateral projection. The height of the thoracic inlet is measured from the ventral border of the spine at the level of the centre of the most cranial rib, to the dorsal border of the manubrium of the sternum where it is thinnest. The diameter of the trachea is measured between the internal aspect of the dorsal border and the internal aspect of the ventral border of the wall, perpendicularly to the longitudinal axis of the trachea and where the line of measurement of the height of the thoracic inlet crosses the trachea (fig. 3.20). This parameter varies depending on the dog or cat breed (Table 3.1). In young animals (under 1 year of age), the normal value is slightly lower than in adults. A poor position of the neck or head when taking a lateral radiograph may cause the trachea to be flexed, which should not be mistaken for a real displacement of this organ caused by adjacent masses. The trachea will also be falsely elevated if the median plane of the thorax is very inclined on the X-ray table when the radiograph is

taken. This is corrected by placing a radiolucent wedge underneath the sternum. FIGURE 3.19. Normal radiographic image of the trachea of a dog. In medium and large- sized dogs, radiographs of the two regions have to be taken separately (due to the size of the animal and to differences in exposure values). An image of apparent tracheal collapse may be seen in obese animals, due to the accumulation of fat around the trachea, especially at the level of the thoracic inlet. On dorsoventral and ventrodorsal radiographs, the trachea appears superimposed with the spine, perfectly centred or slightly to the right of the median line, but never to its left in normal conditions. In obese animals, the trachea may be clearly located on the right side. The tracheobronchial bifurcation, on the other hand, should always be located on the median line. Calcification of the tracheal rings is frequently observed in older animals and patients with Cushing’s syndrome, but this finding alone has no pathological significance. The most common abnormality affecting the trachea is tracheal collapse, defined as the focal narrowing of the windpipe that occurs in relation to the respiratory cycle. This narrowing occurs dorsoventrally, hence only a lateral projection is useful for its diagnosis. Collapse can occur anywhere along the trachea from the middle of the cervical area to the carina. Collapse of the thoracic segment (fig. 3.21) is generally more marked during expiration, while collapse of the cervical part and thoracic inlet (fig. 3.22) is more pronounced during inspiration. Coughing fits can accentuate the collapse of the intrathoracic trachea. It is usually diagnosed in middle-aged or senior dogs of small and miniature breeds. As this is a dynamic process, fluoroscopy is the most suitable radiological technique for diagnosis (see video 3.3). Failing this, one X-ray (including the cervical and thoracic portions of the trachea) could be performed on inspiration and another on expiration, although in practice it is difficult to adjust the moment of the shot with the respiratory cycle. It is important to bear in mind that some healthy animals, especially small and miniature breed dogs, may have a slacker dorsal tracheal membrane and thinner tracheal rings, which causes a variation in the tracheal diameter that is manifested in the following way: during inspiration, the diameter of the cervical trachea is slightly reduced and that of the thoracic trachea increases, while during expiration, the diameter of the cervical trachea is slightly reduced and that of the cervical part increases. However, in normal conditions, this variation

should be minimal. On radiographs, the collapse may be graded according to whether the reduction of the diameter of the trachea reaches 25 %, 50 %, 75 % or from 90 % to 100 %. This grading scale is similar to that used in bronchoscopy, in which the collapse is classified as grade 1 (mild) when the diameter reduction reaches 25 %, grade 2 (moderate), when it reaches 50 %, grade 3 (severe) with it is reduced by 75 % and grade 4 (total) when it is total. A 25% diameter reduction or less is not considered significant (note that the diameter of the normal trachea may vary slightly between inspiration and expiration). A moderate degree of tracheal collapse is frequently observed in small and miniature breed senior dogs with no evidence of significant clinical signs. A fluoroscopic examination in patients with suspected tracheal collapse should examine the entire trachea over several respiratory cycles. It is also recommended to induce coughing (e.g. closing the mouth and plugging the nostrils). In patients with clinical signs suggestive of tracheal collapse, special attention should be paid to the image of the bronchial bifurcation and the larger lobar bronchi, as collapse of these bronchi can occur together with tracheal collapse or as a single alteration. Fluoroscopy is the most suitable technique for evaluating bronchial collapse (see video 3.4) with or without associated tracheal collapse. Bronchial collapse can also vary within the respiratory cycle and is usually most evident in fluoroscopy when cough is induced. Video 3.3. Dynamic radiography of a dog with tracheal collapse Video 3.4. Dynamic radiography of a dog with bronchial collapse Cats rarely suffer from tracheal collapse caused by degeneration of the cartilages. If cervical tracheal collapse is observed in a cat, the possibility of an upper airway obstruction should be considered as this

may cause a significant increase in the inspiratory effort and create enough negative intratracheal pressure to collapse the lumen. Tracheal stenosis is defined as a localised and permanent narrowing of the trachea, not associated with the respiratory cycle, which differentiates it from tracheal collapse. It does not usually cause any clinical signs, unless the reduction of the diameter exceeds 80 %. It usually occurs as a result of previous tracheal lesions, often from bites, foreign bodies or tracheal intubation procedures, although it may also have a congenital aetiology, especially in small breeds. Focal narrowing of the trachea may also be due to external compression, for example, due to major mediastinal lesions (fig. 3.23). In these cases, narrowing of the lumen is usually accompanied by tracheal displacement. The presence of a band of soft tissue density in the dorsal area of the trachea, between the middle of the cervical and the middle of the thoracic portion, may be due to the visualisation of the dorsal tracheal membrane, which can be attributed to its redundancy (redundant dorsal tracheal membrane), but also to a contraction or invagination of this membrane. The degree of narrowing may even vary with the respiratory cycle, as in the case of tracheal collapse, making it difficult to distinguish between both processes. In cases of redundant dorsal membrane, contraction or invagination of the membrane, the dorsal margin of the tracheal wall maintains a normal position (fig. 3.24), while in cases of collapse this margin appears displaced. However, in practice, it is not always possible to clearly establish this differentiation. Other causes of increased dorsal tracheal radiopacity include ventral displacement of the oesophagus plus tracheal rotation or overlapping of the oesophagus with the trachea. Tracheal hypoplasia is a congenital disorder characterised by a uniform reduction in the diameter of the entire trachea, from the larynx to the carina, due to incomplete or abnormal development of the cartilaginous rings. Only very rarely does it affect a single segment of the trachea. Although more common in brachycephalic breeds (fig. 3.25), it can also appear in other breeds on an exceptional basis. It is important to calculate the tracheal diameter to thoracic inlet ratio to avoid subjective evaluations that may lead to misdiagnosis, especially in bulldog breeds (fig. 3.26). Patients with tracheal hypoplasia may

also have other congenital abnormalities such as soft palate elongation, megaoesophagus or congenital heart defects. FIGURE 3.21. Tracheal tears are caused by trauma or incorrect intubation. Following an anaesthetic procedure, a tracheal rupture should be suspected when progressive subcutaneous emphysema develops, which may affect the chest and abdomen. This emphysema will be evident on an X-ray, as well as signs of pneumomediastinum (fig. 3.27), which can spread to the abdomen and cause pneumoperitoneum or pneumoretroperitoneum. Pneumothorax may occur if it is accompanied by injury to the lung or pleura. In cats, it may cause an avulsion of the trachea due to traumas involving a severe extension of the head and neck. Paradoxically, the animal may be taken to the veterinary practice several days or even weeks after the trauma occurred, when the subcutaneous emphysema or the pneumomediastinum may have disappeared. On radiographs, it is possible to observe severe focal dilatation of the

trachea, which appears delimited by a thin wall formed by the intact adventitia or the surrounding mediastinal tissue. FIGURE 3.23. Foreign bodies located in the trachea usually cause severe signs of respiratory obstruction. They may be identified or not on radiographs depending on their location, size and radiopacity. Radiopaque foreign bodies are easily identified, while radiolucent ones may or may not be identified depending on their shape. The accumulation of mucus around the foreign body creates focal areas of increased soft-tissue opacity at the site where it is located. These are usually found near the tracheal bifurcation.

Focal thickening of the tracheal wall may be due to neoplasms, granulomas (e.g. by Oslerus osleri), polyps or haematomas. More diffuse thickening may be due to tracheal haemorrhage caused by trauma or coagulopathy, or diffusely infiltrating neoplasms such as lymphoma, although rare. Inflammatory processes (tracheitis and tracheobronchitis) usually do not cause wall thickening that can be identified on an X-ray. Computed tomography is an appropriate technique to evaluate and confirm cases of collapse, rupture, obstruction and mass in the trachea. Radiographs allow the follow-up of a tracheal stent in order to avoid any possible rupture, displacement or excessive formation of granulation tissue around it. However, computed tomography has the advantage of allowing the differentiation between excessive granulation tissue and accumulations of intraluminal fluid. Oesophagus Radiography is a valuable tool to diagnose diseases that affect the oesophagus. Lateral radiographs are usually used, since the oesophagus is superimposed with the spine and sternum on ventrodorsal and dorsoventral radiographs. The normal oesophagus cannot usually be identified on plain radiographs, since it has the same radiographic density as most of the structures that surround it in the neck and mediastinum. Small accumulations of gas are sometimes visualised throughout its course (fig. 3.28), due to the swallowing of air in nervous patients or patients with respiratory difficulties. It is also common to observe, especially on left lateral projections, minimal fluid retention in the distal part of the oesophagus, just before its entry through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm. This creates an elongated silhouette of soft-tissue density that appears centred between the course of the aorta and the course of the caudal vena cava on lateral radiographs (fig. 3.29). Non- significant, moderate oesophageal dilatation may be observed in

anaesthetised patients (fig. 3.30) or in those in which an oesophageal catheter was placed. Since the information provided by plain radiography is limited, contrast studies are often carried out to examine the oesophagus. Barium is usually used in the form of a paste or mixed with food, so as to slow down the passage of the contrast medium through the oesophagus, as it is very fast in normal conditions, especially when it is liquid. The administration of barium in the form of a paste is useful to examine the mucosa, because it adheres to it. It is usually used when oesophagitis or neoplasms are suspected, but it should not be used if the oesophageal study is going to be accompanied by a gastrointestinal study, as the paste does not fill the stomach or the intestine properly, and does not mix well with liquid barium if this is administered at the same time. Liquid suspensions of barium sulphate at a dose of 3 to 5 ml/kg do not adhere to the mucosa as well as the paste, but they easily surround obstructions. It is sometimes necessary to administer an additional amount to delimit the whole oesophagus when this is very dilated. Barium should not be used when an oesophageal perforation or rupture is suspected, since it may lead to the formation of granulomas if it extravasates. In these cases, hyperosmotic, water-soluble iodinated contrast media may be used, such as meglumine amidotrizoate, or low-osmolarity organic iodinated contrast media, such as iohexol or iopamidol, at a dose of 7 ml/kg. Although the image of the oesophagus is more poorly defined with these contrast media than with barium, they would be absorbed if they extravasated, while barium would not. Despite their higher cost, it is recommended to use low-osmolarity contrast media. Hypertonic contrast media, due to their osmotic effects, may cause pulmonary oedema if they are aspirated or, if they are used in animals with hypovolaemia, the clinical status of the patient may worsen due to the loss of fluid through the gastrointestinal tract. After administering barium, a temporary retention of the contrast medium may be observed between the folds of the oesophageal mucosa, which creates an image of parallel longitudinal bands in dogs. In addition to these longitudinal bands, transverse bands are also observed in the caudal third of the thoracic oesophagus in cats, which has been termed “herringbone” pattern. A minimal temporary

retention of barium at the level of the pharynx or thoracic inlet may also be observed in normal conditions. It is possible to examine functional anomalies of the oesophagus by means of fluoroscopy, as it allows real-time observation of the passage of the contrast medium from the oropharynx to the stomach (see video 3.5). It is recommended to first administer liquid barium and then solid food mixed with barium. This is particularly useful to diagnose stenosis or regional motility disorders. Video 3.5. Dynamic radiography of normal transit through the oesophagus of positive iodinated contrast mixed with food in a dog The term megaoesophagus is used to describe an abnormal dilatation of the oesophagus, generally associated with hypomotility of the wall. The dilatation is usually identified by means of plain radiography, although an oesophagogram may be indicated to confirm the diagnosis in case of doubt, to examine oesophageal motility (using fluoroscopy) or to detect the possible cause of the megaoesophagus. On both plain lateral and ventrodorsal or dorsoventral radiographs, it is possible to identify two thin lines of soft-tissue density in the area of the oesophagus. These lines converge in the diaphragm and correspond to the dilated oesophageal wall (fig. 3.31). These lines are clearly differentiated when the oesophagus is filled with gas but may also be identified when it contains fluid or food (fig. 3.32). The ventral line is sometimes masked by the superimposed caudal vena cava. When dilation is very pronounced, the trachea and cardiac silhouette may appear to be displaced ventrally (fig. 3.33). Ventral tracheal displacement is sometimes the only finding evident on the plain X-ray. On ventrodorsal or dorsoventral views, a moderately dilated oesophagus may be masked by the superimposed spine, although it is common to see a displacement of the trachea to the right. In patients with a megaoesophagus, special attention must be paid to the image of the lung fields, as aspiration pneumonia can often be detected (fig. 3.34).

Oesophagitis does not usually cause significant changes on plain radiographs, although a persistent retention of gas in the oesophageal lumen is sometimes observed. The oesophagogram may show an irregular retention of barium between the folds of the mucosa, which is accompanied by diffuse and non-uniform dilatation of the oesophagus. Foreign bodies located in the lumen of the oesophagus are a common cause of oesophageal dysphagia. The most common sites where oesophageal foreign bodies are observed are: Upper oesophageal sphincter. Thoracic inlet.

Base of the heart. Area cranial to the diaphragm. It is easy to recognise radiopaque foreign bodies (fig. 3.35), but the diagnosis may be more complicated in cases of radiolucent ones. On the oesophago-gram, an accumulation of contrast medium is often observed cranial to the foreign body, although the contrast medium may also be absorbed if the object is porous. Foreign bodies may also cause a partial or complete obstruction or no obstruction at all. The complications associated with oesophageal foreign bodies are perforation and stenosis due to scarring. Diverticula are defined as localised dilatations of the oesophagus and are identified on radiographs by the focal accumulation of gas or granular material (food) in the oesophagus. By administrating a contrast medium, it is possible to determine the size and exact location of the lesion. When they are located in the cranial mediastinum, the diverticulum is usually seen ventral to the trachea (fig. 3.36).
FIGURE 3.31. Lateral radiograph of the thorax a dog with a megaoesophagus. The walls of the oesophagus are shown with white arrows. The trachea appears slightly displaced in ventral direction.

FIGURE 3.32. Lateral projection of the thorax of a dog with fluid-filled megaoesophagus. The arrows point to the dorsal and ventral margins of the dilated distal oesophagus. An oesophageal image that may be confused with a diverticulum is sometimes referred to as a redundant oesophagus, which is characterised by the appearance of folds or kinks in the cranial portion of the thoracic oesophagus. In young dogs or short-necked brachycephalic breeds, this could just be a normal individual variation without clinical significance, but it could also be accompanied by altered motility in this segment, so fluoroscopy is recommended to determine the degree of significance of this finding (see video 3.6). Stenoses are localised narrowings of the oesophageal lumen (fig. 3.37). They may appear as a result of the previous presence of a

foreign body at the site where the stenosis is located, associated with anomalies of the vascular rings or with tumours, and in cases of oesophagitis due to reflux. An oesophagogram is necessary for their diagnosis. A normal peristaltic oesophageal contraction should not be mistaken for stenosis in static images. They can be differentiated by means of fluoroscopy or, if it is not available, by taking several radiographs at different times to observe whether the narrowing remains in the image. Congenital anomalies of the vascular rings cause an external compression of the oesophagus. The most common is the persistence of the right aortic arch, which occurs more frequently in dogs than in cats. It is usually diagnosed in young animals with regurgitation. These anomalies usually cause localised oesophageal dilatation in the cranial mediastinum, cranial to the heart, which can be confirmed with a contrast study (fig. 3.38) (see video 3.7). The image of the caudal oesophagus at the base of the heart is usually normal, although it may sometimes appear dilated. Persistent retention of food is often observed in the dilated area. Video 3.6. The origin of the site of communication may be oesophagotracheal, oesophagobronchial or oesophagopulmonary. On oesophagograms,

their image may be similar to that created when a contrast medium administrated by oral route is accidentally inhaled. Hiatal hernias are usually transitory and may be associated with respiratory movements. They are difficult to diagnose on plain radiographs, in which case contrast and fluoroscopy studies are used. In the most evident cases, the stomach (with its characteristic folds) or part of it may be identified in the thorax (fig. 3.40). In other cases, a less defined soft-tissue density structure is visualised in the caudodorsal part of the thorax, and may disappear on subsequent radiographs. In contrast studies, part of the stomach is identified in the thorax (see video 3.8), although it may move in and out of the thoracic cavity with respiratory movements. Gastrooesophageal invagination or intussusception is an uncommon alteration. The stomach or part of it moves into the lumen of the oesophagus, thus originating an anomalous shadow in the caudodorsal part of the thorax. If a contrast study is performed, the contrast medium may not reach the stomach and may delimit a large intraluminal oesophageal mass instead. In some cases, the intussuception appears intermittently. Gastrooesophageal reflux occurs when stomach acids enter the oesophagus, which usually causes oesophagitis. Plain radiographs do not usually show any significant findings, although focal dilatation of the distal oesophagus with accumulation of gas or fluid is sometimes detected (fig. 3.41). Video 3.8. Pleural space The pleural space is the anatomical space included between the visceral and parietal layers of the pleura (fig. 3.42). The parietal pleura covers the internal aspect of the chest wall, the diaphragm and the mediastinum, and the visceral pleura covers the pulmonary surface and forms the interlobar fissures. It is a potential space, which, in normal conditions, contains a minimal amount of fluid that acts as a lubricant to minimise friction during breathing. Plain radiography allows us to detect the presence of abnormal contents, which generally consist in fluid (pleural effusion) or gas (pneumothorax), in this anatomical space, as well as to identify masses of pleural origin. Calcifications and minimal pleural

thickenings are usual findings in older animals and do not usually have any pathological significance. Ultrasound examinations may provide diagnostic information of great interest in cases of effusion and pleural masses, but not in cases of pneumothorax, since the air contained in the pleural space is easily mistaken for that contained in the lungs. Moreover, this technique will facilitate sample collection for cytology or biopsy. Computed tomography is also an excellent diagnostic alternative to assess the anomalies that affect this anatomical space. Pleural effusion In cases of severe pleural effusion, it is convenient to stabilise the patient first, before performing a radiographic study. Radiographs taken with the animal standing may be useful and, alternatively, the dorsoventral projection may be chosen in order not to worsen the state of the patient. If the respiratory involvement is not severe, a ventrodorsal is preferable to a dorsoventral radiograph, since there is greater fluid accumulation around the heart on the latter making visualisation of this organ more difficult (fig. 3.43 and 3.44), in addition to causing an enlargement of the mediastinum silhouette. On ventrodorsal radiographs, interlobar fissures will be better visualised in cases of mild or moderate effusion, since the fluid tends to enter in the fissures in dorsal recumbency, while it tends to accumulate dorsal to the sternum in sternal recumbency. If the respiratory involvement allows it, in these cases it is recommended to take, in addition, a lateral radiograph.

In normal conditions, the pleural space is a potential anatomical space that only contains a minimal amount of fluid as a lubricant to minimise friction during breathing.

FIGURE 3.43. Schematic representation of the location of a moderate amount of pleural fluid when dorsoventral (DV) and ventrodorsal (VD) radiographs are taken. On the dorsoventral radiograph, the fluid is displaced to the ventral area of the thorax and surrounds the heart, so the cardiac silhouette is less defined. When a ventrodorsal radiograph is taken, the fluid moves to the roof of the thoracic cavity and is separated from the heart, so this latter will be better visualised in the image. In the case of a severe effusion, the cardiac silhouette is masked on both views. The radiological signs of a pleural effusion vary in function of the amount of fluid that accumulates. It could be transudate, exudate, blood or lymph, which are indistinguishable from each other on a radiograph. It starts to be detectable on radiographs from 50–100 ml. If the amount is very small, radiographs will only show thin bands of fluid density at the site of the interlobar fissures (fig. 3.45). As the amount of fluid increases, it is possible to observe retraction and rounding of the lung margins, which will appear separated from the thoracic wall by bands of fluid density. The cardiac silhouette and shadow of the diaphragm may appear partially or totally masked (fig. 3.46). If there is a very large amount of accumulated fluid, the cardiac

silhouette may be elevated and displace the trachea, which may give a false impression of cardiomegaly or mediastinal mass (fig. 3.47), although we must bear in mind that these conditions may coexist with a pleural effusion in some cases. FIGURE 3.44. Lateral (a), dorsoventral (b) and ventrodorsal (c) projections of the chest of a dog with mild to moderate pleural effusion. If the patient’s respiratory compromise is not severe, the ventrodorsal projection is preferred, as the signs of pleural effusion are better seen with this projection than with the dorsoventral projection. In dorsal recumbency, the fluid tends to enter the interlobular fissures, whereas in sternal recumbency it tends to accumulate dorsal to the sternum, somewhat masking the cardiac silhouette as occurs in image (b).

FIGURE 3.45. Enlarged image of the thorax on a lateral radiograph of a dog with mild pleural effusion. Thin bands of fluid/soft-tissue density that delimit the right middle lobe may be observed at the site of the interlobar fissures. It is more common for the pleural effusion to be bilateral (fig. 3.48), as the fluid can pass from one hemithorax to another through the orifices in the mediastinum. However, if these orifices are no longer permeable, the effusion can be located in a single hemithorax. The causes of this loss of permeability may be:

FIGURE 3.46. Lateral radiographs of the thorax of two dogs with pleural effusion, one moderate (a) and the other from moderate to severe (b). In both cases, the lung appears separated from the sternum by areas of fluid/soft-tissue density, but the degree of retraction and rounding of the lung margins is more marked in image (b). In image (a), only the ventral area of the cardiac silhouette and of the dome of the diaphragm is masked by the fluid, while in image (b), neither the cardiac silhouette nor most part of the shadow of the diaphragm can be visualised.

FIGURE 3.47. Lateral radiograph of a cat with a severe pleural effusion. The lungs are slightly distended and the trachea appears elevated. Most of the thoracic cavity has a practically homogeneous fluid/soft-tissue density and neither the cardiac silhouette nor the shadow of the diaphragm can be visualised in the image.
FIGURE 3.48. Dorsoventral radiograph of the thorax of a cat with severe bilateral pleural effusion. The fluid appears distributed in a more or less uniform manner between the two hemithoraces.

FIGURE 3.49. Dorsoventral radiograph of the thorax of a cat with unilateral left moderate pleural effusion. The right lung has an alveolar interstitial pattern that is mainly compatible with pneumonia, oedema or haemorrhage. The presence of a unilateral pleural effusion in cats suggests the presence of a pyothorax, although it may also appear due to other causes. Inflammation or pathological processes that present with fibrin production (e.g. pyothorax, chylothorax, haemothorax or neoplasia). In cats, unilateral pleural effusion is common in cases of pyothorax. Congenital anatomical variations. Diaphragmatic hernia. Lung lobe torsion. When the effusion is unilateral, the radiographic signs vary to some degree:

On lateral radiographs, a more diffuse increase in intrathoracic density may be observed instead of lung retraction (this can even be mistaken for a pulmonary infiltrate). On ventrodorsal and dorsoventral radiographs, lung retraction is only observed on the affected side (fig. 3.49). In severe cases, the entire hemithorax may have a uniform soft-tissue density, whereas the contralateral one remains normal. There may be a displacement of the heart towards the healthy side. A severe pleural effusion may mask a cardiomegaly, the presence of lung infiltrates, a pulmonary, pleural or mediastinal mass, a diaphragmatic hernia or a lung lobe torsion, so the patient should always be reassessed once the effusion has been drained, so as to rule out the presence of any of these conditions. When fluid rich in fibrin has been removed, the lungs may then not fully expand due to pleural thickening, and their margins may remain rounded until the process is resolved. Ultrasonography is used to investigate the primary cause of an effusion, for example to assess cardiac function, identify masses and examine possible pleural thickenings, defects in the diaphragm or lung lobe torsion. It also allows the identification of areas of pulmonary atelectasis and the location of small accumulations of fluid in order to take samples and drain the thorax under ultrasound guidance in complicated cases. In cases of pyothorax and chylothorax, computed tomography is particularly indicated to assess the extension and distribution of the fluid with more precision, as well as to determine the cause in some cases (e.g.: abscesses, fistulous tracts, thoracic duct leaks, etc.). It provides more complete diagnostic information than an ultrasound examination when the effusion is associated with masses, defects in the diaphragm or lung lobe torsion. In cases of chylothorax, a lymphangiogram is performed by administering an iodinated contrast medium through a mesenteric lymph vessel, or by injecting it in a mesenteric lymph node under ultrasound guidance. This way, leaks in the thoracic duct (or one of its branches) and lymphangiectases may be identified.

Pneumothorax Pneumothorax is defined as the accumulation of gas in the pleural space, that is, between the parietal and visceral pleura. It usually occurs as a result of traumatic causes, although it can also occur spontaneously. The accumulation of air in the pleural space leads to pulmonary atelectasis, the degree of which is directly proportional to the severity of the pneumothorax. Atelectasis increases the opacity of the lung, visible on radiographs, as well as separating the lung margins from the normal anatomical borders, which can also be seen to some extent on the radiographs. In the lateral projection, the radiological sign of the heart being elevated is very typical, where it appears separated from the sternum by a band of gas opacity. This image is actually due to the lateral displacement of the heart towards the hemithorax nearest the X-ray table, caused by the collapse of the lower lung (fig. 3.50). Elevation of the heart silhouette from the sternum in the lateral projection may also occur for other causes besides pneumothorax: in dogs with deep chest conformation, in animals with mediastinal deviation, in obese animals and in cases of hypovolaemia. In ventrodorsal or dorsoventral projections, the lateral margins of the lung appear separated from the chest wall by bands of gas opacity (fig. 3.51). This image is best appreciated in the dorsoventral projection, since in the sternal recumbency position the gas ascends and lies between the lungs and the chest wall. Conversely, in the ventrodorsal projection, with animal in dorsal recumbency the gas rises to parasternal positions, more centred on the chest, where it overlaps with the mediastinal structures, and this makes identification difficult in the case of mild to moderate pneumothorax. Taking an expiratory radiograph can also help to identify mild pneumothorax, as the lungs contain less air, which increases their opacity and therefore their contrast with the gas accumulated in the pleural space. In the case of a tension pneumothorax, the pressure in the pleural space is greater than atmospheric pressure throughout inspiration and expiration. This is due to lesions in the lung that act as a one-way valve. The air passes from the lung to the pleural space during inspiration, but it is not returned to the lung during expiration. The

chest wall remains intact, so the pressure in the pleural space increases with each breath. This, therefore, is considered an urgent need for immediate attention. Apart from the radiological signs already described, in tension pneumothorax, there could be signs of expansion of the chest cavity, the lungs are often markedly collapsed, and the heart and caudal vena may appear diminished in size. If it is unilateral, the mediastinal structures will appear displaced to the opposite side to that with the pneumothorax. FIGURE 3.50. Schematic representation of the displacement of the heart, which creates an image of “elevation” of the cardiac silhouette on lateral radiographs in cases of pneumothorax. The heart is not supported as it would normally be by a

healthy lung. The collapsed lung occupies a smaller volume and as a result, the heart is displaced to the centre of the thoracic cavity, which originates an image of elevation on lateral radiographs. In pneumothorax that has evolved over several days, it is common to observe irregular-shaped bands of fluid/soft tissue densities due to the formation of pleural adhesions. If the pneumothorax is unilateral, it will be possible to observe a displacement of the mediastinal structures to the contralateral hemithorax on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal radiographs. On lateral views, the cardiac silhouette may not appear elevated if the animal is placed with the affected side up. A hydropneumothorax (presence of fluid and gas in the pleural space) due to trauma, pulmonary abscesses or oesophageal perforation may be detected. The radiographic findings will depend on the amount and proportion of accumulated fluid and gas. On dorsoventral and ventrodorsal views, folds of skin may create an artefact that may be mistaken for the image of a pneumothorax, which is called false pneumothorax or pseudopneumothorax. The area medial to the fold has a higher opacity than the area lateral to it. If there is a high contrast, the lateral area may be mistaken for free gas in the pleural space (fig. 3.52). To differentiate it from a real pneumothorax, we must carefully examine the most radiolucent area and see if the pulmonary vessels can be identified in it. Their presence confirms that the image is due to an artefact. The small vessels are better visualised if we use a bright light source in the case of conventional images, or by significantly increasing image brightness on digital radiographs. An image similar to a pneumothorax may also be observed when lung radiopacity is reduced due to excessive inflation (for example, secondary to asthma or to chronic bronchial disease) or to cases of pulmonary emphysema, hypovascularisation of the lung or hypovolaemia. It is difficult to distinguish the free gas located in the pleural space from the air contained in the normal lung in an ultrasound image, which is why ultrasonography is not routinely used for the assessment of a pneumothorax. A criterion of differentiation is that the gas contained in the pleural space remains static, while the air contained

in the lungs is displaced with inspiration and expiration. An ultrasound examination may be useful to identify foreign bodies or fistulous tracts located in the thoracic wall when these are suspected to be the cause of the pneumothorax. FIGURE 3.51. Lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) radiographs of the thorax of a dog with a moderate to severe bilateral pneumothorax. In image (a), the cardiac silhouette appears separated from the sternum by a band of gas density and the lung (L) appears collapsed, which is why its radiopacity is increased. In image (b), both lungs are collapsed and separated from the costal wall by bands of gas density, although the degree of lung retraction is greater in the left hemithorax. The cardiac silhouette appears reduced in size, which is a common finding in cases of severe pneumothorax.

FIGURE 3.52. Dorsoventral projection of the thorax of a dog with image of pseudo-pneumothorax, marked with asterisks (a). Image (b) shows the affected area of the left hemithorax enlarged. Image (c) shows the same area after significantly increasing the brightness of the image, allowing identification of small peripheral pulmonary vessels (arrowheads), a finding that confirms that it does not correspond to a real pneumothorax. Computed tomography will provide more complete diagnostic information in cases of recurrent or persistent pneumothorax with no known cause (fig. 3.53). Pleural masses The differential diagnosis of pleural masses includes neoplasia, abscesses/granulomas, haematomas or encapsulated pleural effusion. These lesions usually have relatively large areas of contact with the chest wall, but this criterion is not sufficient to differentiate them from lung masses on an X-ray. Mesotheliomas is the only primary tumour that originates in the pleura. They often present a diffuse distribution, with the formation of very small, disseminated nodules, which may be undetectable on an X-ray. They usually cause pleural effusion, which may be the only radiological sign, or at least initially, identifiable on an X-ray (fig. 3.54). Occasionally, a larger focal pleural thickening may be detected which would usually be identified on an X-ray after chest drainage. Metastatic infiltration of the pleura usually results in associated pleural effusion whose radiological signs, as in the case of

mesotheliomas, may be the only detectable sign on an X-ray. The identification of lung lesions compatible with metastases in these patients may better guide the radiological diagnosis (fig. 3.55). Ultrasonography allows the identification of pleural masses, whether there is a concomitant effusion or not, although it does not clearly differentiate a pleural origin from a possible pulmonary or mediastinal origin. In addition, it facilitates the collection of samples for cytology and biopsies. Computed tomography will give a better definition of the margins of the mass, although in cases of mesotheliomas the pleural effusion may be the only recognisable finding. It is common to find associated pericardial masses or pericardial effusion in the study. Pleural thickenings In older animals, thin lines of soft-tissue or mineral density may be observed at the site of the interlobar fissures. These are normally due to thickenings of the pleura with no clinical significance. Pleural calcifications may also appear as small areas distributed throughout the lung fields on chest radiographs (fig. 3.56). Pathological pleural thickenings appear as bands of soft-tissue opacity with an irregular morphology (fig. 3.57). They may be the sequela of any type of pleural effusion, although they are common and form more rapidly in cases of reactive effusion (pyothorax, haemothorax or chylothorax), in which fibrous adherences that capture and encapsulate small amounts of fluid may form. These focal accumulations of fluid may have a radiographic image similar to that of pleural masses. Mediastinum It corresponds to the anatomical space located between the right and left cavities (fig. 3.58). It communicates cranially with the soft tissues of the neck, through the thoracic inlet, and caudally with the retroperitoneum, through the aortic hiatus. The oesophagus, thoracic trachea, lymph nodes, thoracic lymph duct, thymus, some nerves, the heart and great vessels are located in the mediastinum. Of all these

structures, only the trachea, cardiac silhouette, aorta and caudal vena cava may be identified on a normal chest radiograph of an adult animal. The lumen of the oesophagus can be visualised when it contains air or if fluid or mucus accumulates in its distal portion and the thymus is often identifiable in young animals (up to 6 months of age). The mediastinum may be subdivided into three areas: the cranial portion (between the thoracic inlet and the heart), the middle portion (at the level of the heart) and the caudal portion (between the heart and the diaphragm). Cranioventral and caudoventral mediastinal reflections are sometimes identifiable on the X-rays of healthy patients, although they may be more evident in obese animals due to the accumulation of fat in them. The cranioventral reflection is located slightly left of midline because the right cranial pulmonary lobe extends in that direction, moving the mediastinum to the left. When identified, in dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections, it appears as a slightly curved band of soft tissue density, extending from the T1–T2 vertebrae to the left margin of the cardiac silhouette, at the level of the main pulmonary artery. In the lateral projection, it appears as a band of soft tissue density between the right and left cranial lung lobe, located midway between the thoracic inlet and the heart (this may be mistaken for a gas-filled lung lesion in the cranial area of the lung) (fig. 3.59). The caudoventral mediastinal reflection can sometimes be identified on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections where it appears as a thin band of soft-tissue density located slightly left of midline between the apex of the heart and the diaphragm (fig. 3.60).

Computed tomography image of the thorax of a dog with a hydropneumothorax (accumulation of gas and fluid in the pleural space, although in this image it is only possible to observe the gas –G–) associated with a focal area of pulmonary infection (arrow), possible due to the penetration of a foreign body.

The dorsoventral projection shows focal widening of the left pleural space at the level of the 6th, 7th and 8th intercostal spaces, which is suggestive of a pleural mass. FIGURE 3.55. In older animals, it is often possible to visualise thin lines of soft-tissue or mineral density at the site of the interlobar fissures (white arrow). These are generally due to thickenings or calcifications of the pleura with no clinical significance. The pneumothorax causes a displacement of the cardiac silhouette, which appears separated from the sternum by a gas density band.
