The sternal lymph node also appears increased in size (dorsal to the manubrium and second sternebra).

FIGURE 3.58. Representation of the mediastinum (coloured in red) on a computed tomography image of the thorax of a dog. The mediastinal space contains the oesophagus, the thoracic trachea, and lymph nodes, and thoracic lymphatic duct and thymus, some nerves, the heart and the great vessels of the thorax. On dorsoventral and ventrodorsal radiographs, the shadow of the cranial mediastinum must have approximately the same width as the thoracic vertebrae in cats, while in dogs it should not exceed twice the width of these vertebrae in normal conditions. It should be taken into account that the mediastinum of brachycephalic dogs and obese cats and dogs may be wider, with a displacement of the trachea to the right on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal views, and a significant elevation of

the cardiac silhouette due to an accumulation of fat ventral to it (fig. 3.61). In young animals, it is often possible to identify the shadow of the thymus, which reaches its maximum size at approximately 4 months of age and is no longer visible at 6 months of age (fig. 3.62). On very rare occasions, a vestige of the thymus is observed in adults. Most of the diseases that affect the mediastinum are secondary to pulmonary, oesophageal, pleural and lymphatic diseases. Mediastinal effusion It corresponds to the presence of free fluid (transudate, exudate, blood, lymph) in the mediastinal space. It may appear associated with mediastinitis, coagulopathies, trauma, feline infectious peritonitis, etc. The radiographic image of a mediastinal effusion may be confused with that of a pleural effusion on lateral radiographs, but not on dorsoventral or ventrodorsal radiographs. On these views, there will be no retraction of the lateral margins of the lung, but an abnormal enlargement of the shadow of the mediastinum (fig. 3.63). In some cases, triangular or thorn-shaped shadows will appear with their wider base oriented towards the hilum (which differentiates them from interlobar fissures in a pleural effusion). These are called reverse fissure lines. A mediastinal effusion is often accompanied by pleural effusion. The effusion, whether mediastinal, pleural or both, can mask the presence of localised masses in the mediastinal space, in which case an ultrasound examination will be particularly useful to assess the size and characteristics of the mass, as well as the amount of accumulated fluid. In these cases, ultrasound-guided sampling of the mass and fluid will be indicated. Computed tomography may provide complementary information about the possible origin of the effusion. Pneumomediastinum The presence of free gas in the mediastinal space may be indicative of a rupture of the trachea or oesophagus, or less likely of the bronchi or lung, but it may also be due to the presence of subcutaneous emphysema in the neck, since the gas may go from the spaces

between the fasciae of the neck to the mediastinal space through the thoracic inlet. If all the possible causes are ruled out, the possibility of an idiopathic pneumomediastimum should be considered. FIGURE 3.59. Enlarged images of the lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) projection of the chest of a healthy dog showing the cranioventral mediastinal reflection. In image (a) it appears as a band of soft tissue density (arrow) between the right cranial lobe (RCrL) and the left cranial lobe (LCrL), located midway between the thoracic inlet and the heart. In image (b) it appears as a band of soft tissue density (arrows), extending from the level of the T1-T2 vertebrae to the location of the left margin of the cardiac silhouette, at the level of the main pulmonary artery.

FIGURE 3.60. Enlarged image of the thorax in dorsoventral projection of a healthy dog identifying the caudoventral mediastinal reflection. It appears as a thin band of soft tissue density between the cardiac apex and the diaphragm (arrow).

FIGURE 3.61. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of an obese dog. It is possible to observe a marked accumulation of mediastinal fat located ventral to the cardiac silhouette, which causes its elevation. This should not be mistaken for a pleural effusion. An effusion would mask the image of the cardiac apex, while in this case the definition of the whole ventral margin of the heart is improved due to the contrast between the radiographic density of soft tissue and that of fat.

FIGURE 3.62. Lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) radiographs of the thorax of a young dog, in which the normal shadow of the thymus may be observed. This organ reaches its maximum size at 4 months of age and is usually no longer visible on radiographs from 6 months of age. In cases of pneumomediastinum, it will be possible to identify the shadows of some mediastinal structures, such as for example, the oesophagus or the blood vessels of the cranial mediastinum. It would not be possible to distinguish these structures from one another if no gas was located between them. When the amount of gas is relatively small, the most significant finding is the improved visualisation of the tracheal wall, which appears internally and externally limited by gas (fig. 3.64). If air accumulates rapidly in the mediastinum, the mediastinal pleura may rupture and cause a pneumothorax. That is to say, a pneumomediastinum may progress to a pneumothorax. On the other hand, a pneumothorax is never the cause of a pneumomediastinum. An ultrasound study is not indicated in cases of pneumomediastinum. However, contrast techniques or endoscopy are indicated to rule out a perforation or an oesophageal or tracheal rupture as the causes of the disease. Computed tomography is particularly useful to investigate the cause of a pneumomediastinum.

Mediastinal masses These generally correspond to mediastinal lymphadenopathies (fig. 3.65) or tumours, although abscesses, granulomas, haematomas and cysts may also appear in this location. The lymph nodes that can be found in the mediastinum are divided into: Sternal (there may be one or two in dogs and one in cats): when they increase significantly in size, they appear as a shadow of soft- tissue density dorsal to the second sternebra (fig. 3.66). They drain lymph from the thoracic wall and abdominal cavity. Therefore, if they are enlarged, the cause may be located in the thorax or in the abdomen. Mediastinal lymph nodes: they form a chain of lymph nodes that lies adjacent to the great vessels of the cranial mediastinum (cranial vena cava, brachiocephalic trunk and left subclavian artery). When they increase in size they originate an enlargement of the shadow of the cranial mediastinum, as well as a displacement of the trachea in dorsal direction on lateral radiographs, and to the right on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal radiographs. Bronchial lymph nodes: they are subdivided into pulmonary lymph nodes (often absent, but when present they are distributed throughout the main bronchi) and tracheobronchial lymph nodes (located around the carina). When the tracheobronchial lymph nodes become greatly enlarged, they originate a mass dorsal to the tracheal bifurcation, with a relatively oval morphology on lateral radiographs. The bifurcation of the trachea may be ventrally displaced. This image is similar to that produced by a significant enlargement of the left atrium, but in this case the bifurcation of the trachea appears displaced in the opposite direction –dorsally– and other signs of left cardiomegaly are usually observed. It is more difficult to visualise the mass on dorsoventral or ventrodorsal views, but it may cause a bronchial displacement that is identifiable in the image.

FIGURE 3.63. Lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) radiographs of the thorax of a dog with a mediastinal effusion. On the lateral view, the findings are similar to those of a pleural effusion, but the dorsoventral view does not show a retraction of the lungs (except a minimal separation between the left caudal lobe and the chest wall, due to a mild pleural effusion) but an enlargement of the mediastinal shadow (arrows). It should be borne in mind that brachycephalic dogs have, in normal conditions, wider mediastinal shadows, as also occurs in obese cats and dogs. This patient has, in addition, a pulmonary infiltrate in the caudal area of the left cranial lobe. The most common location of mediastinal tumours is the cranial mediastinum. Heart base tumours are found in the middle mediastinum, and oesophageal tumours can occur in any part of the mediastinum, including the caudal portion. Neoplastic lesions affecting the mediastinum include lymphomas, thymomas, neuroendocrine tumours, lymphomatoid granulomatosis, mastocytomas, melanomas and thyroid carcinomas. The radiological and ultrasound image of mediastinal granulomas, abscesses and haematomas may be identical to that of tumours. Idiopathic mediastinal cysts may appear in older cats, and can grow to a large size.

FIGURE 3.64. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of a dog with a pneumomediastinum caused by a bite in the neck. The gas that penetrates between the fasciae of the neck enters in the mediastinal space through the thoracic inlet. The same image may be observed in cases of tracheal or oesophageal perforation or rupture, since the free gas in the mediastinum may move towards the neck.

FIGURE 3.65. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of a dog with lymphoma. The enlargement of the sternal lymph node or lymph nodes (S) creates a shadow of soft-tissue density dorsal to the manubrium and most cranial sternebrae. The increase in size of the cranial mediastinal lymph nodes (CrM) causes an enlargement of the cranial mediastinal shadow and elevation of the trachea. Finally, the tracheobronchial lymph nodes (TB), which lie dorsal to the tracheal bifurcation, create an approximately oval shadow dorsal to the main bronchi, next to the carina. In general, cranial mediastinal masses usually result in a somewhat marked increase in cranial mediastinal width in lateral, dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections. They also usually cause dorsal displacement of the trachea in the lateral projection and lateral displacement in the dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections (fig. 3.67). Depending on the size of the mass, the heart may also appear displaced, and with its border adjacent to the mass masked (fig. 3.68). Identifying tracheal displacement helps guide the radiological

diagnosis of mediastinal masses when these are masked by pleural effusion, which is relatively common (fig. 3.69). Thymomas usually present initially a more ventral position than masses of nodal origin, so they could be confused with lung masses on lateral projections, although their centred position on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections helps to differentiation them (fig. 3.70). They can grow quite large and extend beyond the lateral margin of the heart. Thymomas are sometimes associated with myasthenia gravis and megaoesophagus; the latter can be identified on X-rays (fig. 3.71). Neoplasms in the middle mediastinum usually correspond to heart base tumours or lymphomas. Heart base tumours can be identified on X-rays as a mass of soft tissue opacity located immediately dorsal to the cardiac silhouette (fig. 3.72). In cases of tracheobronchial lymphoma, the “mass effect” usually occurs dorsally or around the carina. When visualising masses in this region of the mediastinum, other possible aetiologies should also be considered, including abscess, granuloma, oesophageal foreign body or reactive lymphadenomegaly. Neoplasms located in the caudal mediastinum are rare and their origin is usually oesophageal. The radiological image could be confused with that of a pulmonary neoplasm, and may also be very similar to that of abscesses, granulomas, dorsal diaphragmatic or hiatus hernias (see figs. 3.39 and 3.40). An ultrasound examination will allow the evaluation of the size and echogenicity of the mass and the presence of an associated effusion, in addition to allowing ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration or biopsy.

Incomplete (partial) calcification of the costal cartilages is observed, giving a false impression of a rupture. This finding is common in cats.

Lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) projections of a dog with a large mediastinal mass causing marked displacement of the trachea dorsally and to the right (black arrow), also showing a reduction in its dorsoventral diameter in the proximal thoracic portion (this finding indicates compression of the tracheal lumen). The margins of the mass are better identified in image (b) (white arrows). The cardiac silhouette appears displaced caudally in both projections. FIGURE 3.68. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of a dog with thymoma. A large mass (M) that causes a marked dorsal displacement of the trachea and a caudodorsal displacement of the heart (H) may be observed in the cranial area of the thorax.

The marked elevation of the trachea suggests the presence of a mass, although its outline cannot be visualised in the image. Ultrasonography allows the easy identification of the mass.

FIGURE 3.70. Lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) projections of the thorax of a dog with a small thymoma (arrows). In the lateral projection, the lesion could be confused with a pulmonary mass, but its central location in the dorsoventral projection confirms the mediastinal origin as the most probable.

FIGURE 3.71. Lateral projection of the thorax of a dog with a thymoma (black arrows) and megaoesophagus (white arrows). Thymomas are sometimes associated with myasthenia gravis and megaoesophagus. FIGURE 3.72. Lateral projection of the thorax of a dog with a chemodectoma (arrows), which appears as a soft-tissue dense mass located immediately dorsal to the cardiac silhouette. Computed tomography is an excellent technique to identify mediastinal masses and establish their relationship with the other structures in the mediastinum (fig. 3.73).

Displacement of the mediastinum The displacement of the structures that form the mediastinum indicates a change of volume in one of the hemithoraces. If the volume of a hemithorax increases, the mediastinum will be displaced to the opposite side, while if the volume of a hemithorax decreases, the mediastinal content will be displaced to the affected side. The most common cause is iatrogenic, due to a partial collapse of the lung, which has a lower position in patients that remain in lateral recumbency for a long period of time, especially if they are anaesthetised. On radiographs, it is possible to observe a displacement of the heart to the side on which the patient was lying and an increase in the density of the lung of the same side caused by temporary atelectasis. A pathological displacement of the mediastinum may appear due to masses or accumulations located in one of the hemithoraces (unilateral pleural effusion, unilateral pneumothorax), in conditions causing an unequal expansion of the lungs (fig. 3.74), or when adherences that connect the mediastinum with the thoracic wall remain after a chronic pleural effusion. Heart Taking chest radiographs is an essential part of the assessment of patients with a suspected cardiovascular disease. Radiographs allow the assessment of the size and shape of the cardiac silhouette, as well as of the state of the lungs and circulation, thus showing the degree of heart failure of the patient. Thoracic radiographs therefore help to determine the severity of the cardiac disease and allow the evaluation of the efficacy of the treatment.

Contrast studies (angiocardiography) have become less prevalent with the use of echocardiography, which is now an essential routine technique to establish a precise diagnosis of most of the diseases that affect the heart. The diagnostic information obtained by means of radio graphy and echocardiography is often enough for us not to need more advanced diagnostic imaging techniques. Computed tomography is useful for the diagnosis of heart tumours and some diseases of the pericardium. Right lateral and dorsoventral radiographs are used for the radiological assessment of the cardiac silhouette. On left lateral radiographs, the silhouette appears falsely rounded, while on ventrodorsal radiographs it is more magnified than on dorsoventral ones. We should be particularly careful when positioning the animal before taking a radiograph. On lateral views, the rotation of the thorax causes a false increase of the cardiosternal contact and a false elevation of the trachea. On dorsoventral views, any degree of rotation of the thorax causes a deformation of the cardiac silhouette in the image, which does not allow its appropriate examination. Size of the cardiac silhouette The methods to assess the overall size of the cardiac silhouette are based on the measurement of its height and width on right lateral and dorsoventral radiographs. We will distinguish between the classic method and the Buchanan method. According to the traditional method (fig. 3.75), the width of the cardiac silhouette (horizontal craniocaudal diameter) on lateral radiographs should be comprised between 2.5 and 3.5 intercostal spaces in the dog, although this interval varies depending on the conformation of the thorax: In dogs with a narrow and deep thorax (Greyhound type), the heart has a more vertical position in the thoracic cavity, so the limit of normal will be 2.5 intercostal spaces. In dogs with an intermediate conformation (German Shepherd type), the normal interval is from 2.5 to 3 intercostal spaces. In dogs with a wide and shallow thorax (Bulldog type), the normal

range extends to 3.5 intercostal spaces, because the heart is anatomically more inclined on the sternum. In cats, the craniocaudal diameter is not measured horizontally, as in dogs, but perpendicularly to the longitudinal axis of the heart. However, the result obtained is compared to the width of the intercostal spaces horizontally. In normal conditions, its value is 2. This variation in the measurement system is due to fact that, with age, the feline heart tends to lie closer to the sternum because of a progressive elongation of the aorta (fig. 3.76). If the width is measured horizontally, as in dogs, it will therefore seem increased in older cats. Both in dogs and cats, the height of the cardiac silhouette on lateral radiographs –measured from the centre of its base to its apex– corresponds approximately to two thirds of the height of the thoracic cavity at the same level. The width of the silhouette –measured at the level of the 5th intercostal space– should be approximately two thirds of the width of the thoracic cavity on dorsoventral radiographs. The size of the heart in relation to the thoracic cavity is slightly greater in young animals than in adults. The cardiac silhouette also appears slightly larger during expiration when compared to inspiration, and during diastole when compared to systole. However, these changes are minimal and generally do not significantly affect the diagnosis. When assessing the size of the cardiac silhouette, it must be taken into account that the exit of the aorta and pulmonary artery, the pericardium and the pericardial space are part of it. In addition, the abnormal presence of fluid or masses in the pericardial space or the enlargement of the great vessels will cause an increase in the size of the cardiac silhouette in the image. The presence of fat in the mediastinal space may also sometimes create a false impression of increased heart size in obese dogs.

THE BUCHANAN AND OTHER METHODS TO EVALUATE LEFT ATRIUM SIZE The Buchanan method is also known as the vertebral scale system or the vertebral heart score (VHS). Two measurements are taken on the lateral radiograph: first, the distance between the ventral margin of the carina and the apex of the heart (the height), then,

cranial to caudal, the widest portion of the silhouette perpendicular to the height axis. These two measurements are then aligned with the thoracic spine, counting the number of vertebral bodies that each one encompasses, starting at the cranial aspect of the 4th thoracic vertebrae. The sum of these two figures is the cardiovertebral index or VHS (fig. 3.77). The general VHS value is 9.7 ± 0.5 vertebral bodies. By definition, 95 % of a normal population fall within the mean ±2 times the standard deviation of the mean, so the normal VHS range in dogs is 8.7 to 10.7. This value, however, varies with breed (see table 3.2) and it has been shown that it can also vary (by up to one vertebral body) with the respiratory and cardiac cycle in the same individual, hence the importance of always correlating it with the patient’s clinical data. Nonetheless, it can prove extremely useful in the radiological follow-up of patients with heart disease. Breeds with thoracic vertebral malformations (usually shortened) have higher VHS values, which would lead to misdiagnosis of cardiomegaly. In cats, the generic VHS value is 7.5 ± 0.3 vertebral bodies. In a study of 67 cats with respiratory distress, it was concluded that heart disease is highly unlikely with values below 8.0, while values above 9.3 suggested a high probability of heart disease. Furthermore, in recent years, various methods to assess left atrium size in the lateral projection have been described. All of them, however, depend on the correct visualisation of the contour of this cardiac chamber on the X-ray, which is not always possible, especially in patients with increased pulmonary opacity. These methods are as follows: VLAS (vertebral left atrium score): The distance is measured from the centre of the ventral margin of the carina to the caudal margin of the left atrium at its intersection with the dorsal margin of the caudal vena cava. This measurement is then aligned with the thoracic spine, counting the number of vertebral bodies that it

encompasses, starting at the cranial aspect of the 4th thoracic vertebrae (fig. 3.78). According to Malcom et al. (2018) a value greater than or equal to 2.3 is a good indicator of left atrial enlargement. RLAD (radiographic left atrial dimension): a line is drawn bisecting the 90-degree angle formed by the height and width axes of the cardiac silhouette (as per the Buchanan method) from the point of intersection of both axes to the dorsal edge of the left atrium. This measurement is then aligned with the thoracic spine, counting the number of vertebral bodies that it encompasses, starting at the cranial aspect of the 4th thoracic vertebrae (fig. 3.79). According to Sanchez Salguero et al. (2018) a value greater than or equal to 1.8 indicates an increase in the size of the left atrium. M-VLAS (modified-vertebral left atrium size): the distance between the centre of the ventral border of the carina to the caudal margin of the left atrium at the point where it intersects the dorsal border of the caudal vena cava silhouette, and then a second line is drawn perpendicular to the first line, starting from the most distal border of the left atrium. The two measurements are then aligned with the thoracic spine, counting the number of vertebrae that they encompass, starting from the cranial aspect of T4 (fig. 3.80). The sum of the vertebral bodies in these two lines is the M-VLAS index. According to Lam et al. (2021), the left atrium is enlarged with values greater than or equal to 3.4. Table 3.2. Radiographic signs of enlargement of the heart chambers From a didactic point of view, it is useful to describe the signs of enlargement of each of the cardiac chambers separately, although in

practice it is rare to find a significant increase in the size of only one of them. It will be normal to detect signs of enlargement of the left heart (left atrium and ventricle), as well as global cardiomegaly (with or without predominance of the right or left side of the heart) at different degrees. The radiographic signs of enlargement of each heart chamber are summarised in box 3.1 and are illustrated in figures 3.84–3.87. In some cases, the enlargement of the left atrium may appear together with the narrowing of one or both of the main bronchi. This may be caused by the pressure exerted on the bronchi by the enlarged chamber, although it is more likely to be caused by bronchial chondromalacia and dynamic collapse of the bronchi which may be accentuated when the left atrium is significantly enlarged. This left atrium enlargement and bronchial collapse due to chondromalacia may cause the dog to cough, which the clinician should not confuse with a sign of heart failure. The radiological signs of left atrial enlargement are less evident in cats. The most evident sign is usually the widening of the heart base silhouette in the dorsoventral projection (fig. 3.88). If the enlargement is very pronounced, it can produce what is known as the valentine- shaped cardiac silhouette, traditionally associated with biatrial enlargement in cases of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. We now understand that visualisation of the valentine-shaped silhouette does not necessarily imply enlargement of the right atrium, in fact, it has been seen that most feline patients with this radiological sign present only a marked enlargement of the left atrium. Radiographic signs of left cardiac failure may be observed when the left heart is enlarged: vascular congestion and pulmonary oedema. Dilatation of the pulmonary veins is the radiological sign that may be detected most early, although it is not always identified. Pulmonary oedema starts in the interstitial tissue, which makes the visualisation of the small pulmonary vessels more difficult. However, these remain visible until the oedema progresses and also affects the alveoli, which is when air bronchograms appear in the affected area. Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema in dogs is typically located in the perihilar area, although it extends to the median and peripheral area of the lung at advanced stages. It usually affects the right lung more than the left one. In cats, cardiogenic pulmonary oedema may appear

in any part of the lung, often with a more patchy pattern. Pleural effusion is also common in cats as a sign of left heart failure (fig. 3.89). When the right heart is enlarged, it is possible to detect signs of right cardiac failure, which include dilatation of the caudal vena cava, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and pleural effusion. Pleural effusion due to right heart failure in cats differs from that caused by left failure: the patient does not also present associated hepatomegaly or ascites with left heart failure which do occur in cases of right failure. If cardiomegaly is global, the silhouette will appear increased in width and height in the two projections (fig. 3.90). In many cases, the signs of an enlarged left heart predominate; in the other cases it is possible to observe signs of enlargement of the right heart, or a more or less uniform enlargement of both sides of the heart. Depending on which are the most affected chambers, the radiographs may show associated signs of left and/or right cardiac failure. Moderate or marked cardiomegaly is a quite reliable indicator of cardiac disease, but mild cardiomegaly should be interpreted carefully, and always in correlation with the rest of the patient’s clinical data. On the other hand, a heart that appears normal on an X-ray may not be a healthy heart as some diseases do not have a significant impact on heart size or shape. Recently, Huguet et al. (2021) published a study of 175 dogs and concluded that X-ray imaging is more accurate for diagnosing left heart enlargement than right heart enlargement, based on the correlation of radiographic findings in these patients with echocardiography. The authors found numerous false negatives in radiographic identification of right-sided cardiomegaly when it was mild, and false positives of right-sided cardiomegaly in cases of severe left-sided cardiomegaly, which can cause significant alteration in the overall morphological appearance of the cardiac silhouette even in the absence of right-sided heart enlargement (fig. 3.91).

BOX 3.1. SIGNS OF ENLARGEMENT OF THE CARDIAC CHAMBER Left ventricle It is located immediately ventral to the left main bronchus. The enlargement of the atrium leads to its dorsal displacement and to a prominence of the cardiac silhouette at this level, which are both visible on lateral radiographs. On dorsoventral radiographs, it is located between the two main bronchi, caudal to the tracheal bifurcation. An increase in the size of the atrium leads to a greater separation of these two bronchi, although this will only be visible on the radiograph if it is taken with a high kilovoltage so it is intentionally overexposed. In addition, the left atrial appendage is displaced, which originates an image of a prominent cardiac silhouette in the 2 to 3 o’clock position. Right ventricle When this chamber increases in size, it tends to do so in height, which therefore leads to an increase in the height of the cardiac silhouette and to a dorsal elevation of the trachea (along its whole length, from the thoracic inlet to the carina) on lateral radiographs.

The caudal vena cava is also displaced dorsally. On dorsoventral radiographs, the left margin in the interval from 2 to 5 o’clock becomes rounded and lies closer to the thoracic wall. Right atrium On lateral radiographs, the increase in size of the atrium causes a dorsal displacement of the caudal part of the trachea (on the cranial part of the base of the heart), while the carina tends to maintain its normal position. It is difficult to assess on dorsoventral radiographs, although it may give rise to a prominence of the margin of the cardiac silhouette in the 9 to 11 o’clock position.

Left atrial appendage When this chamber increases in size, it tends to do so in width, which therefore leads to an increase in the width of the cardiac silhouette and to a greater cardiosternal contact on lateral radiographs. On dorsoventral radiographs, the margin of the cardiac silhouette becomes rounded in the 5 to 9 o’clock position, and even acquires a “inverted D” shape when the enlargement is significant.

Great vessels Changes in the image of the great vessels may provide additional information about possible alterations of the heart. The diameter of the caudal vena cava (CVC), between the cardiac silhouette and the diaphragm, can be compared with the diameter of the descending aorta (Ao), measured at the same intercostal space and if possible, during inspiration (fig. 3.92). A CVC/Ao ratio > 1.5 is very indicative of right cardiac failure. A CVC diameter that exceeds T5 or T6 vertebral body length is another reference indicating enlargement, when measured on the lateral projection. Before reaching a definitive diagnosis of decreased size, we should bear in mind the diameter of this vessel varies slightly with both the respiratory and the cardiac cycles. If the decreased diameter size is maintained on serial radiography, hypovolaemia would be considered as the most likely cause. The diameter of a normal aorta is similar to the height of the adjacent vertebral bodies. It may appear increased in cases of aortic valve stenosis, and occasionally, in patients with patent ductus arteriosus. On dorsoventral radiographs, an increase of the aortic diameter creates a prominence of the cardiac silhouette in the 11 to 1 o’clock position according to the clock-face analogy, while on lateral radiographs the aortic arch is more marked. In senior healthy cats, the aorta may be elongated, and its curvature may be more pronounced or it may even follow a more undulating course, which has been termed “redundant aorta” (see fig. 3.76). In these cases, the contour of the aortic arch may appear lateralised to the left in the dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections, which can be mistaken for a pulmonary nodular lesion.

The main pulmonary artery (pulmonary trunk) may appear enlarged in cases of pulmonary stenosis, patent ductus ateriosus, pulmonary hypertension or dirofilariasis, essentially. On ventrodorsal radiographs, its enlargement gives rise to a prominence of the cardiac silhouette in the 1 to 2 o’clock position according to the clock-face analogy in dogs. In cats, its location is more medial. On lateral views, it is more difficult to identify its enlargement, although the superimposition with the trachea may facilitate its visualisation. FIGURE 3.86. Acquired heart diseases Acquired valvular disease Primary acquired valvular disease in cats and dogs is usually degenerative (endocardiosis) or, on a less frequent basis, infectious (bacterial endocarditis).

Myxomatous mitral valve degeneration, also called mitral endocardiosis or chronic myxomatous mitral valve disease, is the most common heart disease in dogs. Clinical signs are generally observed in old animals, especially in small breeds. The incompetence of the mitral valve caused by valvular degeneration leads to the backflow of blood to the left atrium, which initially originates its dilatation, and will be followed by an enlargement of the left ventricle. As the process progresses, signs of left heart failure may appear. Degeneration of the tricuspid valve is uncommon as an isolated lesion. It usually appears associated with degeneration of the mitral valve. It causes signs of enlargement of the right atrium and ventricle and may be accompanied by signs of right heart failure (dilatation of the caudal vena cava, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and pleural effusion). Bacterial endocarditis is rare in cats and dogs. Radiography does not provide any relevant information in most cases, at least in the early stages. The cardiac silhouette may appear normal, or show signs of enlargement of the left atrium and pulmonary oedema. Cardiomyopathies Dilated cardiomyopathy is one of the most frequent heart diseases in dogs. It usually produces signs of global cardiomegaly (fig. 3.93). In advanced stages, the silhouette may resemble that of pericardial effusion, and secondary signs of left and right heart failure may appear. In the Doberman, dilated cardiomyopathy may cause a very remarkable enlargement of the left atrium only. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the most common acquired heart disease in cats which usually presents with substantial left atrium enlargement (fig. 3.94). The valentine-shaped cardiac silhouette sign may appear, with widening of the cardiac base in the dorsoventral projection. As the disease progresses, signs of associated left and/or right heart failure may appear. Dilated cardiomyopathy is much less frequent in cats, and usually causes global cardiomegaly with rounding of the apex. The cardiac silhouette is often masked by pleural effusion in these cases.
The diagnosis of cardiomyopathy is always confirmed by means of echocardiography.

Dirofilariasis This is one of the main causes of pulmonary hypertension, which in turn causes right ventricular hypertrophy. Adult parasites inhabit the pulmonary arteries and sometimes the right ventricle and atrium. On chest X-rays, signs of right ventricle enlargement can be visualised, as well as the dilatation and tortuous course of the pulmonary arteries. When transverse silhouettes of these enlarged vessels are identified, their image may be confused with that of pulmonary nodules (see fig. 3.113c). The enlarged main pulmonary artery creates a prominence of the cardiac silhouette contour from the 1 to 2 o’clock position according to the clock-face analogy (fig. 3.95). A focal or multifocal alveolar lung pattern may appear in peripheral areas due to thromboembolism caused by the accumulation of parasite debris or secondary inflammation (pneumonitis). The latter may also cause an unstructured interstitial lung pattern. Dirofilariasis is rare in cats. When present, enlargement of the main pulmonary artery is not usually evident, but enlargement of the peripheral pulmonary arteries can be identified. They may have a bronchointerstitial pattern similar to that of feline allergic or inflammatory lung diseases. This pattern may appear even in the absence of a vascular pattern, so this differential diagnosis should be taken into account in cats that present this radiological pattern, especially in geographical locations with the highest incidence of this disease.

Congenital cardiac diseases The value of plain radiography in the diagnosis of congenital diseases of the heart and great vessels is limited. Contrast techniques have been almost totally replaced by echocardiography, which is the method of choice for the diagnosis and assessment of these diseases. The most common congenital heart defects in dogs are patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis, ventricular septal defect and tetralogy of Fallot. Mitral valve dysplasia, atrial septal defect, tricuspid valve dysplasia, cor triatatum dexter and mitral valve stenosis are diagnosed on a less frequent basis. Persistent truncus arteriosus, tricuspid valve stenosis, right ventricular

hypoplasia, double outlet right ventricle and transposition of the great vessels are rarer. In cats, the most frequent defects are mitral valve or tricuspid valve dysplasia, patent ductus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, ventricular septal defect, aortic valve stenosis, tetralogy of Fallot, persistent common atrioventricular canal or endocardial fibroelastosis. In some cases, plain radiography provides data that may help or guide us in case of a clinical suspicion of a congenital heart or vascular disease. Patent ductus arteriosus In the foetal circulation, the ductus arteriosus shunts the oxygenated maternal blood to the aorta. The permanent closure of this duct occurs soon after birth, thus forming the ligamentum arteriosum. A failure in the closure of the duct maintains a communication between the aorta and the main pulmonary artery, and is called patent ductus arteriosus. The consequences of this failure to close will depend on the diameter of the duct and on the pulmonary vascular resistance. When the pulmonary vascular resistance is normal, there is a continuous shunt flow from the aorta (high resistance) to the pulmonary circulation (low resistance). This type of flow (systemic to pulmonary) is termed left-to-right shunt and is the most common pattern. Reverse or right-to-left patent ductus arteriosus refers to those cases in which blood flows back from the pulmonary artery to the aorta (pulmonary to systemic), and occurs because the pulmonary vascular resistance is higher than the systemic vascular resistance.

FIGURE 3.95. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the thorax of a dog with dirofilariosis. It is possible to observe signs of enlargement of the right ventricle and dilatation and tortuous course of the pulmonary arteries (indicated by white arrows). In image (b), the enlarged main pulmonary artery creates a prominence of the cardiac silhouette in the 1 to 2 o’clock position (black arrows) according to the clock-face analogy. The radiographic signs of a patent ductus arteriosus considerably vary depending on the volume of blood being shunted, the age of the animal and the degree of cardiac decompensation. In left-to-right shunts, it is possible to observe a mild to moderate enlargement of the left atrium and ventricle due to volume overload and vascular congestion. It is common to observe three prominences in the margin of the cardiac silhouette on dorsoventral radiographs: in the 11 to 1 o’clock position due to aortic arch enlargement; in the 1 to 2 o’clock position due to enlargement of the outflow tract of the pulmonary artery; and in the 2 to 3 o’clock position, due to lateral displacement of the left atrial appendage. Pulmonary oedema occurs with the development of left heart failure. In animals with severe pulmonary hypertension, caused by a right-to-left patent ductus arteriosus, an

enlargement of the right ventricle and tortuous pulmonary arteries (fig. 3.96) are observed. Pulmonary stenosis It is a narrowing of the outflow tract of the right ventricle at the valvular (pulmonary valve dysplasia), subvalvular or supravalvular level. The most common type is the first one. When blood passes through the area of narrowing, the flow accelerates and poststenotic turbulences that cause dilatation of the main pulmonary artery appear. The pressure overload in the right ventricle leads to its enlargement. The radiographic signs of this condition depend on the degree of narrowing, although it is often possible to see signs of enlargement of the right heart and main pulmonary artery in the two projections. It is easier to see the prominence of the pulmonary artery on dorsoventral radiographs, in the 1 to 2 o’clock position according to the clock-face analogy (fig. 3.97), although its shadow may be seen superimposed with the trachea on lateral radiographs (as a kind of “hat”). The pulmonary arteries may appear normal or have a reduced diameter.

FIGURE 3.96. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) radiographs of the thorax of a dog with patent ductus arteriosus. These images show marked global cardiomegaly with a prominence of the cardiac silhouette in the 12 to 2 o’clock position (black arrow) according to the clock-face analogy, which indicates an enlargement of the main pulmonary artery, and, to a lesser extent, of the aortic arch. Dilatation of the pulmonary arteries and veins may also be observed (white arrows). Aortic stenosis It is a narrowing of the outflow tract of the left ventricle at the subvalvular (fibrous or muscular ring), valvular or supravalvular level. The subvalvular type is the most common type in dogs (subaortic stenosis). When blood passes through the area of narrowing, the flow accelerates and poststenotic turbulences that cause dilatation of the aortic arch appear. Secondarily, the left ventricle dilates due to pressure overload. The radiographic signs of this disease depend on the degree of the narrowing. An enlargement of the aortic arch and signs of increased height of the left ventricle may be observed on lateral radiographs (fig. 3.98), as well as a prominence of the cardiac silhouette in the 1 to 1 o’clock position, and in the 2 to 5 o’clock position on dorsoventral radiographs. Signs of enlargement of the left atrium will appear at advanced stages. Ventricular septal defect Interventricular septal defects may occur in any area of the septum, but they are more frequent in its membranous part, in its most dorsal area. They may be isolated defects or be associated with other congenital anomalies, such as atrial septal defects or patent ductus arteriosus. If the right and left ventricular pressures are normal, the blood flow will be shunted from left to right because the left ventricular systolic pressure is higher than the right one. However, if the defect is very dorsal, the blood will flow directly into the pulmonary artery, which causes almost no effects on the right ventricle. The blood that is shunted to the pulmonary circulation returns to the left atrium and ventricle, which causes pulmonary (arteries and veins) congestion and enlargement of the left heart. If the defect has a more ventral

location, a large volume of blood may enter the right ventricle, so this latter may also appear enlarged in these cases. Small defects do not usually cause any alterations on chest radiographs. If the defect is large, there will be signs of enlargement of the left ventricle and atrium, although this will be less marked in the later, as well as signs of enlargement of the right ventricle on some occasions (if the defect is ventral) and pulmonary congestion. FIGURE 3.97. Lateral (a) and dorsoventral (b) radiographs of the thorax of a dog with pulmonary stenosis. Image (a) shows a prominence of the cranioventral margin of the silhouette and image (b) its right margin appears rounded, with marked prominence at 1 to 2 o’clock position (arrow), according to clock-face analogy, due to the enlargement of the main pulmonary artery. Tetralogy of Fallot Tetralogy of Fallot is the congenital defect that most often causes cyanosis. It is the result of the combination of pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defects, secondary hypertrophy of the right ventricle and several degrees of dextroposition and overload of the aorta. The radiographic signs of this disease may greatly vary depending on the severity of the pulmonary stenosis and size of the ventricular

septal defect. An enlarged right heart and reduced pulmonary vessels are usually observed. Diseases of the pericardium The disease that most frequently affects the pericardium is pericardial effusion. It causes a generalised enlargement of the cardiac silhouette, which acquires the aspect of a water bottle when the volume of fluid that has accumulated in the pericardial sac is very large (fig. 3.99). When the amount of fluid is minimal or moderate, the cardiac silhouette does not necessarily acquire a characteristic water- bottle shape and its enlargement is variable. On radiographs, the globally rounded shape of the cardiac silhouette in the two projections and the fact that the heart chambers cannot be identified help us to differentiate this image from that of global cardiomegaly. Even so, it is necessary to perform an echocardiogram to establish a differential diagnosis between both conditions. In many cases, this technique will also allow detection of tumours as the cause of the effusion. Peritoneopericardial hernias may have a congenital origin and are characterised by a communication between the peritoneal space and the pericardial space through a defect in the diaphragm. The identification of clumped abdominal structures that mask the image of the normal cardiac silhouette in the centre of the thorax is a typical radiological finding in this anomaly (fig. 3.100). The liver is the most frequently herniated organ, followed by the gallbladder, the stomach, the intestine and the omentum. If there is communication but passage of abdominal contents to the pericardial sac is minimal, the cardiac silhouette may appear enlarged with an asymmetric morphology (fig. 3.101). In such cases, the communication and abnormal content in the pericardial space can be confirmed via echocardiography. The oral administration of barium may confirm the anomalous position of the stomach and intestine if these are herniated. Cardiac tumours Most cardiac tumours are associated with a pericardial effusion. Haemangiosarcoma is the most frequent tumour in dogs, while lymphoma is the most frequent type in cats. Haemangiosarcomas

originate in endothelial cells and may appear in any part of the heart, although their most common location is the wall of the right atrium. Chemodectomas originate in neuroepithelial cells and are typically located at the base of the heart, where they create a more or less defined “mass effect” on radiographs depending on their size (fig. 3.72). Other tumours (myxomas, ectopic thyroid carcinomas, fibrosarcomas, etc.) are less frequent. Microcardia The term microcardia is used to describe the reduction of the size of the heart. The decrease in the size of the cardiac silhouette may be real or apparent on radiographs. An increase in the amount of air in the lungs (emphysema) or in the pleural space (pneumothorax) may create an image suggestive of microcardia. Real decreases in size are always the result of conditions that cause hypovolaemia, mainly haemorrhage, severe dehydration or Addison’s disease. In the latter, the image may be particularly remarkable because hypovolaemia is accompanied by atrophy of the muscular mass of the heart. The size of the pulmonary vessels is usually reduced (hypovascularisation) as an associated finding in cases of microcardia (fig. 3.102). Microcardia and pulmonary hypovascularisation can sometimes be encompassed with the identification of signs of megaoesophagus in patients with Addison’s disease.

A dilated cardiomyopathy may give rise to a similar image, although it is usually possible to distinguish the cardiac chambers to some extent, while in the image of a pericardial effusion it is not. However, an echocardiogram is necessary to confirm the diagnosis with certainty.

Cor pulmonale The radiological identification of an enlargement of the right ventricle in a patient with a pulmonary or vascular disease is very indicative of cor pulmonale, which is defined as a right heart failure caused by a pulmonary or thoracic disease. By definition, there must be pulmonary hypertension in cor pulmonale for right heart failure to happen. In dogs, the most common cause of cor pulmonale is dirofilariasis, although any obstruction of the pulmonary vessels may cause hypertension and, therefore, cor pulmonale. The obstruction of the pulmonary arteries may occur as a result of the presence of blood clots (pulmonary thromboembolism) or by embolisation of fat, septic material, neoplastic cells or nematodes of the genus Dirofilaria. Lung In cats and dogs, the right lung is divided into four (cranial, middle, caudal and accessory) lobes and the left lung is divided into two (cranial and caudal) lobes. The approximate areas occupied by each lung lobe are shown in figure 3.103. The lungs contain air in the alveoli and in the lumen of the bronchi and bronchioles, and are formed by structures of soft-tissue density, which include the alveolar walls, the interstitial tissue, the blood vessels and the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles. Of these latter, only the blood vessels and walls of the bronchi with a larger diameter can be identified on a radiograph of a normal thorax. If we divided the radiograph in three concentric areas –perihilar area, middle area and peripheral area of the lung–, in normal conditions it would only be possible to visualise the walls of the bronchi in the area most proximal to the pulmonary hilum, since these are usually too thin to be identified in the image in the middle and peripheral areas. The blood vessels, however, are visible in the three areas as they have soft-tissue density walls and content. They appear as structures with a linear morphology that branch out and become narrower as they run from the hilum to the periphery of the lung. Following this criterion, the concept of normal lung pattern refers to the lung that appears basically radiolucent, due to its air content, and

in which the pulmonary vessels–with a normal size and morphology– and the walls of bronchi with a larger diameter are identified (fig. 3.104). The pulmonary vessels and bronchi follow a parallel path. In lateral projections, the arteries are dorsal to the veins, while in dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections, the arteries are lateral to the veins. The path of the main bronchi can be identified among the silhouettes of the larger arteries and veins (fig. 3.105). Cranial lobar pulmonary vessels are better appreciated on lateral projections. There is generally less overlapping between them in the left lateral projection, which improves their assessment in this projection compared to the right lateral projection. Caudal lobar pulmonary vessels are better evaluated in dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections. However, dorsoventral are preferred as these vessels appear more magnified, their path is more perpendicular to the X-ray beam and there is less pulmonary atelectasis in adjacent areas compared with ventrodorsal projections. In healthy patients, the arteries and veins should be equal in size. In the lateral projection, the width of the cranial lobar vessels where they cross the 4th intercostal space should not exceed the width of the proximal third of the 4th rib. The caudal lobar vessels are evaluated in the dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections, the width of which under normal conditions should not exceed the width of the 9th rib at the point where they overlap. In cats, it is easier to visualise the cranial lobar arteries and veins than the caudal ones.

The arteries are situated dorsal to the veins in the lateral projection, while in the dorsoventral projection the arteries are located laterally, and the veins are medial. The bronchi lie between the arteries and the veins. As discussed above, the factors that have the greatest impact on lung radiography are: Exposure values: on underexposed conventional radiographs, the lung has a higher radiopacity, which may be mistaken for an interstitial infiltrate of the parenchyma, while on overexposed conventional radiographs, all the structures in the image appear darker, which may be confused with emphysema, and on overexposed digital radiographs, only the lung areas with less thickness would appear as black areas which cannot be corrected with post-processing tools. Moment of the respiratory cycle: if the radiograph is taken during expiration, the lungs contain a lesser amount of air, which slightly increases their radiopacity.

Obesity: an excess amount of subcutaneous fat leads to a slight increase in pulmonary radiopacity, as the density of fat is added to that of the lungs. In addition, the accumulation of intrathoracic fat somewhat limits lung expansion, which also contributes to the increase in pulmonary radiopacity. Age: the lungs of young animals may be more radiopaque than those of adults because they contain more water. The lungs of old animals may be slightly more radiopaque due to interstitial fibrosis, as well as to calcification or fibrosis of the bronchial walls, which make these more visible on radiographs (it will also be possible to visualise them in the middle area of the lungs). Prolonged lateral recumbency: the animals that remain in a recumbent position for a relatively long period of time, especially if they are anaesthetised, will have a partial collapse of the lung that corresponds to the side on which they had been lying. In the ventrodorsal and dorsoventral view, a deviation of the mediastinum towards the affected side is observed, which helps to differentiate atelectasis caused by a recumbent position from a true pulmonary pathological alteration. Digital radiographs: digital radiographs have a much higher contrast resolution than conventional radiographs and make the lungs appear less radiolucent. They also improve the visualisation of soft-tissue density structures, such as the pulmonary vessels and walls of the bronchi, which will sometimes be identified in the middle area of the lungs despite having no anomalies. Lateral and ventrodorsal radiographs are recommended for a general assessment of the lungs. If ventrodorsal and dorsoventral views are compared, the capacity of the lungs to expand is greater with the first one, which improves the definition of the lung in the image. On a lateral radiograph, the lung that is higher will be better visualised, since its capacity of expansion is at its maximum, while the lung that is lower will always have some degree of partial collapse, which may limit its radiological examination. The right lateral projection is usually used as the standard view. However, in the specific case of an assessment of pulmonary metastases, the

combination of the two lateral projections, right and left, is used, since if there are small lesions, these will be better viewed in the most distended lung (higher position). In case of doubt, a ventrodorsal radiograph is added in order to obtain complementary information, although small lesions that are visible on one or the two lateral views often cannot be identified on the ventrodorsal view. Ultrasound examinations of the lungs have important limitations. It will only be possible to visualise areas of the lungs that do not contain air and are in contact with the thoracic wall, since the presence of air will hinder the examination in other locations. In cases of pleural effusion, the fluid facilitates the visualisation of the pulmonary content. Ultrasonography is indicated in the study of pulmonary masses and consolidation, since it provides information about the internal structure of the lesion, its vascularisation may be examined with Doppler ultrasound and it allows the collection of samples for cytology or biopsies under ultrasound guidance. As opposed to magnetic resonance imaging, which provides low- quality lung images with conventional equipment, computed tomography will be indicated whenever the findings on the radiographs are suspicious, when a torsion is suspected, in cases of bronchial foreign body or pulmonary thromboembolism, for a thorough examination of metastases and for the assessment of masses (it allows the determination of its exact location and examination of the rest of the lung to rule out any associated lesions), as well as for guided punctures or biopsies of lesions that are not identifiable by means of ultrasonography. Abnormal lung patterns The radiological assessment of the lungs is based on the identification of abnormal lung patterns, which have been classified in function of the affected components of the lung: Bronchial. Vascular. Alveolar. Interstitial.

Mixed (combination of two or more of the previous patterns). The identification of the pattern may be more or less difficult depending on the location and extension of the lesions. Once it is identified, a differential diagnosis is made for each abnormal lung pattern. The length of the list of diseases may vary depending on the correlation of the radiological findings with the rest of the patient’s clinical data (anamnesis, examination, laboratory tests, etc.). The main limitation in the interpretation of lung radiographs lies in this fact: very different diseases may have a similar radiographic image. Bronchial pattern A bronchial pattern is identified when bronchial walls that could not be observed become visible in normal conditions, in general in the middle or peripheral area of the lung, although we must remember that digital radiography can allow the visualisation of walls of normal bronchi in the middle area. The typical radiological sign is the visualisation of “ring-” or “donut-”shaped images, which correspond to transverse shadows of bronchial walls (of those bronchial branches with a course that is parallel to the X-ray beam), and “train track” images, which correspond to the longitudinal shadows of these branches (bronchial branches with a course that is perpendicular to the X-ray beam). The bronchial pattern may be due to the thickening of the bronchial walls, the presence of peribronchial infiltrates (indistinguishable from wall thickening on an X-ray) (fig. 3.106) or increased radiopacity caused by bronchial wall calcification (fig. 3.107). The latter is usually due to a degenerative process associated with the advanced age of the patient, although in some cases it may appear secondary to primary pathological alterations such as Cushing’s disease. A radiographic finding of bronchial wall calcification is not considered significant. It is, however, not always easy to differentiate on an X-ray a bronchial pattern caused by some disease from that caused by bronchial wall calcification. It is important to keep in mind that the absence of any identifiable bronchial pattern on the X-ray does not rule out bronchial pathology,

especially in acute processes. Identification of bronchial lung patterns should always be correlated with the patient’s clinical data. Patient’s age and whether or not they have clinical signs consistent with bronchial pathology at the time the X-rays are taken should be taken into account. In a young patient, a radiographic finding of a bronchial pattern is usually due to pathological causes that is either occurring at the time of the X-ray or the after-effects of previous bronchial pathologic processes. In a senior animal with no clinical signs consistent with bronchial pathology, this pulmonary pattern is usually associated with an age- related degenerative process. Finally, when an adult patient, senior or not, presents clinical signs consistent with a bronchial process, the radiographic visualisation of a bronchial pattern should be considered a priori as significant, although, as in a young patient, it may also be a sequela of previous pathological processes. If in doubt, a transtracheal wash will allow a more precise diagnosis to be established. The typical lung pattern of feline asthma is bronchial (fig. 3.108), although it may be associated with other lung patterns. The severity of the clinical signs often does not directly correlate with the magnitude of the radiological findings. In patients with feline asthma, it is common to observe secondary atelectasis of the right middle lobe and emphysema. In chronic or severe bronchial diseases, the bronchi may have irreversible sac-like dilatations, a condition known as bronchiectasis (fig. 3.109). These may also be caused by obstructions of the airway or smoke inhalation. Bronchial neoplasms rarely produce an evident bronchial pattern but tend to cause pulmonary consolidation and nodular lesions. Computed tomography is of great interest in the study of the diseases of the bronchi. It allows the visualisation of bronchi and bronchioles with a small diameter, bronchiectases that are not detectable by means of radiography or bronchial ruptures, and the differentiation between foreign bodies, presence of intraluminal mucus and bronchial masses (fig 3.110). In the case of bronchial neoplasms, it also facilitates the identification of pulmonary metastases and lymphadenopathies. With CT virtual bronchoscopy, it

is possible to follow the course of the trachea and large bronchi (fig. 3.111). FIGURE 3.106. Schematic diagram of the bronchial lung pattern caused by thickening of walls or peribronchial infiltrates (a) and lateral (b) and ventrodorsal (c) projections, as well as the enlarged image of the cranioventral area of the lung in lateral projection (d) of the thorax of a dog with marked bronchial pattern due to allergic bronchitis. White arrows (d) point to “ring-like” shadows of varying sizes. Vascular pattern

The pulmonary vascular pattern is characterised by changes in pulmonary blood vessel size and/or morphology. It is inadvisable to evaluate the size and shape of the vessels subjectively. The image of the cranial lobar vessels in the lateral projection and the caudal lobar vessels in the ventrodorsal or dorsoventral projections should be taken as reference. Vascular patterns may be arterial, venous, or mixed. In a venous vascular pattern, the width of the veins exceeds that of the arteries (fig. 3.112); in an arterial vascular pattern, the width of the arteries exceeds that of the veins (fig. 3.113); and in a mixed vascular pattern, both the arteries and the veins appear enlarged (fig. 3.114). In the latter case, it is important to use reference landmarks comparing vessels against rib diameter (as explained earlier), rather than relying on subjective assessments which could lead to misdiagnoses. The most common causes of venous vascular lung pattern are:

Left heart failure. Fluid overload (iatrogenic). Left atrial obstruction (thrombus, neoplasm). Intracardiac communication with right-to-left flow (e.g.: Tetralogy of Fallot). On rare occasions, intracardiac communication with left-to-right flow. An arterial vascular lung pattern may appear in patients with: Dirofilariasis, Angiostrongylus vasorum infection or Aelurostrongylus infection (cats). Large left-to-right intracardiac communication (e.g. septal defects). Pulmonary thromboembolism. Pulmonary hypertension. Chronic lung disease. Peripheral arteriovenous fistula. A mixed vascular pattern, with enlargement of both arteries and veins, may be observed in patients with: Fluid overload (iatrogenic). Intracardiac communication with left-to-right flow (e.g. patent ductus arteriosus, inter-ventricular or atrial septal defects). Feline cardiomyopathy. Pulmonary congestion prior to pneumonia. Left heart failure. Chronic anaemia. Hyperthyroidism. Arteriovenous malformations.

Upper airway obstruction. Visualisation of tortuous (wavy) pulmonary vessels is also considered to be an abnormal vascular pattern (fig. 3.115). It is common to observe this type of image in pathologies that cause pulmonary hypertension, such as dirofilariasis. FIGURE 3.113. The white arrowhead points to the left caudal (lateral) lobar artery and the black arrowhead points to the left caudal (medial) lobar vein. FIGURE 3.115. Schematic diagram of the vascular lung pattern caused by tortuosity of the pulmonary arteries (a) and enlarged image of the left caudal hemithorax (b) of a dog with dirofilariasis. The white arrowhead points to the left

caudal lobar artery, which is extremely enlarged and following a slightly wavy path, and the black arrowhead points to the left caudal lobar vein, which is normal in size, but also slightly wavy. A reduction in the size of the pulmonary vessels is also considered a pathological vascular pattern, which is called pulmonary hypovascularisation (fig. 3.116), which appears in processes that cause hypovolaemia, such as haemhorrage, severe dehydration or Addison’s disease. It can also occur in some congenital conditions with right-to-left flow and in severe cases of pulmonary stenosis. As the size and number of vessels visible on the X-ray decrease, the lung fields appear darker, and it may be difficult to identify vessel silhouettes in peripheral areas. Alveolar pattern This occurs when the pulmonary alveoli fill with fluid (oedema, pneumonia, haemorrhage) or when they become deflated (atelectasis). Alveolar pattern due to the proliferation of neoplastic cells, at least in isolation, is much less common. Figure 3.117 shows the different phases in the evolution of an alveolar lung pattern. When a small number of alveoli are affected by one of these processes, the increased opacity of the affected areas may be negligible or very difficult to identify on an X-ray. This means that, at very early stages, oedema, pneumonia, haemorrhage or pulmonary atelectasis may not be detected on an X-ray examination. As the affected areas in the lung expand, the possibilities for radiographic identification also increase. They appear on the image as areas of soft tissue/fluid opacity with irregular morphology and poorly defined borders (fig. 3.118), distinguishing them from nodular lung lesions which have regular morphology and usually well-defined borders. When the areas of increased alveolar opacity become larger and surround the bronchial branches, the air content of the latter will be highlighted on the radiographic image, a sign known as air bronchogram. An air bronchogram occurs when the normal lumen of the bronchi is made visible on the X-ray by the opacification of the surrounding pulmonary parenchyma. In other words, the lumen of the

bronchi is normal and what is altered is the parenchyma surrounding them. Air bronchograms on the lung image are considered the hallmark sign of an alveolar pattern. But air bronchograms are not always identified in an alveolar pattern. If the affected areas are small and close to a relatively large diameter bronchial branch, the lumen of the bronchi will not be highlighted and therefore the bronchograms will not be noted. Air alveolograms are the areas of lung parenchyma that retain some air but appear surrounded by parenchyma zones with alveoli filled with fluid or without any air (fig. 3.119). FIGURE 3.116. Schematic diagram of the vascular lung pattern caused by a decrease in the size of the pulmonary vessels (a) and lateral projection of the thorax of a dog with pulmonary hypovascularisation (b). The left cranial lobar artery (white arrowhead) and vein (black arrowhead) are indicated, both reduced in size; other radiographic findings suggestive of hypovolaemia are also noted, such as microcardia and decrease in the size of the caudal vena cava (asterisk).

FIGURE 3.117. Schematic representation of the different phases (1-6) in the evolution of an alveolar pattern. When all the alveoli are fluid-filled or deflated in a large area of pulmonary parenchyma, this area acquires a homogeneous fluid/soft

tissue opacity, without alveolograms, which is called pulmonary consolidation. Air bronchograms may be observed in an area of pulmonary consolidation (fig. 3.120), but if they collapse or become filled with fluid, they will no longer be visible in the affected area. This is what is known as complete consolidation and would represent the most advanced phase of an alveolar pattern (fig. 3.121). When a consolidated area coincides with the margin of a pulmonary lobe and the contiguous lobe is not affected, we get what is known as a lobar sign, so called because the lobe margin can be seen which is not possible on an X-ray of a healthy lung. The alveolar pattern may also cause a silhouette sign (also termed loss of silhouette sign or loss of outline sign) in areas where the affected lung parenchyma abuts other soft tissue opaque anatomical structures, such as the heart, pulmonary vessels or diaphragm. As they are in contact and are of the same opacity, it is not possible to distinguish the margins of one structure from the other on the X-ray (fig. 3.122). The most common causes of an alveolar lung pattern are pulmonary oedema, pneumonia and pulmonary haemorrhage. As all these pathologies produce the same pulmonary pattern, they cannot be differentiated by radiological study alone. However, the rest of the patient’s clinical data, other radiographic findings identifiable on the image (fig. 3.123), the location of the area of pulmonary involvement and, in some cases, treatment response and progression may adequately guide the differential diagnosis. For example, oedema may develop and disappear in a few hours if the appropriate treatment is administered (fig. 3.124). However, a haemorrhage or aspiration pneumonia may appear in a few minutes, but it may take days before they disappear. On the other hand, bacterial pneumonia develops within a few hours or days, but takes several days or weeks to resolve when treated. Oedema of cardiogenic origin (due to left heart failure) appear in patients with heart disease which can generally be identified on an X- ray as cardiomegaly, with some exceptions, such as endocarditis. In dogs, its location is typically perihilar in the early stage, spreading first to the middle and then to the periphery (fig. 3.125). In cats, however, cardiogenic oedema can occur in any location and its pattern is often multi-focal (“patchy”). If cardiogenic pulmonary oedema is suspected,

the radiological image of the lung should be reassessed after appropriate treatment. FIGURE 3.118. Lateral radiograph (a) and computed tomography image (b) of the thorax of a dog with an alveolar pattern due to pneumonia. In image (a), areas of soft-tissue density with an irregular morphology may be observed in the peripheral areas of the lung, where some air bronchograms can be identified, though with difficulty. The affected areas and air bronchograms are much more evident in the computed tomography image.

In these cases, a lung ultrasound or computed tomography is indicated.

The time an alveolar pattern takes to appear and disappear may be of help to establish a differential diagnosis. An oedema takes several hours to disappear or reduce with the appropriate treatment, while a haemorrhage or pneumonia will take days to do so. Non-cardiogenic oedema is uncommon. While it can occur in any part of the lung, dorsocaudal lung involvement is more common, and especially the right caudal lobe. Medical history and examination findings can help guide the radiological diagnosis in these patients who present with an episode of acute dyspnoea. The most common causes are upper airway obstruction, neurogenic (e.g. secondary to seizures), electrocution and near-drowning. Pneumonia may present at any location in the lung, with involvement of one or more lobes. Bacterial pneumonia is often found in the cranioventral area (fig. 3.126). Ventral location is also common for aspiration pneumonia, although it may appear in other locations depending on the patient’s position at the time of aspiration. If aspiration occurs as a result of an alteration of the oesophagus, the X-ray may also provide some information about this. Foreign body penetration of the lung (e.g. grass awns) usually causes focal pneumonia, sometimes difficult to identify on X-rays, especially when the affected area overlaps with other chest structures, such as the heart (fig. 3.127). Peripheral involvement may suggest

Angiostrongylus infection. The absence of cardiomegaly and venous congestion on the image may help distinguish pneumonia from cardiogenic oedema. Pulmonary haemorrhages usually occur as a result of trauma to the chest but can also be due to coagulation disorders. In the event of trauma, the most affected area is usually closest to the impact (fig. 3.128). They may present a more diffuse pattern of distribution or cause more focal haematomas (fig. 3.129), usually adjacent to the chest wall. The accumulation of cells in the alveoli is uncommon, although it may occur in some types of neoplasia (e.g. bronchoalveolar carcinoma). In the case of pulmonary atelectasis, the alveolar pattern is accompanied by radiographic signs of decreased volume of the lung or the affected area of the lung. This is usually identified on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal radiographs by the displacement of mediastinal structures toward the affected lobe or lobes (fig. 3.130), unless the atelectasis affects both lungs to a similar extent, as may occur in pneumothorax or bilateral pleural effusion. It is more difficult to appreciate the signs of decreased volume in a lung or lung area in lateral projections. In cases of more pronounced atelectasis, the cardiac silhouette can appear elevated over the sternum by the displacement of the heart towards the affected hemithorax (fig. 3.131) or towards the most affected in the case of atelectasis of both lungs.

Interstitial pattern The lung interstitial pattern is characterised by abnormalities affecting the pulmonary interstitium. Two types of patterns are clearly distinguished: nodular interstitial, due to the focal proliferation of cells in the interstitium that leads to the formation of nodular lesions, and

unstructured interstitial pattern, when involvement of the pulmonary interstitium occurs diffusely. Nodular interstitial pattern The differential diagnosis of a nodular pattern varies in function of the number and size of the lesions. A nodular lesion may be distinguished from an area of alveolar infiltration because a nodule has a regular shape (typically round or oval) and well-defined borders, while an area of alveolar infiltration has an irregular morphology and poorly defined limits (fig. 3.132). Nodular lesions may be identified on radiographs when they reach a diameter of 5 mm or more. With smaller diameters, they may be confused with transverse images of the pulmonary blood vessels. However, if the lung has an elevated number of nodular lesions smaller than 5 mm (referred to as a miliary nodular interstitial pattern), these will no longer be mistaken for vessels. The differential diagnosis of a nodular interstitial pattern with lesions larger than 5 mm (fig. 3.133) includes: pulmonary metastases (the most common diagnosis), primary lung neoplasms, abscesses and pulmonary granulomas (not frequent). A miliary nodular interstitial pattern (fig. 3.134) may be due to metastases or mycotic pneumonia as the most probable diagnoses, followed by mycobacterial or haematogenous bacterial pneumonia, pulmonary lymphoma or disseminated intravascular coagulation. Pulmonary bone metaplasia (fig. 3.135), which is a benign process characterised by the appearance of numerous very small, calcified nodules in the lung parenchyma, should not be confused with a miliary pattern caused by metastases, mycosis, lymphoma, etc. The calcification of nodular lesions caused by metastases, even from osteogenic tumours such as osteosarcoma, is very rare.

The displacement of the cardiac silhouette (displacement of the mediastinum) to the left hemithorax indicates a loss of volume in the affected lung lobe. A mass was detected by means of bronchoscopy in the bronchus of the caudal segment of the left cranial lobe. FIGURE 3.131. Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) projection of the thorax of a dog with partial atelectasis of the left lung. In the lateral projection, elevation of the cardiac silhouette and a slight retraction of the ventral pulmonary border can be observed.
