FIGURE 3.132. Schematic representation of a nodular interstitial pattern in comparison with an area of alveolar infiltration. A nodular lesion has a regular shape (generally round or oval) and well-defined limits, while the area of infiltration has an irregular morphology and ill-defined borders.

FIGURE 3.133. Lateral projection of the thorax of a dog with pulmonary metastases. The arrows point to several of the pulmonary nodular lesions, measuring over 5 mm in size (nodular interstitial lung pattern) presented by the patient. The use of the terms pulmonary “nodule” or “mass” depends on the size of the lesion: if its diameter is less than 3 cm, it is called nodule, and if it exceeds this value, the term “mass” is used. It is important not to confuse nodules with transverse images of pulmonary vessels, images created by the superimposition of ribs and other structures, or with calcified pulmonary or pleural plaques. The most probable cause of a single pulmonary mass (fig. 3.136) is primary lung neoplasm, although abscess, granuloma, haematoma or fluid-filled bulla should also be included in the list of possible differential diagnoses. Pulmonary masses may occasionally be

calcified in the centre due to dystrophic calcification, or have a more or less irregular central area with gas density (cavitary mass). The most likely diagnoses of a cavitary pulmonary mass are a tumor with necrotic center and an abscess (fig. 3.137). It is important not to confuse a cavitary mass with a pulmonary bulla (also called pneumatocele), which often appears as an incidental finding. A pulmonary bulla is due to a focal accumulation of gas in the lung caused by loss or rupture of the alveolar walls, which may be of congenital, traumatic or idiopathic origin. The wall of the bulla is usually thin and is formed by pulmonary connective tissue and the visceral pleura (fig. 3.138). When a large lung mass is observed next to others with a smaller diameter, these latter usually correspond to metastases of the first mass. In dogs, lung metastases usually appear as well-defined, round lesions, while in cats they often have a more irregular shape and a more poorly defined outline. The metastases of haemangiosarcomas may also appear less defined because they are usually accompanied by haemorrhage. A large lung mass may mimic the image of lung lobe consolidation due to other causes, such as lobar pneumonia (fig. 3.139). One criterion that facilitates their differentiation is that masses generally have convex margins, not consistent with the normal morphology of interlobular fissures. It is uncommon to identify air bronchograms in a lung mass, but when visualised they are usually narrow or distorted.

FIGURE 3.134. Lateral projection of the thorax of a dog with pulmonary metastases. There are very numerous pulmonary nodular lesions measuring less than 5 mm (miliary nodular interstitial lung pattern).

FIGURE 3.135. Lateral projection of the thorax of a dog with pulmonary osseous metaplasia, a benign process characterised by the appearance of numerous tiny, calcified nodules in the lung parenchyma. When a mass is located adjacent to the thoracic wall, it is possible to assess it by means of an ultrasound examination, and thus to determine whether it is solid or cystic, to examine its vascularisation and to perform an ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration or biopsy. Computed tomography is particularly indicated to look for metastases (nodules smaller than 2 mm can be detected) and for the study of lung masses, since it allows us to determine their exact location for a possible surgical treatment, assess their extension to adjacent structures (fig. 3.140) and perform a guided biopsy if this cannot be done by means of ultrasonography.

Unstructured interstitial pattern The unstructured interstitial pattern (also called diffuse interstitial) is the most difficult to identify on X-rays. It causes a discrete diffuse increase in pulmonary opacity in the affected areas, which makes it difficult to differentiate the pulmonary vessels, although these are still visible in the image (fig. 3.141). It differs from the alveolar pattern in that the latter causes a more marked increase in opacity, which completely obscures the image of the pulmonary vessels in the affected areas. In fact, if a pathological process affects the interstitium and alveoli, the unstructured interstitial pattern will be masked by the alveolar component, which is common in the case of oedema, pneumonia or haemorrhage that affects both pulmonary components. Cardiogenic oedema is only interstitial in the earliest phase (often difficult to identify on radiographs due to the typical perihilar location in dogs). Afterwards it evolves towards greater alveolar interstitial

involvement at which point the alveolar radiological pattern predominates and masks the interstitial pattern. The increased pulmonary opacity caused by the unstructured interstitial pattern is usually homogeneous in appearance, although it can sometimes acquire a reticular or linear appearance (fig. 3.142). The most common causes of pure unstructured interstitial pattern (not associated with an alveolar component) are interstitial oedema (initial or resolution phase), viral or protozoan pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis, diffuse neoplastic infiltration (lymphoma or metastasis of mammary carcinoma), herbicide poisoning and haemorrhage (initial or resolution phase). Pulmonary fibrosis may appear as a degenerative sign associated with ageing in older animals and causes a slight increase in interstitial radiopacity. It may also appear as the final consequence of a great variety of lung diseases leading to an irreversible alteration of the support tissue of the interstitium. The initial cause may be inflammatory, infectious or idiopathic. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis mainly affects senior dogs of the Terrier breeds, especially the West Highland White Terrier and Cairn Terrier (fig. 3.143).

FIGURE 3.140. Computed tomography image of the thorax of a dog with a 6-cm mass in the left lung (long red line), previously diagnosed by means of radiography. Computed tomography allowed the determination of the exact location of the mass and the detection of small metastases (short red line) that had not been identified in the right lung.

FIGURE 3.141. Schematic representation of the unstructured interstitial pattern, which is characterised by a diffuse increase of lung radiopacity, which reduces the visibility of the pulmonary vessels. Mediastinal lymphadenopathies are also often found in patients with pulmonary lymphoma, especially in dogs. It may also be accompanied by pleural effusion and/or pulmonary oedema. Ultrasound examination of the abdomen usually reveals organomegaly and intra-abdominal lymphadenopathies in these patients. Computed tomography is very sensitive to detect or confirm this type of lung pattern (fig. 3.144).

In image (a) the increased opacity is more homogeneous, while image (b) has a more reticular appearance. The pattern obstructs proper visualisation of smaller diameter pulmonary vessels.

Mixed pattern Pathological processes affecting the lung often cause abnormalities in more than one pulmonary component, so it is very common to identify mixed lung patterns on the X-ray (fig. 3.145). Bacterial bronchopneumonia, for example, usually elicits a mixed pattern with bronchial, alveolar and interstitial components, although the latter is usually masked by the alveolar. In pulmonary fibrosis, the co- appearance of an unstructured interstitial and a bronchial pattern is also common. Whereas with primary pulmonary neoplasms, an interstitial component (nodular and/or unstructured), a bronchial

component and in some cases an alveolar component (secondary atelectasis or alveolar infiltration) are common. The predominant pattern is usually taken into account when establishing the order of probability of the possible differential diagnoses. Lung hypertranslucency Generalised hypertranslucency may appear due to an increase in the volume of air contained in the lungs (due to an obstruction of the intrathoracic airways or emphysema) or as a result of a reduction in the size of the pulmonary vessels. Real hypertranslucency should not be confused with an overexposed radiograph. Pulmonary emphysema is characterised by an excessive, focal or diffuse, accumulation of air in the lung parenchyma, and may be congenital or acquired. Acquired emphysema usually occurs secondary to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which causes irreversible expansion of the alveoli or destruction of their walls. One or more lung lobes may be affected showing up as hyperlucent (less opacity than normal) and this does not vary with the inspiration and expiration cycle. The chest cavity may appear expanded, with the ribs more perpendicular to the spine and the diaphragm flattened and displaced caudally, with little variation in its position with inspiration and expiration. The cardiac silhouette may appear diminished in size and more distant from the diaphragm (fig. 3.146). If only one lung is affected, the mediastinal structures tend to lean toward the unaffected lung, and if only a single lobe is affected, it can partially collapse the adjacent lobe, causing a sharp contrast in the opacity between the affected and the adjacent lobe. Pulmonary bullae can also be identified in these patients.

FIGURE 3.146. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of a cat with hyperlucency and increase of the lung volume due to emphysema. The cardiac silhouette appears reduced in size and the diaphragm is flattened and caudally displaced. Emphysema is a common complication of feline asthma. Pulmonary neoplasia The most common radiological image of primary lung neoplasms is characterised by the appearance of a solitary mass with a regular and clearly defined contour. Multiple nodules, homogeneous lobar consolidation, a diffuse reticulonodular pattern or an interstitial- alveolar pattern may also be observed. Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma may produce a mixed pattern with nodules of irregular morphology and peribronchial infiltrates. Areas of consolidation, that appear associated with a primary lung neoplasia, may correspond to the tumour itself but could also be caused by pulmonary atelectasis due to secondary inflammatory changes or tumour invasion of the airways.

In dogs, pulmonary histiocytic sarcomas are most commonly found in the right middle lobe (predominantly in the ventral area) and the left cranial lobe, and usually involve the peripheral area of one lobe or the whole lobe. The appearance of air bronchograms in the lesion is more common in histiocytic sarcomas than in other primary tumour types. Identifying chest lymphadenopathies associated with primary lung neoplasms on X-rays is not common. However, studies have been published indicating that they are more common in dogs with histiocytic sarcomas, in which greater sternal and tracheobronchial node involvement was observed compared with cranial mediastinal nodes. The radiological pattern that can be identified on X-rays of patients with pulmonary lymphoma varies greatly in both dogs and cats. In dogs, the most common radiological pattern is unstructured interstitial, followed by nodular interstitial (single or multiple lesions), alveolar infiltration and bronchial infiltration. In cats, pulmonary masses and/or nodules and bronchial infiltration are the most common findings. In some cases, the pulmonary infiltration pattern appears together with images of sternal, cranial mediastinal and/or tracheobronchial lymphadenopathies, and less frequently pleural effusion. Pleural effusion associated with a primary lung neoplasm is more common in cats than in dogs. In these patients, ultrasound may facilitate more accurate identification of lung lesions, provided that they extend to the peripheral area of the lung. To properly assess the lung image, the X-ray should be repeated after thoracentesis. In addition to the increased frequency of associated pleural effusion, other common radiographic findings in cats with primary lung neoplasia are: The radiological pattern is usually that of a well-defined mass, although the margins can often be irregular. The most common location is in the caudal lobes, with a predominance of the right. Bronchioloalveolar carcinoma may generate a mixed bronchial pattern that is more alveolar, with no evident nodular component, a

focal alveolar pattern or one or more cavitary masses (fig. 3.147). Gas-filled cavities are more common in tumours of bronchial origin, although they can also appear with other types of lung tumours. If calcification appears in association with these lesions, this further increases the suspicion of neoplasia. Adenocarcinomas, squamous cell carcinomas and bronchogenic carcinomas can metastasise to the distal phalanges, and can affect various digits and phalanges. If lysis is identified in one or more distal phalanges in the cat, which may spread to the middle phalanges, metastasis of a lung carcinoma should be considered as a differential diagnosis. Cases of monoparesis as a result of arterial thromboembolism have also been described in patients with primary lung carcinoma, hence a chest X-ray is recommended in senior cats without heart disease presenting this clinical sign. Lung lobe torsion Lung lobe torsion can occur spontaneously, especially in deep-chest dogs, or it can be secondary to pathologies that cause lobar collapse and the presence of air or fluid around it, which facilitates lobe mobility. The most affected lobe is the right middle, followed by the cranial part of the left cranial lobe (especially in Pugs) and the right cranial lobe; caudal lobe involvement is unlikely. Initially, signs of increased volume of the affected lobe can be observed, but when secondary necrosis develops, the volume of the lobe tends to decrease, and its margins may appear concave. Consolidation can be observed, sometimes with small identifiable air bronchograms. The appearance of a “vesicular pattern”, with numerous small “sponge-like” areas of trapped gas is relatively typical; a finding that is highly indicative of lobe torsion. The lobar bronchi may present a sudden interruption of their path or an abnormal direction. The development of a secondary pleural effusion is common, which can be located in both hemithoraces, only in the affected lobe or only around the affected lobe. Pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum may also appear if there is a rupture of the bronchi.

Doppler ultrasonography may be of great help in the diagnosis as it allows the detection of the absence of venous flow and of the reduction or absence of arterial flow in the affected lobe. However, in practice, good quality images may not be obtained due to the breathing difficulties of patients with torsion. The most appropriate diagnostic technique is computed tomography, as it provides accurate data on the abnormal bronchial and vascular structure positioning as well as an evaluation of their permeability. The administration of an intravenous contrast medium allows the differentiation between the vascularised collapsed lung and the necrotic lobe with torsion. Pulmonary thromboembolism This is caused by blockage of an artery by a blood clot or migration of an embolus, which may be composed of small blood clots as well as other components such as bacteria, parasites, fat, air or foreign bodies (e.g. an intravenous catheter). The patient presents with lethargy, weakness and tachypnoea and poorly response to oxygen and other support measures. Computed tomography or pulmonary angiography are usually required to confirm the diagnosis. X-rays may show no obvious abnormalities, even in patients with severe clinical signs. Up to 27 % of dogs and cats with a necropsy-confirmed pulmonary thromboembolism do not show any anomalies on chest radiographs. In an animal with tachypnoea that does not respond to oxygen administration, a normal chest radiograph will strongly suggest the presence of thromboembolism.

The affected vessel is rarely identified; it may appear dilated in the segment prior to the obstruction point and appear sharply reduced in size in the segment after it. Appendicular skeleton4 Normal radiographic anatomy of the appendicular skeleton https://goo.by/oKtDO Principles of interpretation Radiography is an excellent technique for skeleton assessment. As with other anatomical regions, the main difficulty in the radiological diagnosis of some appendicular diseases is that the same radiological findings are shared by different diseases. In such cases, it is essential to correlate findings with other clinical data (history, examination, laboratory data, etc.) from the patient. Useful information for the diagnosis can be obtained in some cases by assessing the evolution in time of the radiographic image of a lesion. This is why serial radiographs are often performed. When studying the appendicular skeleton, a comparison of the obtained images with those from radiographic atlases is of special interest, especially when examining complex anatomical joints, such as the tarsus or the carpus. When an animal has a lesion only in one limb, we can obtain a better reference of normality by radiographing the contralateral limb. A few technical tips to optimise appendicular skeleton images are summarised below: Projections: in general, two radiographic projections should be always taken at a 90º angle, although in some cases it may also be useful to obtain oblique radiographs or radiographs taken in forced flexion, extension or lateralisation of a joint. When radiographing a

large bone, the corresponding proximal and distal joints should be included. Positioning: in order to avoid image distortions caused by obliquity, it is important to correctly centre the anatomical region that is to be radiographed. In addition, the median plane of the bone structures should be parallel to the cassette, if possible. Collimation: it is very important to correctly collimate the anatomical region that is to be radiographed. Thus, the image quality will be optimised, unnecessary radiation to other anatomical regions of the animal can be avoided, and the amount of diffuse radiation that can affect the operator who holds the patient can be reduced. Anti-scatter grid use: only needed when radiographing anatomical regions over 10-cm thick, which generally correspond to the scapula, the scapulohumeral joint and the humerus in the forelimb, and the hip and femur in the hind limb. The rest of limbs are radiographed without the grid. Image observation: on a conventional radiograph, small-sized lesions can be better observed using an intense focal source of light (e.g.: placing the film next to a halogen lamp). On a digital radiograph, the same effect can be achieved using image post- processing tools. A good appendicular skeleton radiograph should provide good detail of the trabeculae of bone and the cortex. At the same time, it should offer sufficient contrast of soft parts, so soft tissues and fat (e.g.: the infrapatellar fat pad) can be differentiated. Ossification and closure of growth plates Calcification of bone structures begins during gestation. At birth, only the diaphyses of long bones and the cranial bones are calcified, whereas the epiphyses are still cartilaginous, thus having the density of soft tissue, and cannot be distinguished from the soft tissues surrounding the bone. Subsequently, progressive calcification of the ossification centres located in the epiphyses, the apophyses and smaller-sized bones occurs. Table 4.1 shows the ages of onset and fusion of the different ossification centres in dogs and cats.

The metaphysis, located between the epiphysis and the diaphysis of long bones (fig. 4.1), can present slightly irregular margins in growing animals, especially in large breeds. It should not be mistaken for a periosteal reaction or for pathological osteolysis. It is important not to mistake growth plates for fracture lines in young animals. In case of doubt, radiographic atlases can be consulted, although the best reference of normality is obtained by radiographing the contralateral limb of the same animal (provided the disease is not bilateral). In adult animals, the closed growth line can appear as a sclerotic band that binds the epiphysis with the metaphysis.

FIGURE 4.1. Dorsopalmar radiograph of the carpus of a healthy 10-week-old dog. The growth line (physis) appears as a soft tissue density band that separates the epiphysis from the metaphysis. The latter can present slightly irregular edges

during growth, especially in large breed dogs. The metaphysis is joined to the bone diaphysis. Osteolysis and osteogenesis Bone lesions basically present in two forms: with bone destruction (osteolysis) and with new bone production (osteogenesis). The terms osteolysis and osteogenesis should not be mistaken for osteopaenia and sclerosis, although they are related. In osteopaenia, general reduction in radiopacity of a bone is observed, and the term sclerosis is used to describe increased bone radiopacity. Several patterns in osteolysis and osteogenesis are described, and correct identification of the pattern leads to a more precise radiological diagnosis. Patterns of osteolysis (fig. 4.2) Geographical pattern One or more areas of osteolysis appear, generally more than 1 cm in diameter and with well-defined edges, with a narrow zone of transition between the lesion and normal bone. Geographical lesions may or not have a sclerotic margin and are usually found in the bone marrow. The adjacent cortical zone can appear interrupted, thinned or displaced (expansile lesion). This pattern usually appears in benign or low-grade malignant lesions. Moth-eaten pattern Multiple osteolytic areas appear in different sizes, usually 3–10 mm in diameter, and may coalesce in the central area to form a bigger lesion. Margins are not well-defined and show a relatively wide area of transition to normal bone. They can be localised both in the bone marrow and cortex. The affected cortical zone usually appears irregularly eroded. This pattern usually appears in more aggressive processes, such as malignant tumours, osteomyelitis and multiple myeloma.

Permeative pattern Many small-sized osteolysis zones appear, 1–2 mm, with pinpoint shapes. The margins of the lesion are ill-defined and show a relatively wide area of transition to normal bone. The cortical zone usually appears irregularly eroded. It is characteristic of more aggressive bone lesions, such as highly malignant tumours or severe osteomyelitis. Table 4.1. Age at appearance and fusion of ossification centres in the dog and cat (taken from F.J. Barr, 2006; R. Dennis et al., 2001; J.P. Morgan, 1981; R.N. Smith, 1968, 1969 and G. Summer–Smith, 1966).
Mixed pattern A combination of the above-mentioned patterns can be found in a lesion, usually indicating evolution to the most aggressive type. This

can be observed when a benign process becomes more active, becomes fractured or when it progresses to malignancy. Osteopaenia It is defined as a general reduction in bone radiopacity. It is usually accompanied by thinning of the cortices and apparent sclerosis of the subchondral bone. The most frequent causes of osteopaenia are: Osteoporosis: decreased bone calcification with reduced bone mass. A frequent cause for osteoporosis is secondary hyperparathyroidism of nutritional or renal origin. It can also appear after immobilisation of a limb (disuse osteoporosis) or as a sequela of distal fractures (post-traumatic osteoporosis). Osteomalacia: decreased bone calcification maintaining bone mass. It is caused by vitamin D deficiency and it is rare in small animals. Patterns of osteogenesis (fig. 4.3) A common characteristic of many skeletal lesions is new bone formation. This happens as a direct or indirect result of a lesion, infection, tumour or other local or systemic diseases. Most of the new bone is formed in the periosteum (periosteal reaction), although it can also be formed in the endosteum or bone trabeculae. It therefore corresponds to the bone response after an abnormal stimulus that can be short, repeated or maintained over time. Several classifications of periosteal reactions have been made. The classification below has been sorted from moderate to high aggressiveness. Solid periosteal reaction Cortical thickening occurs, and may have smooth (chronic mild trauma, subperiosteal haematoma, panosteitis) or rough margins (trauma, inflammation of tissue adjacent to the bone). Lamellated periosteal reaction

It is also known as “onion skin”. New bone forms in layers due to repeated periosteum elevation periods. This reaction type is observed in many pathological processes, from focal trauma to bone infections and tumours. Palisading periosteal reaction It presents as a series of small bone columns perpendicular to the cortex. This type of reaction is usually observed in bacterial osteomyelitis and hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy. Brush border periosteal reaction Thin and short bone spicules are formed very close together and perpendicular to the cortex, occupying a wide cortical area. It can appear due to inflammation of tissue adjacent to the bone, in acute osteomyelitis or in early stages of bone neoplasms. Spiculated periosteal reaction Bone spicules are formed roughly set apart and perpendicular to the cortex. It is considered suggestive of malignancy. Sunburst periosteal reaction Bone spicules that irradiate from the lesion in various directions are formed. It is suggestive of lesion expansion through the cortex into adjacent soft tissue. Amorphous periosteal reaction Different sized, shaped and oriented new bone deposits appear in the soft tissues surrounding the damaged area of the bone. It is considered highly suggestive of malignancy. Aggressive bone lesions versus non-aggressive In order to classify a bone lesion as aggressive or non-aggressive several factors should be considered: Degree of lesion margin definition.

Width of the zone of transition between damaged and healthy bone. Pattern of osteolysis. Pattern of osteogenesis. Cortex involvement. Occurrence of sclerotic margins. Progress of the lesion over time. Findings suggestive of aggressive and non-aggressive lesion are summarised in Table 4.2. When a lesion presents a combination of signs of both columns of the table, those which are more suggestive of aggressiveness should be considered. Soft tissues Soft tissues can show alterations associated to the presence of lesions in the appendicular skeleton. They often appear thicker due to inflammation or because of the presence of masses, although a reduction in size due to muscular atrophy can also be appreciated (fig. 4.4). Presence of gas in soft tissues (subcutaneous emphysema) is usually due to air penetration from the outside, in case of penetrating wounds (fig. 4.5) or after surgery in the area, although it can also be caused by anaerobic infections. In soft tissue, radiopaque foreign bodies or areas of calcification can also be identified on radiographs (fig. 4.6). The latter can be mistaken for small bone fragments or overgrowths when localised next to the bone.

It is usually used to examine soft tissues and is of special interest in the study of muscular and tendon

lesions. The associated joints and ligaments can also be examined, although very high resolution transducers and wide experience are required to correctly interpret the images for small animals. Rapid progress. Computed tomography offers excellent images of bone structures. It is specially indicated to evaluate less-evident bone lesions or those difficult to detect by radiography, or to examine anatomically complex joints such as the carpus or tarsus. It is also indicated for the preoperative assessment of bone deformations and complex fractures because three-dimensional image reconstruction at different angles enables the surgeon to know the exact location and morphology of the deformed bone or fragments in order to decide the most appropriate surgical approach. In human medicine, magnetic resonance is the imaging technique of choice for the diagnosis of diseases of joints and soft tissues of the limbs. It is, however, limited for assessing bone structures, especially in those lesions that can mostly affect the bone cortex, given that it produces no signal. Despite this, it is most useful to evaluate bone tumours, osteomyelitis, haematomas and processes which cause bone necrosis. Due to the smaller size of the joints, its use in small animals is limited by the patient size and the resolution offered by the equipment. Congenital, hereditary and developmental abnormalities

Chondrodysplasia The term chondrodysplasia is applied to a wide group of diseases, all of them due to abnormal cartilage growth. It can affect long bone epiphyses, vertebral body epiphyses, long bone epiphyses and metaphyses, or a combination of the above. One or several of the following radiological signs can be observed: Slower growth of long bones, which may appear shorter and thicker than normal. The physes can appear wider. Retained growth cartilage can be observed in the metaphyseal region. Calcification of the epiphyseal ossification centres can be delayed. Punctated or distorted epiphyses may be observed. Vertebral epiphyses can be partially or irregularly ossified. Chondrodysplasia is classified based on the bone region that is mostly affected, as described below. Epiphyseal chondrodysplasia In dogs, it has been described in Beagles and Poodles. It is characterised by a delay in the calcification of the epiphyseal ossification centres. The epiphyses can have a punctate appearance and although ossification may be completed, they are often deformed, thus causing early onset of osteoarthritis. It has also been described in some cat breeds. Physeal chondrodysplasia It has been described for the Pointer breed and causes a disproportionate dwarfism. Marked widening of the physis is radiologically observed, especially in the radius, ulna and tibia. Long bones are shortened and curved. It is accompanied by articular cartilage erosion, thus causing early onset of osteoarthritis. The same

process occurs in the Alaskan Malamute, although without articular cartilage erosion. It has also been described in cats. Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia It has been described in the Pyrenean Mountain Dogs. It basically affects long bone metaphyses and vertebrae. All long bone metaphyses appear wider, especially in the radius, ulna, tibia, metacarpals and metatarsals. Vertebral body epiphyses are irregularly or incompletely ossified. In the Labrador Retriever and the Samoyed, a form of oculoskeletal dysplasia has been described. It causes shortening and deformation of the limbs, associated with ocular defects Retained core of growth cartilage In growing large and giant breed dogs, a retained core of growth cartilage can be observed, generally affecting the distal physis of the ulna, although it has also been described at other sites, such as the distal physis of the radius or the femur. It appears as a radiolucent triangular area that spreads from the physis to the metaphysis, with a sclerotic margin (fig. 4.7). It may cause limb deformity. Retained core of growth cartilage can be observed associated with other pathological alterations of the physis, but in those cases the lesion usually has non sclerotic, ill-defined margins. Polymelia It indicates a higher number of limbs or parts of a limb than normal. Supernumerary fingers (polydactyly) are most frequent, especially observed in cats and other dog breeds such as the Pyrenean Mountain Dogs. Supernumerary fingers often start at the medial part of the limb and can include full or partial metacarpals or metatarsals and a variable number of phalanges. This abnormality is not usually clinically significant. Ectrodactyly The distal part of the limb appears split, with split phalanges, metacarpals, and carpal bones and associated abnormally to the radius and ulna (fig. 4.8). Aplasia, hypoplasia or fusion of distal bones in the

limbs can occur. It is a rare alteration in cats and dogs, and considered hereditary in the latter. Hemimelia Absence or hypoplasia of one of the bones forming a pair (most frequently affecting the ulna–radius, but also can affect the tibia–fibula) (fig. 4.9). Osteochondrosis and osteochondritis dissecans Osteochondrosis is defined as a failure of endochondral ossification, resulting in thickening of the cartilage. The thickest areas do not receive enough quantity of nutrients, which results in necrosis and fissure formation in the affected area. When a chondral flap or an osteochondral fragment is separated from the adjacent subchondral bone, the process is called osteochondritis dissecans. The cartilage flap or even the osteochondral fragment cannot be radiologically identified in many patients, thus generally receiving the name osteochondrosis. This developmental disease appears in young dogs of large and rapid growth breeds. Clinical signs usually appear between 6–9 months of age. It is usually bilateral, even though the animal may only present with lameness in one limb. It usually appears at specific anatomical locations and affects weight-bearing joint surfaces: Caudal or caudolateral surface of the humeral head (fig. 4.10). Distal and medial surface of the humeral condyle (fig. 4.11). Distal surface of the lateral femoral condyle (fig. 4.12) and less frequently, in the same area of the medial condyle. Medial or lateral trochlear edge of astragalus. Flattening or concavity of the affected subchondral bone surface is radiologically observed, as well as sclerosis of the subchondral bone surrounding it. The cartilage flap is usually not observed, unless it is calcified. If osteochondral fragments are identified inside the joint, the clinical signs are usually more evident.

At times, a subchondral defect can be identified on the joint surface opposite the lesioned joint, which is known as a “kissing lesion”. Although rare, the appearance of intra-articular gas has also been described in dogs with shoulder osteochondrosis, known as “vacuum phenomenon”, which is attributed to an accumulation of nitrogen gas due to the negative pressure exerted during the traction of the joint for X-ray positioning. When the lesion is located in the lateral margin of the astragalus, overlapping of the calcaneus in the dorsoplantar projection may impede its identification. A dorsolateral–plantaromedial oblique or a flexed dorsoplantar view may be useful in these cases. Sacral osteochondrosis, which affects its craniodorsal edge, has also been described. It basically affects the German Shepherd and, less frequently, the Boxer and Rottweiler. Irregularity of the dorsal edge of the cranial vertebral endplate of the sacrum is observed. As in other sites, the osteochondral fragment is occasionally identified; in this example, on the vertebral canal floor.

Elbow dysplasia Elbow dysplasia is a non-specific term that refers to a triad of developmental lesions which include: Osteochondrosis of the humerus. Failure of anconeal process to fuse with the ulna. Fragmentation of the medial coronoid process of the ulna. One, two or all three lesions can be observed in one animal, and most frequently there is affectation of both limbs. Elbow joint incongruity, due to non-uniform contact of the joint surfaces that form the elbow, can lead to ununited or fragmented anconeal process and hyperostosis or fragmented medial coronoid process of the ulna. X-ray can identify severe elbow joint incongruity, but CT is much more accurate in diagnosing this abnormality, especially if the severity of the lesion is mild or moderate. The anconeal process should fuse with the ulna at 5 months of age. Lack of fusion at this age is considered pathological. It affects large dog breeds, especially the German Shepherd. To adequately observe the lesion, the elbow radiograph should be taken in lateral projection, forcing flexion of the joint (fig. 4.13).

FIGURE 4.13. Mediolateral radiograph with hyperflexion of the elbow of a dog with an ununited anconeal process of the ulna (arrow). The hyperflexion makes it easier to identify the lesion. Fragmentation of the medial coronoid process of the ulna affects large or medium breed dogs, more males than females, and clinical signs usually appear between 4–6 months of age. It is the primary cause of elbow dysplasia in dogs. The radiological study of these patients should include the two standard orthogonal projections, mediolateral and craniocaudal elbow, plus the craniolateral- caudomedial oblique view with limb pronated 15 to 25º, which reduces the overlapping of the medial coronoid process of the ulna with the

radius, thus improving its evaluation. In many cases, the fragment is not identified on the radiograph due to superimposition with the radius, because it is partially adhered to the ulna or when it is basically made of cartilage. Thus, the radiological diagnosis is very frequently based on the observation of degenerative signs secondary to the primary lesion. The radiographic signs that indicate fragmentation of the medial coronoid process of the ulna (fig. 4.14) are: Visualisation of the bone fragment at the area where the medial coronoid process is located (uncommon). Loss of definition or irregularity of the cranial edge of the medial coronoid process in mediolateral projection. Rounding of the medial edge of the medial coronoid process in the craniocaudal projection. Incongruence or subluxation of the elbow joint. Computed tomography is much more precise than radiography to evaluate joint incongruency (nonuniform contact of joint surfaces). Degenerative secondary signs: osteophyte formation at the proximal edge of the anconeal process, distal humerus, proximal radius, trochlear notch, and in the medial coronoid process itself; also, trochlear plate sclerosis. Computed tomography is an excellent alternative to accurately diagnose this anomaly (fig. 4.15). Hip dysplasia The term hip dysplasia refers to an abnormal development of coxofemoral joints. It is a hereditary disease that can appear in any dog breed, but especially in large breeds, although also in medium and small breeds, as well as in cats. It is usually bilateral although it can also be unilateral (in approximately 11% of cases). At birth, the coxofemoral joint is normal but, due to the increase in joint laxity experienced by these animals, they develop a greater or lesser degree of subluxation/luxation and signs of degenerative joint disease (coxarthrosis).

The standard projection that is normally used when assessing hip dysplasia is ventrodorsal. In order to avoid diagnostic errors, a correct positioning is essential (fig. 4.16): Symmetric pelvis (it can be checked by comparing the two obturator foramina, which should be of the same size in the image, and the width of the wings of the ilium, which should also be the same). The femurs should appear in parallel. The patellas should appear aligned with the trochlear groove (to achieve this, internal rotation of the knees should be forced). The full pelvis and both knees should appear on the radiograph. This projection is used to assess dysplasia when issuing official certificates, usually from 1 year of age. Radiographic signs for dysplasia include: Femoral head subluxation or luxation: usually the acetabular coverage of the femoral head is at least 50 %. When there is coxofemoral subluxation, widening of the medial joint space will be observed (fig. 4.17). The degree of luxation is also measured by the Norberg angle, that requires specific templates or angle-measuring devices. In digital radiography, the angle can be measured using specific post-processing tools (fig. 4.18). Signs of joint degeneration (fig. 4.19): Acetabular remodelling (usually flattening), with rounding of the cranial acetabular edge. Femoral head and neck remodelling. Periarticular osteophyte formation on the edges of the femoral head and the acetabulum. A sclerotic line appearing on the femoral neck called Morgan’s line. It is due to osteophyte formation at the caudal surface of the femoral neck and is considered an early sign of coxarthrosis. Subchondral sclerosis of the acetabular edge.

FIGURE 4.14. Mediolateral (a), craniocaudal (b) and oblique caniolateral- caudomedial radiographs of a dog with fragmentation of the medial coronoid process of the ulna. Image (a) showing flattening of the cranial margin of the medial coronoid process of the ulna (white arrow), remodelling of the cranial margin of the radial head (black arrow) and sclerosis in the trochlear notch of the ulna (asterisk). Image (b) shows a slight rounding of the margin of the medial coronoid process of the ulna (arrow), while image (c) identifies a small bone fragment adjacent to the medial coronoid process of the ulna (arrow) thanks to the oblique projection. Dysplasia is less prevalent in cats than in dogs. In the cat, most degenerative changes appear at the craniodorsal edge of the acetabulum, whereas remodelling of the femoral head and neck is less frequent. The Norberg angle is measured at the intersection of two lines: one drawn between the centres of both femoral heads, and another one starting at the centre of each femoral head and moving tangentially to the craniolateral acetabular edge. The Norberg angle measures 105° or more in most healthy dogs, and at least 95º in healthy cats. Inferior measurements are suggestive of dysplasia. The smaller the angle value is, the higher the subluxation degree, and therefore the severity of the dysplasia. Nevertheless, it is important to remark that there are many factors influencing the correct measurement of this angle, such as the positioning of the femurs and pelvis and changes in the acetabular edge.

To correctly assess coxofemoral joints, the pelvis should appear symmetric, the femurs in parallel and the patellas aligned with the trochlear channel. The PennHIP method is a way to assess the degree of laxity of the coxofemoral joint at an earlier stage, from 16 weeks of age. Three

radiographic projections are used: the standard ventrodorsal with the femurs pulled into extension; a ventrodorsal projection with compression of both coxofemoral joints; and a ventrodorsal with distraction of both joints. A specific device is used to cause the distraction. The distraction index is calculated by dividing the distance from the femoral head centre to the centre of the acetabulum, between the radius of the femoral head. The value of this index can vary from 0 to 1. A value of 0 indicates perfect joint congruity and a value of 1 indicates complete luxation. This method was developed by researchers from the University of Pennsylvania, where an international database is elaborated and there are specific courses to obtain official certification as a PennHIP certified technician. Hypertrophic osteodystrophy Also called metaphyseal osteopathy or metaphyseal osteodystrophy. It affects young dogs between 2 and 7 months of age, generally large and giant breeds. It is uncertain how this disease is originated, but in some cases it has been related to distemper and nutritional alterations (an excessive administration of vitamin complexes is thought to cause onset, but this is not clear). Great Danes and Weimaraners could be somewhat predisposed. Clinically, the animal can develop fever and the metaphysis area of long bones appears swollen, warm and painful. It is generally self-limiting and is usually resolved in a few weeks, although most severe cases can cause premature or abnormal closure of growth lines as a sequela. Radiological signs (fig. 4.20): Lesions are usually bilateral and symmetrical. A radiolucent band usually appears at the metaphysis, parallel to the epiphyseal line. This sign is more evident in the distal metaphysis of the radius, ulna and tibia, although it may affect the metaphyses of all long bones. A sclerotic band usually appears at the metaphysis, parallel to the radiolucent band. Inflammation of the soft tissues adjacent to the affected metaphysis. In advanced stages, calcified areas are formed around the metaphysis, apparently separated from the bone cortex by a radiolucent band. These areas can extend to the diaphysis. Remodelling of the affected areas takes place over time. Sometimes, the growth plate is prematurely or abnormally closed, thus causing deformation of the affected bone(s).

FIGURE 4.20. Mediolateral projection of the radius and ulna of a dog with an early stage (a) and advanced stage (b) hypertrophic osteodystrophy. Image (a) shows an irregular radiolucent band in the metaphysis (arrows), parallel to the epiphyseal line. Image (b) shows a solid periosteal reaction (black arrow) and mineralised areas around the metaphysis and part of the diaphysis (white arrows). Panosteitis This disease causes inflammation of the diaphyses of long bones in youngs large breed dogs. It affects more males than females, and German Shepherds could be more predisposed. It typically appears in animals between 5 and 18 months of age, but it has also been detected in dogs up to 7 years. It is clinically characterised by episodes of acute lameness, that may affect one or several limbs and it does not always appear simultaneously in all affected limbs (alternating lameness).

During the examination, pain is observed at deep palpation of the affected limbs. With regard to the radiographic signs (fig. 4.21): They may appear in one or several bones. Areas of focal increased density (sclerosis) are observed in long bone marrow, usually in the femur, humerus, radius, ulna and tibia. An irregular thickening of the cortical endosteum can be observed. A solid and smooth periosteal reaction can be appreciated. With time, resolution of bone marrow sclerotic lesions can make the bone trabecular pattern seem to be more marked than usual. Cortical thickness may persist.

FIGURE 4.21. Images of the radius and ulna in mediolateral projection of two dogs with panosteitis. Image (a) shows a focal area of sclerosis in the proximal half of the ulna shaft (arrow). In image (b) increased bone marrow density is more diffuse and affects the radius and the ulna, that also present endosteal and periosteal growth of solid type. Femoral head avascular necrosis

It is also called Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease or femoral head aseptic necrosis. It is a developmental disease that appears in young dogs between 4 and 11 months of age, of small or miniature breeds. Normally, the process is unilateral (fig. 4.22) and less frequently bilateral (fig. 4.23). It results from a deficit in vascular supply to the femoral head epiphysis that produces subchondral bone necrosis. In early stages of the disease, small radiolucent areas (osteolytic) are observed with an irregular morphology at the femoral head, which then evolves to deformation and flattening of the femoral head and neck, that may cause coxofemoral subluxation. Incomplete ossification of the humeral condyle It is a hereditary disease mainly affecting dogs from Spaniel breeds, although it has also been described in dogs from medium and large breeds. The two ossification centres that appear at the humeral condyle fuse at approximately 84 days from birth. Once skeletal maturation is complete, those animals with incomplete ossification will maintain a thin fissure between both halves of the condyle, thus predisposing them to pathological fractures at that site. Spontaneous capital femoral physeal fracture in cats Spontaneous femoral head fractures have been reported in young cats, with a mean age of 2 years. These fractures are not associated with trauma, are more frequent in males and may be unilateral or bilateral. If only one femur is fractured, the contralateral may show delayed physeal closure. They have been linked with obesity, early neutering and delayed capital femoral physeal closure (neutering could cause delayed physeal closure). The initial radiographic finding is a slipped capital femoral epiphysis, followed by different degrees of osteolysis (due to bone resorption) and sclerosis of the affected femoral head and neck (fig. 4.24). Mucopolysaccharidosis Mucopolysaccharidosis is a hereditary disease caused by a deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme responsible for breaking down glycosaminoglycans, which disrupts the development of the epiphyses

of vertebrae and long bones, as well as facial malformation. It is a very rare anomaly in dogs and cats, although the incidence in the latter is higher, especially in the Siamese breed. In long bones it causes malformation of the epiphysis with shortening and stiffness of the limbs. In the spine, it causes shortening and deformation of the vertebrae, bone neoformation around the articular processes and ankylosing spondylitis, which can present with paresis and paraplegia. Facial shortening and widening can be seen in the skull, with alteration of the pattern of the nasal turbinate. It also causes corneal abnormalities, and patients may have cardiac abnormalities and hydrocephalus. FIGURE 4.22. FIGURE 4.24. Ventrodorsal projection of the hip of a 2-year-old cat with right spontaneous femoral capital physeal fracture. Early neutering may be a

predisposing factor for this injury in cats. Fractures Fractures are classified as: Closed (intact skin) or open (skin defect in the area) (fig. 4.25). Simple (single fracture line), comminuted (several fracture lines interconnect at one point or plane, thus dividing the bone in three or more fragments) or multiple (several fracture lines that do not interconnect, in the same or different bones). Transverse, oblique, spiral or irregular, depending on the fracture line direction. Complete (affects the whole bone diameter) or incomplete (e.g. greenstick fracture). Articular or nonarticular fracture, if it affects the joint or not. Avulsion fracture: it separates the insertion site of a muscle (fig. 4.26), ligament or tendon. Stress or fatigue fracture (caused by repeated mild trauma). Compression or impacted fractures: the end of one of the fragments jams into the other (fig. 4.27); shortening of the bone can be observed and it is more frequent in vertebrae. Salter–Harris fractures (see Box and fig. 4.28 and 4.29): they affect the physis. Pathological fractures: they are caused by another disease (processes that cause osteopenia, tumours, bone cysts, osteomyelitis) (fig. 4.30).

profundus are inserted. SALTER-HARRIS FRACTURES Fractures that affect the physis are classified in 6 types (Salter-Harris classification) (fig. 4.28): Type I: the fracture occurs along the physis. Type II: the fracture line crosses the physis and also divides part of the metaphysis. Type III: the fracture line crosses the physis and also divides part of the epiphysis. Type IV: the fracture line crosses the physis and also divides part of the metaphysis and of the epiphysis (fig. 4.29). Type V: impacted or compressed fracture hat occurs at the physis level. It may completely or partially affect the physis. This is the type of fracture that may cause premature closure of the distal growth plate in the ulna. Type VI (rare): it is a consequence of trauma that only affects part of the physis thus causing its partial closure (asymmetric). This type has been added later to the classification and some authors think it should not be included.
FIGURE 4.27. Enlarged image in ventrodorsal projection of the right coxofemoral joint of a dog with an impacted femoral neck fracture. Femoral neck shortening is caused by the fracture.

FIGURE 4.28. Diagram of the classification of Salter type fractures. Immediately after surgical resolution of the fracture, a radiograph will allow the assessment of: the degree of fracture reduction (contact between the fragments); the alignment of the fragments; and the correct placement of the osteosynthesis material. In further radiological checks, the following will be examined: bone callus evolution; possible displacement of the fragments or the osteosynthesis material; rupture of the osteosynthesis material (fig. 4.31); and abnormalities in the adjacent soft tissues. The occurrence of radiolucent bands surrounding the osteosynthesis material indicates mobility of the material or infection (fig. 4.32). Nevertheless, an artefact with the same appearance (radiolucent lines surrounding metallic implants) has been described in digital radiography, due to overuse of the edge-

enhancement tool. This has already been corrected in many modern equipment. Follow-up X-rays of fractures are recommended every 2–4 weeks to evaluate progression and for the early detection secondary complications. In the first 2 weeks, a haematoma and a non-calcified callus form between the fragments, leading to an increase in soft tissue volume around the fracture. During this period, there is a certain degree of bone resorption at the ends of the fragments blurring their definition on the X-ray. The callus begins to calcify 10–12 days after the fracture and with this it can be identified in the images. From about 3 to 4 weeks, the calcification of the callus should already be marked and evident. This calcification usually progresses from the periphery toward the centre of the focus, with the fracture line gradually disappearing. Cortical remodelling occurs in the final phase, usually between 8 and 12 weeks after fracture reduction and stabilisation. These times spans are for general reference only. Progression in the resolution of a fracture depends on many factors, including bone type, fracture type, patient age, treatment methods and the existence of other systemic diseases. Post-traumatic osteoporosis is a common sequela of many long bone distal fractures and can be especially acute in young animals. It is often wrongly called disuse osteoporosis. Post-traumatic osteoporosis develops distal to the fracture (fig. 4.33), whereas disuse osteoporosis (caused by limb immobilisation) affects the whole limb. Once the fracture has formed a solid callus and the bone is again rigid, bone density returns quickly to normal in both types of osteoporosis.

Type II Salter-Harris fracture of the epiphysis plus part of the distal radius metaphysis (b). Type IV Salter-Harris fracture of part of the epiphysis plus part of the distal metaphysis of the humerus (c).

The main complications from fractures are: Delayed union: callus formation is slower than normal. Non-union: callus is not formed; it can be atrophic (end of fragments are pointed) (fig. 4.34) or hypertrophic (bone forms around the ends of the fragments, but they do not bind; the shape of the ends looks like an “elephant’s foot” (fig. 4.35). Defective consolidation: fragments are bound, but not correctly aligned (fig. 4.36). Exuberant callus: splinters of bone incorporate to the callus, due to mobility of the fracture focus or to infection. Osteomyelitis: infection will be suspected when osteolysis is observed surrounding the material, together with an atypical periosteal reaction and marked soft-tissue tumescence, that may look like emphysema (focal gas accumulations) in some cases. Neoplastic development: it may appear after several years, especially if the osteosynthesis material was not removed or the fracture resolution was very complicated. Its cause is unknown but it could be related to chronic inflammation.

the rod can be seen, as well as rupture of several screws. FIGURE 4.33. The osteoporosis develops distal to the fracture (in this case, more marked in the tarsus and metatarsals), unlike desuse osteoporosis that affects the whole limb.

FIGURE 4.34. Craniocaudal radiograph of the tibia and fibula of a dog with atrophic nonunion of a tibial fracture. The fragment ends appear pointed. The external fixators and a double fibula fracture can be observed in the image. Deformities due to growth plate alteration

Growth plate lesions cause slowed-down or arrested growth, and its consequences can be: Shortening of the affected bone(s). Angulation of the affected bone(s). Subluxation of adjacent joints. The degree of bone shortening depends on the specific contribution that the damaged plate has in global bone growth and on the stage of growth when the lesion is produced (fig. 4.37). Angulation or curvature of the affected bone takes place when the lesion affects more than one area in the plate, or when the affected bone is part of a pair (e.g. radius–ulna). The most significant deformities occur by lesion of the proximal or distal growth plate of the radius and of the distal growth plates of the ulna, femur or tibia. Due to its conical shape, the distal growth plate of the ulna is especially prone to lesions. Sometimes, premature growth line closure can be observed with no previous evident trauma. When distal growth of the ulna is slowed-down or arrested and the radius continues growing at a normal pace, cranial and medial curvature of the radius occurs, as well as valgus (lateral) deviation of the hand, elbow subluxation and proximal migration of the ulna styloid process (fig. 4.38). This deformity is called radius curvus.

FIGURE 4.35. Mediolateral radiograph of the radius and the ulna of a dog with hypertrophic nonunion of the radial fracture. The fragment ends appear separated, sclerotic and new bone is forming around them. Nonunion of an ulnar fracture is also observed, with the proximal fragment looking atrophic and the distal, hypertrophic.
FIGURE 4.36. Craniocaudal radiograph of the elbow of a dog with poor consolidation of a distal humerus fracture.

FIGURE 4.37. Craniocaudal projection of the femurs and tibias of a dog with premature closure of the distal growth line of the right femur, causing shortening of this bone (17 cm) compared with the left (18.43 cm). When the lesion affects the distal radial growth plate, the radius is shortened with respect to the ulna, that keeps growing at a normal pace. The radial head separates from the humeral condyle, widening the joint space (fig. 4.39). Medial widening of the distal radial epiphysis occurs, which usually causes valgus deviation of the hand, although it is sometimes in the opposite direction (in varus, to the medial area). Proximal growth plate lesions of the radius are much less frequent and cause similar radiographic signs to those of the distal plate, but the distal radius remains normal and there is no hand deviation. Bone tumours and osteomyelitis Bone tumours Benign bone tumours are uncommon. They include osteomas, generally appearing as radiodense masses of amorphous bone; chondromas, with less radiopacity than osteomas; and osteochondromas, appearing as single cartilaginous exostoses. Malignant bone tumours (osteosarcoma, fibrosarcoma, haemangiosarcoma, chondrosarcoma) appear as aggressive bone lesions, usually single, mainly located at the following metaphyses: proximal of the humerus, distal of the radius, distal of the femur and proximal or distal of the tibia (fig. 4.40). Chondrosarcomas usually affect the ribs, pelvis, or skull.

FIGURE 4.38. Radiographic images in mediolateral (a) and craniocaudal (b) projection of the radius and ulna of an 8-month old dog with radius curvus. Computed tomography image of the same patient (c). As previous trauma has caused premature closure of the distal growth line of ulna, the radius is curved cranially and medially. This causes elbow subluxation and valgus deviation of the hand. Accessory carpal bone deformity can be also observed, as well as a fragment caudal distal to the distal epiphysis of the radius. Both findings are related to the prior trauma. The image (c) shows computed tomographic-based volumetric reconstruction of both limbs, where the damaged limb can be compared in detail to the normal limb. The degree of deformity can therefore be easily assessed, as well as the degree of angulation of the affected limb. This is of special interest when planning surgical treatment. Primary bone tumours can appear as lesions with various degrees of osteolysis and osteoproliferation. The zone of transition between the lesion and normal bone is usually wide and poorly defined, and the periosteal reaction of spiculated, sunburst or amorphous type. For years, tumours were thought to have a characteristic periosteal reaction that was called Codman triangle (fig. 4.41), and corresponds to a small triangular bone area located at the edge of the lesion. Today, it is known that it is formed when the periosteum gets broken and lifted “for

any reason” and, although it is generally considered suggestive of malignancies, it can also be associated to subperiosteal haematoma and inflammatory processes. Primary tumours do not normally “cross” the joint and extend to adjacent bone. They can be the cause for secondary pathological fractures. As lung metastases are frequent, it is advised to always perform a radiological thoracic study when these types of bone lesions are observed. Bone metastases usually appear as multiple aggressive lesions (fig 4.42). Multiple myeloma results from neoplastic proliferation of bone marrow plasma cells. It produces multiple focal lesions that affect long bones, ribs and vertebrae at the same time (see Chapter 5). Malignant soft-tissue tumours adjacent to the bone may secondarily affect nearby bone structures. In these cases, the typical radiological finding is marked tumefaction of soft tissues together with osteolytic, rather than osteo-proliferative changes in the adjacent bone (it may affect several bones depending on the primary tumour extension) (fig. 4.43). Subungual squamous cell carcinoma is a typical example of a malignant tumour of soft tissues usually affecting adjacent bones (fig. 4.44), which appears more frequently in large breed dogs with black coat.

The distal part of the ulna and the radius seems deformed. Osteomyelitis It is usually a sequela of surgical fracture repair (fig. 4.45), although it can also appear in open fractures. Sometimes the infection is produced haematogenously. In the acute phase, aggressive periosteal reaction is observed, with some degree of cortical and trabecular osteolysis and inflammation of the adjacent soft tissues. In chronic phases, bone may proliferate around the lesion. A complication of osteomyelitis is the formation of sequestra (fig. 4.46), which are defined as avascular bone fragments that are isolated from the main bone and enclosed in a radiolucent area. Radiotranslucency of the bone surrounding the fragment is due to necrosis. This area is delimited by a peripheral sclerotic margin, referred to as involucrum. The appearance of sequestra is more common after the use of external fixation devices (fig. 4.46). In practice, it is not possible to safely differentiate osteomyelitis from a bone neoplasm only by radiological imaging. A biopsy is always required to confirm diagnosis.

The lesion was identified after removal of the osteosynthesis material. Nutritional and metabolic alterations Balanced bone production and resorption is maintained in healthy adults. Numerous factors play a role to control this equilibrium, mainly the level of some hormones such as the parathyroid hormone and calcitonin (both are produced in the parathyroid gland), growth hormone, glucocorticoids and vitamin A, among others. Bone is a living tissue that can reflect metabolic alterations and nutritional imbalances, that sometimes lead to increased bone production, although they more frequently cause increased resorption with subsequent bone density loss. Density changes in bone can be detected by conventional radiography but not at an early stage. In order to be evident on a radiograph, 30–50 % of bone calcium should be lost to reduce its opacity. Bone densitometry, a more sensitive and precise technique, is used in human medicine to evaluate changes in bone density. Secondary nutritional hyperparathyroidism It is also called nutritional osteodystrophy. It usually affects growing animals, especially cats, that feed on a low-calcium diet, or with an inappropriate calcium/phosphorus ratio (e.g. when they feed exclusively on meat, with a high phosphorus and low calcium content). Hypocalcaemia stimulates parathyroid hormone production. Radiographic signs are (fig. 4.47): Decreased bone radiopacity. Thinning of long bone cortex. A double cortical line caused by resorption of intracortical bone may be observed (rare). Secondary pathological fractures may be observed.

Deformed bone limbs due to old pathologic fractures may be observed. Pelvic and vertebral deformity can appear. Fast calcification of bone structures after introducing a balanced diet. Secondary renal hyperparathyroidism It appears in animals with chronic renal failure. The reduction in the degree of glomerular filtration causes retention of phosphorus, which reduces calcium levels in blood. This stimulates the production of parathyroid hormone. It usually appears in older dogs, but it can also be detected in young patients with renal dysplasia. The radiographic findings in long bones are similar to those described in secondary nutritional hyperparathyroidism, but the most significant bone changes usually affect the skull (see Chapter 6). Hypophyseal dwarfism It mostly affects the German Shepherd and it is caused by abnormal growth hormone production (sometimes also with hypothyroidism). Unlike other metabolic or hereditary diseases also causing dwarfism, it causes proportional dwarfism. Radiographic signs are: Delayed calcification of the epiphyseal ossification centres. Delayed closure of growth lines. Incomplete epiphysis ossification when the skeletal maturation of the animal concludes. Hypervitaminosis A This disease affects cats that ingest excessive amount of vitamin A (usually in liver-based diets). Clinically these animals have spine stiffness, lameness and pain when the neck is being handled. In young animals, delayed development may occur. Radiographic signs are: Irregular bone growths in long bone metaphyses and around the joints (fig. 4.48).
Exostosis in vertebrae, usually cervical and thoracic, sometimes causing the spinous processes to fuse. It is important not to mistake the radiographic image for a neoplasm.

Joint disease Joints are the regions of the locomotor system where movement takes place. Apart from this dynamic function, they are responsible for the skeleton functioning as an elastic set, and therefore, better prepared to bear pressure and stretching than a rigid block. The bones that integrate joints should keep interrelated in order to fulfil these functions. Radiographic signs of joint disease Numerous radiographic signs can be pinpointed on an X-ray that are indicative of joint disease as described below. Increased synovial volume The appearance of this sign is usually due to an increase in synovial fluid (synovial effusion), although this cannot be differentiated from the joint capsule, synovial membrane or articular cartilage on an X-ray as they are all of fluid/soft tissue density. The joint in which increased synovial volume can most reliably be evaluated is the knee thanks to the anatomical landmark, the infrapatellar fat pad. This is located between the patellar ligament and the synovial components of fluid/soft tissue opacity in the joint, so a narrowing of its silhouette in the mediolateral projection is indicative of increased volume of synovial fluid and/or synovial soft tissues (fig. 4.49). Altered thickness of the joint space An actual increase in joint space width is usually due to an increase in the volume of the fluid/soft tissue opacity components of the joint (fig.

4.50), while a reduction in joint space usually appears in the advanced stages of degenerative joint disease. However, it is important to note that the radiographic assessment of joint space width is generally not very precise as it can vary significantly with patient positioning and depending on the fixation methods used. FIGURE 4.48. Mediolateral radiograph of the knee of a cat with hypervitaminosis A. The cat has a localised osteo-proliferative lesion on the cranial aspect of the

joint. In these cases, similar lesions can be observed in long bone metaphyses and vertebrae. FIGURE 4.49. Mediolateral radiographs of the knee of a dog with signs of increased synovial volume. The narrowing of the silhouette of the infrapatellar fat (G) is a fairly reliable indicator of this increase in volume, which is usually due mainly to synovial effusion.

Decreased subchondral bone opacity The subchondral bone is located adjacent to the articular cartilage. Any pathology that causes the articular cartilage to erode can, secondarily, affect the integrity of the subchondral bone. When eroded, it shows radiolucent areas, which are called subchondral defects (fig. 4.51). These can appear in cases of severe or chronic degenerative joint processes and are also very typical in cases of inflammatory or infectious joint processes (inflammatory and infectious arthritis). Subchondral defects with rounded, well-defined morphology are described as subchondral cysts. Increased subchondral bone opacity The increased opacity of the subchondral bone is called subchondral sclerosis. This finding is usually associated with degenerative joint disease and usually occurs as a result of bone remodelling on the joint surface, caused by the degenerative process (fig. 4.52). Osteophytes and enthesophytes Osteophytes are defined as small new bone formations, which develop at the joint margin (periarticular osteophytes) or adjacent to the joint margin (extra-articular osteophytes). Periarticular osteophytes are the most characteristic finding in degenerative joint disease (fig. 4.53). Enthesophytes are distinguished from osteophytes only by their location, since they appear at the point of insertion of a ligament (fig. 4.54), tendon or joint capsule to the bone. On radiographs, they are often indistinguishable from osteophytes.

FIGURE 4.50. Standard mediolateral (a) and forced flexion mediolateral (b) projections of both scapulohumeral joints of a dog with increased left shoulder joint space width. It is important to be cautious when assessing joint space width, as the image can be significantly influenced by patient positioning and the degree of traction applied when taking the radiographs.
FIGURE 4.51. Mediolateral projection of the knee of a dog with severe degenerative joint disease. The arrow points to subchondral defects.

Soft tissue calcification Calcification or mineralisation of intra-articular or periarticular soft tissues is a common finding in joint pathology. In the intra-articular components it may be due to calcification of the synovial capsule or synovial membrane (fig. 4.55). In some cases, especially in cats, meniscus calcification may be the cause (fig. 4.56). These findings are generally indicative of degenerative joint disease, although meniscus calcification in cats may be incidental. The appearance of calcification foci associated with various types of tendinopathy is also common. The presence of very numerous and large areas of periarticular calcification may be due to what is called synovial chondrometaplasia or osteochondromatosis, which may be primary or secondary to an underlying pathology. It usually appears on the hip (fig. 4.57), knee, tarsus or shoulder.

Intra-articular bodies (arthroliths) Intra-articular loose bodies (arthroliths), more colloquially referred to as joint mice, are small fragments of bone that move around the intra- or peri-articular area (fig. 4.58). They usually come from the joint or peri- articular bone, although they may also correspond to osteochondral components from injured joint surfaces or small synovial osteochondromas.

Joint incongruence The lack of congruence between the surfaces of the bones that form a particular joint is a clear sign of joint disease. A typical example is hip dysplasia, in which the articular surfaces of the acetabulum and femoral head are incongruent to a greater or lesser extent, depending on the degree of coxofemoral joint laxity (fig. 4.59). Joint malformation A morphological abnormality of the bone components of the joint is an obvious sign of joint pathology that can be easily diagnosed by X-ray (fig. 4.60). Intra-articular gas Intra-articular gas is most commonly associated with iatrogenic causes, following joint puncture, arthroscopy or arthrotomy, although it may also be associated with penetrating trauma or anaerobic joint infection. The so-called “vacuum phenomenon” has also been described, in which intra-articular nitrogen gas accumulates spontaneously due to the negative pressure exerted by traction of the joint during radiographic positioning. It has been observed in dogs and cats when excessive distraction of the coxofemoral joint is applied, and it has also been described in 20 % of shoulder radiographs in dogs with osteochondritis dissecans of the humeral head. This sign is best appreciated on computed tomography scans.

Ligament injuries In general, ligaments cannot be identified on X-rays because they have fluid/soft tissue density and, therefore, are indistinguishable from other joint components of similar radiopacity. The only exception is the patellar ligament of the knee, which is surrounded cranially by subcutaneous fat and caudally by infrapatellar fat, allowing its identification on the image. When instability is observed in the orthopaedic examination of a joint, this would suggest the existence of some ligament injury, that is, a sprain. In these cases, X-rays in forced or stress projections are

required, which must always be performed with patient under sedation. Some projections can be carried out without the operator in the room, using mechanical clamping (fig. 4.61), while others require the operator to be present. Lead gloves or mittens must be worn (fig. 4.62). Exposure to the main beam must be avoided whenever possible as the most energetic X-rays get through the leaded protection layer and irradiate the hands. When hyperextension, hyperflexion, valgus lateralisation or varus lateralization movements are forced, straps can be used to avoid hand exposure to the main X-ray beam. However, when radiographs are made with rotation of the joint, this movement cannot be performed with accessories so must be carried out by the operator. Sprains are classified clinically as grade I (mild), grade II (moderate) and grade III (severe). Table 4.3 summarises the most common radiographic findings according to the sprain grade. These findings should always be correlated with orthopaedic examination. In these patients it is very important to compare the image of the injured limb with the contralateral limb and forced or stressed projections should always be performed (fig. 4.63).

FIGURE 4.61. Patient positions for forced or stress projections of the carpus using straps as positioning accessories: forced flexion (a), forced extension (b) and valgus lateralisation (c). The most common ligament lesion in clinical practice is the cranial cruciate ligament rupture in the knee. Although cranial tibial displacement or subluxation with respect to the femur is described as the typical radiographic sign of this pathology (fig. 4.64), in order to visualise this displacement on an X-ray a mediolateral projection forcing the displacement of the tibia is usually required and this often implies operator exposure. In practice, it is not necessary to perform a forced projection if the “cranial drawer sign” is evident in the orthopaedic examination. In a standard mediolateral projection in neutral position, we would rarely observe tibial subluxation. Radiological imaging of this joint would, however, allow us to assess whether signs of secondary degenerative joint disease have already developed at the time of diagnosis (fig. 4.65). Tendon lesions X-ray is usually not very useful for assessing diseases affecting tendons. Ultrasound, on the other hand, provides quite accurate diagnostic information but also requires extensive operator experience and very precise knowledge of the ultrasound anatomy of the musculoskeletal system. A radiographic indicator of tendon pathology is the appearance of focal calcificated areas where the tendons are located, fundamentally at the insertion sites. For example, the appearance of mineralised areas immediately proximal to the greater trochanter of the femur, often bilaterally, is indicative of calcific tendinitis of the gluteus medius (fig. 4.66). Biceps and supraspinatus tendinopathies in the shoulder may present with focal calcification of these tendons. Small calcifications may go undetected in a radiological study and be identified on an ultrasound.

Sprain grade Radiographic signs Mild (Grade I) The only radiographic finding is usually an increase in soft tissue thickness at the ligament location, although this may not even be evident on the image. No associated bone lesions are observed.

Forced projections show no abnormalities of joint spaces. Modera te (Grade II) A moderate to marked increase in periarticular soft tissue thickness is generally seen. Associated bone lesions are rare. Abnormalities in joint spaces are usually not identified in neutral position projections but are identified in radiographs in forced projections. Severe (Grade III) A marked increase in periarticular soft tissue thickness is usually observed. It is common for associated bone lesions to appear, which in many cases are small avulsion fractures. Abnormalities in joint spaces are usually seen in both neutral and forced positions.
