The radiological image will suggest biceps tendinopathy when we observe areas of calcification at the location of this tendon, i.e. coinciding with the bicipital groove (fig. 4.67). Calcifications of this tendon may be confused with osteophytes located in the intertubercular groove of the humerus. The biceps tendon originates from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, so an irregularity in the margin of this tubercle may also be indicative of pathology of this tendon. The location of the supraspinatus tendon is more cranial, coinciding with the cranial part of the greater tubercle of the humerus. The appearance of mineralisations in this location further suggests supraspinatus tendinopathy (fig. 4.68). Tangential projections of the shoulder (fig. 4.69) may help distinguish them, since the location of the supraspinatus tendon is immediately cranial to the greater tubercle of the humerus, while that of the biceps is at the height of the sulcus intertubercularis and bicipital grooves. However, it is important to always correlate these radiographic findings with ultrasound examination of the joint. Achilles or calcaneus tendon lesions usually cause soft tissue tumefaction at the insertion point, that is, around the proximal margin of the calcaneus, which may also present an irregular margin as a result of the tendon injury (fig. 4.70). Sesamoids Sesamoids that appear in the appendicular skeleton of dogs and cats are summarised in Table 4.4 (figs. 4.71 and 4.72). When a sesamoid divided into several parts is visualised, it may correspond to a multipartite sesamoid (fig. 4.73), which is considered an incidental finding of no clinical significance, or it may be a sesamoid fracture (fig. 4.74). A syndrome called fragmented palmar metacarpophalangeal sesamoids has been described which generally affects large dog breeds, with a greater incidence in Rottweilers. The fragmentation can be caused by bone necrosis (osteonecrosis), which in turn may be caused by developmental disorders, trauma or degenerative changes. The 2nd and 7th sesamoids, corresponding to the 2nd and 4th digits respectively, tend to be more affected. In the case of the Rottweiler, it has been shown that this syndrome can cause lameness in puppies in a very high percentage of cases. The margins of fragments of a multipartite sesamoid are usually smooth and regular, while those of a

fragmented sesamoid usually have less defined or irregular edges, which would help differentiate them on an X-ray. FIGURE 4.66. Variation in the position of sesamoids may be incidental or have pathological causes. For example, it is very common for the medial sesamoid of the gastrocnemius muscle to appear in a more medial and distal position than the lateral sesamoid. If this finding is bilateral, it is more likely to be incidental, due to anatomical variation in the patient (fig. 4.75). If it is unilateral, although it may also be incidental, injury to the gastrocnemius muscle may not be ruled out as a cause of this variation in location. The most common example of sesamoid displacement is patella dislocation (luxation). Patellar luxation or subluxation may be of congenital or traumatic origin, with the former being much more

common. The cause of patellar luxation is considered to be associated with conformational deformities and to be multifactorial. The patellar extension mechanism is made up of the quadriceps muscles, patellar tendon, patella, patellar ligament and tibial tuberosity. This extension mechanism should form a straight line between the median plane of the proximal femur and the median plane of the tarsus. Most patients with patellar luxation have poor alignment of this extensor mechanism, which is considered a predisposing factor. Most dislocations are considered congenital because they occur in relatively young animals and are not associated with trauma. Although the patient may not have patellar dislocation at birth, it may well have some limb deformation that will cause this luxating at a later date. In these patients, the tibia appears curved medially. This alteration in the tibial conformation is believed to be compensatory, in other words, it was not always present, but this is not clear. In addition, the lack of pressure from the patella on the trochlear groove of the femur makes it appear more shallow or even flattened. FIGURE 4.74. Mediolateral (a) and craniocaudal (b) projections of the knee of a dog with old fragmentation of the lateral sesamoid of the gastrocnemius muscle.

FIGURE 4.75. Enlarged image of the knees in a ventrodorsal projection of the hip, in which the arrows point to both medial sesamoids of the gastrocnemius muscle, which appear displaced medially and distally. This finding is usually incidental, especially if it is bilateral. Medial dislocation of the patella is much more frequent than lateral. Approximately 75–80 % of knee dislocations occur medially (fig. 4.76). In general, patellar luxation is much more common in small or miniature dog breeds. In large breeds, in which this condition is much less common, lateral luxation is considered to be more frequent (fig. 4.77), although it appears that in recent years the diagnosis of medial luxation has increased significantly in large and giant breeds, especially in Labrador, Siberian Husky, Alaskan Malamute and Akita Inu. It has also been seen to occur concurrently with cranial cruciate ligament rupture in up to 20 % of cases. Clinically, patellar dislocation has been classified into four grades based on orthopaedic examination and not radiographic findings. In fact, when a patient is classified as grades 1 and 2, on the craniocaudal or caudal projection of the knee, the patella may appear in its normal position. Apart from the standard projections, in some cases a tangential projection of the knee will be necessary (fig. 4.78), which will allow a more precise evaluation especially of the flattening of the trochlear groove, in addition to the position of the patella (fig. 4.79).

Luxations and subluxations Luxations are the complete loss of the normal congruity between the joint surfaces of two bones (fig. 4.80). When there is still a certain amount of apposition between them, the term subluxation is used (fig. 4.81). Luxations and subluxations are relatively easy to diagnose radiologically, although they are sometimes not evident on one of the orthogonal views. They may be caused by trauma, although they can also have a congenital origin or appear secondarily to developmental abnormalities. The most frequent congenital luxations are those affecting the elbow (fig. 4.82) and the shoulder, although they can affect other joints. They cause marked remodelling of the articular surfaces by degeneration.

Degenerative joint disease The most common joint disease in dogs and cats is degenerative joint disease, also called osteoarthritis or arthritis. It can be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to other developmental or acquired diseases. Radiologically it is characterised by the appearance of increased volume of the joint fluid/soft tissue, formation of osteophytes and enthesophytes, increased or decreased subchondral bone opacity, appearance of intraarticular or periarticular soft tissue mineralisations (fig. 4.83) and, in advanced or severe cases, a decrease in the width of the joint space can be seen. It is, however, uncommon to observe the latter radiographic finding.

FIGURE 4.80. Mediolateral radiograph of the carpus of a dog with antebrachiocarpal joint luxation. FIGURE 4.81. Mediolateral (a) and craniocaudal (b) radiographs of the elbow of a dog with scapulohumeral subluxation. Infection Septic arthritis may appear as a consequence of penetrating wounds affecting the joint, although they are also spread haematogenously. In the latter, one or several joints may be affected. Although the image could be mistaken for severe arthritis, the increase in the volume of joint fluid/soft tissue is normally higher, the appearance of subchondral bone defects is more frequent and the periarticular osteophytes and enthesophytes tend to have a more aggressive appearance (fig. 4.84). Secondarily, infection can spread to the bone. The diagnosis is confirmed by cytology and joint fluid culture.

Immune-mediated polyarthropathy The term refers to the set of joint diseases with an immune-mediated origin. They are classified as erosive and non-erosive. It typically affects multiple joints, thus the term polyarthropathy. When inflammation of multiple joints is observed, haematogenous septic arthritis or immune-mediated polyarthropathy must be considered in the differential diagnosis. In non-erosive immune-mediated polyarthritis, an increase in joint fluid/soft tissue volume is usually observed on radiographs, with no apparent bone abnormalities. Erosive immune-mediated polyarthropathy is less frequent. In addition to the changes described in the non-erosive form, joint edge erosion is observed (fig. 4.85) and in many cases, aggressive periosteal reaction. The most common type of erosive polyarthropathy in the dog is rheumatoid arthritis. However, it is rare in dogs and cats. It usually affects the distal joints (mainly the carpus and tarsus, followed by metacarpus and metatarsus) of small and miniature breed dogs. In cats, the most striking radiographic finding is periosteal reaction and it has only been described in young male cats. Diagnosis is confirmed by the rheumatoid factor blood test, joint fluid analysis and synovial biopsy.

FIGURE 4.82. Mediolateral (a) and craniocaudal (b) radiographs of the radius and ulna of a dog with congenital luxation of the elbow. The proximal part of radius and ulna is very deformed and normal alignment between the humerus and the radial head is lost.

Osteophytes appear in the femoral trochlea, proximal and distal margins of the patella, sesamoids of the gastrocnemius and popliteus muscles, tibial plateau, medial margin of the medial epicondyles and lateral margin of the lateral epicondyles of femur and tibia, which are all typical locations of osteophytes appearing in this joint. In addition, intra- articular (white arrow) and peri-articular (black arrows) soft tissue mineralisations are identified. The mediolateral projection shows moderate narrowing of the infrapatellar fat pad (asterisk), which suggests the existence of moderate synovial effusion. Joint tumours Joint tumours are rare in dogs and very rare in cats. They most commonly affect medium or large dog breeds, and their most frequent location is the knee or elbow, although they can appear at any location. They usually cause a marked increase in volume of joint fluid/soft tissue, significant widening of the joint space due to soft tissue

proliferation and marked erosion of the joint margins and subchondral bone, with well-defined osteolysis areas (fig. 4.86). Other appendicular skeleton abnormalities Pulmonary hypertrophic osteopathy It is also called Marie’s disease, hypertrophic osteopathy or pulmonary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. This disease is usually associated with the presence of lesions in the thorax (generally masses), although it has also been described linked to abdominal diseases. It is clinically characterised by affecting older dogs, that present with hot and painful inflammation of the distal limb area, as well as lameness. The first affected bones are the phalanges. If the primary cause is resolved, it is a reversible process. Radiographic signs are (fig. 4.87):

Palisading periosteal reaction. Initial lesions tend to be distal and may affect the four limbs.

Lesions may be bilaterally symmetrical. Marked soft-tissue inflammation. To evaluate the presence of possible lesions in both anatomical regions, thoracic and abdominal radiographs should always be taken. Circumscribed calcinosis It presents as ectopic calcification foci in soft tissues, generally periarticularly located (fig. 4.88). It usually affects young large breed dogs, especially the German Shepherd. Multiple cartilaginous exostoses It is an benign osteoproliferative disease that appears in growing dogs. Exostoses in long bone metaphyses, vertebrae and ribs are evident on radiographs. It usually does not have clinical significance, unless the lesions cause excessive compression of certain anatomical structures such as the spinal cord, but this is rare. Lesions cease to grow when skeletal maturation of the animal concludes. Exceptionally, cases of affected adults and continued growth of the lesions after skeletal maturation have been described.

Spine 5 Normal radiographic anatomy of the spine https://goo.by/Gspgz Principles of interpretation Both dogs and cats have 7 cervical vertebrae, 13 thoracic vertebrae, 7 lumbar vertebrae, 3 sacral vertebrae and a variable number of coccygeal vertebrae. Each anatomical region of the spine has different characteristics, and it is necessary to know them in order to interpret radiographs correctly. These are described in the following boxes. Thoracic spine T11 is the anticlinal vertebra (its spinous process is vertical instead of being directed caudally or cranially). T10–T1 is the anticlinal1 intervertebral space, which is the narrowest intervertebral space. The heads of the ribs appear cranial to their corresponding vertebrae. Lumbar spine The cat’s lumbar vertebrae are longer than those of the dog. The ventral border of L3 and L4 can appear slightly blurry in

dogs, especially in large breeds, which is due to the crura of the diaphragm being superimposed (this image should not be confused with that of a lesion). Good-quality images are essential to carry out a thorough assessment of the spine. That is why it is recommended to take radiographs under sedation, using appropriate positioning accessories (radiolucent blocks, tape and sand bags). In lateral projection, the longitudinal axis of the spine has to be parallel to the cassette, which is achieved by placing a radiolucent block under the cervical area and another one under the lumbar area (fig. 5.1). To ensure that the sagittal plane of the vertebrae is parallel to the cassette, it is necessary to place blocks in order to slightly elevate the position of the limbs. If the spine is twisted when taking a lateral radiograph, the transverse processes of each vertebra will be separated in the image (fig. 5.2). Cervical spine C1 has a large transverse process (wings of the atlas). C2 is the largest vertebra and has a process in the cranioventral area of its body, called the odontoid process. The C2–C3 and C7–T1 intervertebral disc spaces are usually narrower than the rest. C6 has a large, characteristic ventral lamina. The spinous process of C2 must be adjacent to or superimposed on the arch of C1. Sacrum and coccygeal vertebrae The three vertebrae that form the sacrum are usually fused. Coccygeal vertebrae have haemal processes, which should not

be confused with spondylosis deformans. Lateral rotation of the spine should be avoided when taking a radiograph in ventrodorsal projection. If the position of the patient is correct, the spinous processes will be aligned and centred with the vertebral bodies in the image (fig. 5.3). A complete study of the spine should include two cervical radiographs (one centred on C3–C4 and another one on C6–C7), a thoracic radiograph (centred on T6–T7) and a thoracolumbar radiograph (centred on T13–L1). Usually, the previous clinical assessment of the patient allows the location of the region or regions of the spine that may be injured, which narrows the radiographic study down to the affected area. Spinal radiographs taken in forced flexion or extension may be useful for the diagnosis of certain diseases, such as atlantoaxial, cervical or lumbosacral in- stability. However, they should always be taken after standard radiographs in a neutral position. If these radiographs show an abnormal position of the vertebrae, radiographs in forced positions will not be recommended, since they can cause serious compressive lesions of the spinal cord. We should also always handle the patient very carefully when a fracture of luxation of the spine is suspected, since we could worsen the clinical picture.

In the first radiograph, it is not possible to assess the intervertebral disc spaces in an appropriate way, since the X-ray beam penetrates obliquely through them.

Enlarged images of the lumbar region of a dog, obtained in lateral projection, before (a) and after (b) placing a positioning block that slightly elevates the position of the limbs, so the sagittal plane of the vertebrae is parallel to the cassette. The perfect superimposition of the transverse processes of each vertebra (arrow) indicates that the radiograph was taken correctly. Myelography

Myelography is the contrast technique most frequently used to assess the spine (fig. 5.4). It is based on the introduction of a contrast medium in the subarachnoid space. As it involves certain risks, it should be carried out only when considered absolutely necessary, generally when the choice of surgical treatment depends on the results of this test. Magnetic resonance imaging is an excellent alternative. Myelograms must be performed under general anaesthesia. Before administering the contrast medium, it is necessary take plain radiographs with correct positioning. The contrast media of choice are low-osmolarity, nonionic iodinated contrast agents, such as iohexol or iopamidol, since they are less neurotoxic and remain longer in diagnostic concentrations in the subarachnoid space than other water-soluble agents. They are used at concentrations from 200 to 350 mg I/ml (the higher the concentration of iodine, the better defined the contrast columns will be in the images) and at doses of 0.3 ml/kg or 50 mg I/kg. The administered volume depends on the size of the animal and on the region that is going to be examined: Small dogs and cats (1–5 kg): 1.5–2 ml. Medium–size dogs (5–15 kg): 1.5–3 ml. Large dogs (15–35 kg): 3–5 ml. Giant breed dogs (+ 35 kg): 8–9 ml maximum. The contrast medium may be introduced in the cisterna magna or in the lumbar area. Spinal needles are used for this purpose (25-mm needles for cats and small dogs, 40-mm needles for medium-size dogs and 75–90-mm needles for large dogs) and maximum asepsis should be maintained when performing the injection.

FIGURE 5.3. Ventrodorsal radiograph of the lumbar spine in a dog. The centred position of the spinous processes with respect to the vertebral bodies indicates that the radiograph was taken correctly. FIGURE 5.4. Usual myelographic pattern of the cervical region in lateral projection (a), thoracolumbar region in lateral projection (b) and lumbar region in ventrodorsal projection (c). In order to perform a cisternal injection (cisternal myelography), the patient should be placed in lateral recumbency and its head bent at a 90º angle with respect to the neck. It is important to make sure this movement does not cause the obstruction of the airways. If the table can be inclined, it should be tilted 15º upwards approximately. Alternatively, radiolucent positioning blocks may be used to elevate the patient’s head and neck. The technique is described in the box below. It is recommended to allow an amount of cerebrospinal fluid similar to the volume of contrast medium that is going to be injected to flow out and analyse a sample. The injection of the contrast medium is performed slowly, in 2 to 3 minutes approximately. If the head has not

previously been elevated, it is indispensable to do it at that moment, to ensure that the contrast material flows caudally and does not leak into the cerebral ventricles. If resistance is felt when administering the contrast medium, the injection should be stopped and the needle withdrawn. Puncture technique for cisternal myelography In order to carry out the puncture, the depression between the external occipital protuberance and the dorsal lamina of the atlas should be palpated. The needle is inserted in the median line of this depression, at a slight angle in cranial direction and slowly moving forward. The bevel should be directed caudally. It is possible to feel some degree of resistance when going through the nuchal ligament. If the needle is positioned correctly, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) will flow out. If blood flows out together with CSF, it is usual to carry on with the procedure. However, if only blood flows out, the needle must be removed and the injection should be attempted again with a new needle. In case of piercing through the bone, the needle should be redirected. If there is a compression site, the contrast column may fail to pass beyond the lesion, in which case it is not possible to determine the real extension of the area of compression. In lumbar myelography, the contrast medium is injected in the subarachnoid space in the lumbar area. It is more difficult to perform and more traumatic, since the needle is inserted into the spinal cord. Two advantages of this technique are that the lumbar and thoracic areas are properly filled and that, in many cases, the contrast material can reach sites located cranial to an area of compression. The technique is described in the box below. Puncture technique for lumbar myelography

In order to carry out a lumbar myelogram, the animal is placed in sternal recumbency, with the spine arched. This is achieved by extending the hind limbs forward. The spinal needle is inserted in the L5-L6 disc space in dogs and in the L6-L7 disc space in cats. The needle is moved forward, going through the spinal cord, until reaching the floor of the canal. The bevel of the needle should be directed cranially. When reaching the floor of the canal, the needle is removed slightly and the introducer needle is withdrawn. If CSF flows out, this indicates that the needle has correctly been placed. If no CSF flows out, the position of the needle may be checked by taking a radiograph or by means of fluoroscopy. An additional check can be made by introducing a small amount of contrast and examining its position in a radiographic image. Attempting to enter in the dorsal subarachnoid space without going through the spinal cord is possible, by frequently removing the introducer needle to check if CSF flows out, but this is not easy. The injection of a contrast medium in the spinal cord may be lethal (severe paresis or paralysis in lumbar injections cranial to L4–L5, or death of the animal in cisternal injections). If the contrast medium is injected in the epidural space, the contrast columns will be very irregular and difficult to analyse. Although it would be recommended to inject the contrast agent as close as possible to the area where the lesion is suspected to be located, the simplest and safest technique is cisternal myelography, with which the area of most lesions can be determined. Lumbar myelography is usually reserved for the defining of the caudal margin of lesions that have been delimited cranially with a cisternal myelogram. The subarachnoid space is larger in the cisterna magna. The spinal cord has a larger diameter in the cervical–thoracic region and in the central area of the lumbar region. The ventral column often appears slightly elevated at the intervertebral disc spaces, which should not be confused with spinal cord compression. It should be borne in mind that the contrast medium is progressively absorbed, and will therefore no longer be evident in the

image after approximately 50 minutes. An extradural lesion causes the contrast column to be elevated or displaced at the site of compression. This is accompanied by a narrowing of the opposite column (fig. 5.5). This type of lesions includes herniated discs, thickening of the dorsal longitudinal ligament, thickening of the ligamentum flavum, haematomas, epidural fat deposits, deformations of the vertebral body, luxations, vertebral subluxations and fractures, cervical or lumboscral spondylopathy and abscesses, granulomas and extradural tumours. An intradural–extramedullary lesion causes focal enlargement of the subarachnoid space (fig. 5.6). This type of lesions includes intradural tumours (e.g. neurofibroma, meningioma), as well as haemorrhages, oedema or intradural granulomas. FIGURE 5.5. Myelographic pattern of an extradural lesion.

FIGURE 5.6. Myelographic pattern of an intradural-extramedullary lesion. The contrast medium surrounds the lesion located in the subarachnoid space. An intramedullary lesion causes divergence of the contrast columns at the site of the lesion (fig. 5.7). There may be an interruption of the contrast column at the site of the lesion, cranial to the lesion in a cisternal myelogram, or caudal to the lesion in a lumbar myelogram. This type of lesions includes intramedullary tumours (e.g. ependymoma, astrocytoma), intramedullary haemorrhage or oedema, hydromyelia, syringomyelia and granulomatous meningoencepahlitis. Other contrast techniques may be used to examine the spine instead of myelography, but their application is much more limited. Epidurography involves introducing the contrast medium (intentionally, not by mistake) in the epidural space, generally at the sacrococcygeal junction. It has been recommended for the detection of lesions in the cauda equina. The interpretation of the results of this technique is often difficult. Discography involves introducing a contrast medium in the intervertebral disc space, but is hardly used in cats and dogs. Computed tomography offers excellent images of the bones that form the spine, but it is not as good as magnetic resonance imaging for the definition of its soft tissues. Congenital disorders

Hemivertebra It is due to an incomplete development of the vertebral body. It may affect one or several vertebrae. Hemivertebrae may have a butterfly shape on ventrodorsal radiographs (fig. 5.8) or a “wedge” shape on lateral or ventrodorsal radiographs (fig. 5.9). Compensatory morphological changes in the adjacent vertebrae can usually be observed. FIGURE 5.7. Myelographic pattern of an intramedullary lesion. The width of the contrast columns decreases around the spinal cord lesion. An enlargement of the dorsal contrast column, cranial to the site of the lesion, can be observed.
FIGURE 5.8. Ventrodorsal radiograph of the thoracic spine of a Bulldog with several “butterfly” vertebrae (arrows).

FIGURE 5.9. Lateral radiograph of the thoracic spine of a dog with several “wedge” vertebrae (arrows). Hemivertebrae generally appear in the thoracic spine and are often associated with kyphosis and, to a lesser extent, lordosis or scoliosis. Block vertebra Two or more adjacent vertebral bodies appear partially or totally fused, with no intervertebral disc (fig. 5.10). The intervertebral space may be visualised as a thin radiolucent line or may not be visible at all if fusion is complete. Generally, this is not clinically significant, although some authors suggest that it may increase the risk of disc disease in adjacent intervertebral spaces. Transitional vertebra This occurs when the vertebrae of the atlantoaxial, cervical–thoracic, thoracolumbar, lumbosacral or sacroccygeal junction have morphological characteristics of the vertebrae of both regions (they totally or partially have the shape of the previous or next vertebra): Lumbarisation: the S1 vertebra appears separated from the rest of the sacrum, and may have one or two transverse processes, similar to those of the lumbar vertebrae. Sacralisation: the transverse process of L7 is fused with the wing of

the sacrum and may articulate with the ilium. This alteration may cause lumbosacral instability and degeneration of the intervertebral disc (fig. 5.12), leading to cauda equina syndrome. It may also make the correct positioning of the animal more difficult when taking a ventrodorsal radiograph of the hip. Partial or complete fusion of S3 with Cc1. A transitional T13 vertebra may have a transverse process instead of the rib (fig. 5.13). Vestigial ribs may be observed, and appear as structures with mineral density in soft tissues. This variation is relatively frequent. Therefore, when planning a spine surgery, it is recommended to always take radiographs in the two projections, since an image in lateral projection could lead to an error when locating the exact vertebra or intervertebral disc space. A transitional L1 vertebra may have one or two ribs instead of a transverse process. A transitional C7 vertebra may have ribs instead of a transverse process. Occipitalisation of the atlas.

Lateral (a) and ventrodorsal (b) views of the lumbosacral area of the spine of a dog with lumbarisation of the sacrum. On the lateral view, a radiolucent line (white arrow) can be seen, which separates the S1 vertebra from the rest of the sacrum. On the ventrodorsal view, a transverse process (black arrow) can be identified on S1. Spondylosis at L7–S1 can be observed on both radiographs.

Morphological changes may be unilateral or bilateral and, except for those affecting the lumbosacral junction, they do not usually have any clinical significance. Spina bifida It is a very uncommon anomaly. It is due to a failure in the closure of the neural arch and may affect one or more vertebrae. It can be associated with a protrusion of the meninges through the defect. It is best viewed on ventrodorsal radiographs. If there is a failure in the fusion of the spinous processes, the image will show a double spinous process in the affected vertebrae. In mild cases, the patient may not display any clinical signs. Instability syndromes They are associated with congenital anomalies that may worsen with growth, or with acquired lesions secondary to instability. They affect three anatomical regions: atlantoaxial, cervical and lumbosacral. Atlantoaxial instability Atlantoaxial instability or subluxation usually appears as a congenital anomaly in small and miniature breeds, such as Yorkshire Terriers, Chihuahuas, Pomeranians or Poodles. It may be due to agenesis or hypoplasia of the odontoid process, to a lack of fusion of this process with the axis, or to a stretching or rupture of the ligament holding it. It may also have an acquired origin in any breed, due to trauma that fractured the apophysis or caused injury to the ligament. On lateral radiographs, an increase in the distance between the dorsal arch of the atlas and the spinous process of the axis can be observed, accompanied by an angulation of the floor of the spinal canal at the atlantoaxial junction (fig. 5.14). Odontoid aplasia, hypoplasia or dorsal articulation with the axis may sometimes be identified. When this condition is suspected, the patient should be

carefully positioned. Slightly bending the animal’s neck can help identify these findings, although there is a risk of worsening the patient’s clinical picture. Flexed positions should not be attempted if the patient has tetraparesis. The ventrodorsal projection is generally unhelpful for diagnosis and might exacerbate the patient’s clinical condition in the presence of spinal cord compression. Some authors suggest using an oblique ventrodorsal projection to enhance the visualisation of the odontoid process. Although the diagnosis is usually made by radiography, computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging may provide additional diagnostic information useful for surgical planning. Cervical instability It is also called Wobbler disease, cervical spondylopathy, caudal cervical spondylomyelopathy, cervical vertebral malformation or cervical stenotic myelopathy. It is a developmental abnormality affecting young or middle-aged dogs, especially large breeds. It encompasses a series of alterations that manifest differently in each patient, including vertebral subluxation and malformation, deformation of joint apophyses, disc protrusion, and compensatory ligament hypertrophy. These changes culminate in the compression of the cervical spinal cord within the affected intervertebral spaces. It particularly affects Great Dane and Doberman breeds, and to a lesser extent Basset Hound, although it has also been described in other breeds. The affected animals present with progressive discoordination of the hind limbs and, on occasions, of the forelimbs. The symptoms usually appear between 3 to 10 months of age, although they may also appear at a later age, especially in the Doberman breed. The C2–C4 location is more common in the Basset Hound, C3–C7 in young and C4–C7 in older Great Dane dogs, while in young and middle-aged Doberman the segment usually affected is C5–C7.

The general radiographic signs that may be observed are: Alteration in the shape of the affected vertebra or vertebrae. Narrowing of the cranial part of the affected vertebra or vertebrae, which gives the spinal canal the aspect of a “funnel” or triangle. The cranial articular processes may appear deformed or be absent. If there is subluxation (fig 5.15), lateral images obtained with the neck flexed will show the cranial end of the affected vertebra protruding dorsally towards the spinal canal. It should be taken into account that, when the neck is flexed, the cranial end of the vertebrae is always raised to some degree, which should not be confused with a pathological subluxation. The intervertebral disc space cranial to the affected vertebra may be enlarged and the affected discs may be calcified. There may be new bone formation and sclerosis of the end-plates of the vertebral bodies. The myelogram may show spinal cord compression. This should not be confused with the normal image obtained with the neck flexed, in which a certain degree of elevation of the contrast column is observed in the areas located on the intervertebral disc spaces. Ventral compression indicates a prolapsed disc or hypertrophy of the dorsal longitudinal ligament, while dorsal compression indicates hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum. Taking radiographs in flexion, extension or with cervical traction can reveal subluxations undetected in a neutral position. These lesions are termed dynamic lesions. In the case of adynamic lesions, there are no differences with the image obtained in neutral position. These neck movements should be performed with care, especially

the forced flexion and extension, as they can aggravate the patient’s clinical picture. Traction is also useful and poses less risk. Although radiological findings may be sufficient to establish the diagnosis, advanced imaging tests (computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging) are necessary to establish the exact location and severity of the spinal cord compression causing the clinical symptoms. Lumbosacral instability Lumbosacral instability is also called lumbosacral stenosis or lumbosacral malarticulation. Cauda equine syndrome is a broader term, which applies to numerous degenerative, inflammatory, traumatic or neoplastic disorders that affect the lumbosacral junction causing pain and neurological dysfunction in the hind limbs. The most common causes are degenerative, including degenerative disc disease at L7–S1 and bone remodelling causing spinal canal or foraminal stenosis at L7–S1. However, fractures, discospondylitis, osteochondrosis and neoplasms in lumbosacral locations may also cause the clinical signs that are included under cauda equina syndrome. The radiographic findings most commonly identified with lumbosacral instability or stenosis are the associated degenerative changes, particularly spondylosis deformans and sclerosis of the caudal end of L7 and cranial end of the sacrum (fig. 5.16). The intervertebral space may be narrower or collapsed. It is sometimes possible to identify a reduction of the spinal canal dorsoventral diameter at the level of L7 or of the sacrum, or a ventral displacement of the sacrum relative to the position of L7 (fig. 5.17). This latter finding may be constant or inconstant, and may appear alone, or become more noticeable when a radiograph is taken in hyperflexion or hyperextension. There is no direct correlation between the clinical signs and the radiological findings. In fact, some patients with symptoms show a normal image of the lumbosacral junction on plain radiographs while many patients with radiographic evidence of L7-S1 spondylosis do not present with any clinical signs. Myelography, epidurography or discography may help with the diagnosis, although computed

tomography and, above all, magnetic resonance imaging are the most appropriate techniques to evaluate this disease (fig. 5.18). Degenerative intervertebral disc disease Each disc is formed by an annulus fibrosus (fibrous ring) and a nucleus pulposus. This latter is composed of a homogeneous gelatinous material. The annulus fibrosus is much thicker in its ventral part than in its dorsal part (this is why ventral protrusions are rare, and would not affect the spinal cord in any case). Discs are covered dorsally by the longitudinal ligament, which runs through the floor of the spinal canal. This ligament is reinforced by other ligaments in the area between T1 and T10, so herniated discs in this area are rare. FIGURE 5.15. Lateral radiograph of the cervical spine of a Great Dane with Wobbler disease. The C6 vertebra is subluxated, which causes a marked narrowing of the spinal canal in this area.

FIGURE 5.16. Lateral radiograph of the lumbosacral area of the spine of a dog with spondylosis deformans at L7–S1 and sclerosis of the caudal end of L7 and of the cranial end of the sacrum. These findings of a degenerative nature are suggestive of lumbosacral instability.

FIGURE 5.17. These findings indicate lumbosacral instability. The most appropriate projection to examine intervertebral disc spaces (IVDS) is the lateral one. Radiolucent positioning blocks or wedges should be placed under the cervical and lumbar spine in an attempt to align the spine parallel (not curved) to the cassette. The obliquity of the peripheral X-rays of the beam makes it necessary to centre the radiograph appropriately on the IVDS where a lesion is suspected (fig. 5.19). On each radiograph, it is only possible to assess the centred IVDS and the spaces immediately cranial and caudal to it. If the area that we are going to examine is wider, several radiographs should be taken, centring the images on different sites.

FIGURE 5.18. Magnetic resonance images in sagittal and transverse plane of the L7–S1 disc in a dog with lumbosacral instability. The images show degenerative changes and protrusion of the disc, which causes a compression of the cauda equina.

FIGURE 5.19. Representation of the direction of entry of the X-ray beam through the intervertebral spaces. Since the X-ray beam is divergent, only the central rays of the beam are aligned with the intervertebral disc space on the radiograph. The entrance direction of X-rays into other intervertebral spaces will be more oblique the farther away the spaces are from the center of the beam. The IVDS at the cervicothoracic junction and at the lumbosacral junction are slightly narrower than the others. The IVDS located between T10 and T11 may also be slightly narrower in normal conditions. If no radiolucent positioning blocks are placed under the cervical or lumbar spine, the width of the IVDS may appear falsely reduced, due to the curvature of the spine. Disc degeneration is a phenomenon related with age. Problems occur when the degeneration process is faster than usual. Two types of degeneration are distinguished: Hansen type I: it is generally observed in chondrodystrophic breeds, in which a degeneration of the nucleus pulposus at early ages is frequently observed (many animals have calcified discs, with no clinical significance). With time, the annulus fibrosus also degenerates, which can cause its rupture and subsequent bulging out of the nucleus pulposus into the spinal canal, which is called extrusion of the disc material. Hansen type II: more common in non-chondrodystrophic breeds, in which degenerative changes occur more slowly, and rarely cause calcification. A protrusion of the disc (with no rupture of the annulus fibrosus) usually occurs. The disc moves to a greater or lesser extent towards the spinal canal and may cause different degrees of spinal cord compression. In cases of type I extrusion, clinical signs appear in an acute manner, with pain, neurological deficiency and paralysis. In cases of type II protrusion, the clinical picture is less dramatic, and progressive ataxia and neurological deficiency are usually observed. A variant of type I extrusion, described later, is that which occurs acutely from a non-degenerated disc. This variant is also known as

high-velocity low volume or type III disc extrusion. It is due to a rupture of the annulus caused by the exit of disc material of low volume, and presumably at high speed, towards the vertebral canal. Secondary spinal cord damage is caused by the impact and haemorrhage (spinal contusion). The radiological signs that may appear in degenerative intervertebral disc disease are: Disc calcification (more frequent in chondrodystrophic breeds). This finding alone is not diagnostic of disc prolapse, but does indicate its degeneration (fig. 5.20). Narrowing of the affected IVDS (fig. 5.21). Observation of calcified disc material in the spinal canal (fig 5.22). It is also sometimes possible to identify non-calcified disc material when this is located in the area of the intervertebral foramen. Appearance of a pattern of ventral or ventrolateral extradural lesion on the myelogram. FIGURE 5.20. Lateral radiograph of the cervical spine of a dog with calcification of the C5–C6 intervertebral disc (arrow). Calcification is a finding that indicates disc degeneration. The radiological signs should always correlate with the clinical symptoms, although the finding of spinal cord compression on the

myelogram is always significant. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging provide much more precise diagnostic information about this condition. An acute disc protrusion may produce a normal image in plain radiographs. Old lesions may not have any clinical significance, and may be accompanied by sclerosis of the end-plates of the adjacent vertebral bodies and spondylosis deformans (fig. 5.23). Other disorders of the spine Scoliosis, kyphosis and lordosis Scoliosis is defined as an abnormal curvature of the spine in lateral direction, and is therefore best visualised on ventrodorsal radiographs (fig. 5.24). Kyphosis is defined as an abnormal curvature of the spine in dorsal direction (fig. 5.25), while lordosis occurs in ventral direction (fig. 5.26). These are therefore best observed on lateral radiographs. FIGURE 5.21. Lateral radiograph of the lumbar spine of a dog with a narrowing of the L5–L6 intervertebral disc space (arrow), which indicates disc disease.

These disorders may be congenital, idiopathic or may appear associated with other diseases affecting the spine. As in people, the degree of kyphosis determines the likelihood that secondary neurological dysfunction may occur, usually due to progressive myelopathy as a result of spinal canal stenosis or spinal instability in the affected segment. Scoliosis, on the other hand, is not usually associated with significant neurological dysfunction. The degree of angulation of the spine in dogs with kyphosis can be quantified using the Cobb angle which is formed by the intersection of two lines: one parallel to the cranial margin of the vertebra immediately cranialward of the malformed vertebra and the second line parallel to the caudal margin of the vertebra immediately caudally to the malformed vertebra. This can be calculated more accurately with post-processing tools in digital radiography. If the patient has several non-contiguous affected vertebrae, the angle is measured for each of them. On the other hand, if several contiguous malformations appear, the angle is measured considering the vertebra with the most marked malformation (fig. 5.27). A Cobb angle greater than 35 ° has been associated with a high probability of the appearance of secondary neurological deficits. The angle may vary progressively in these animals, so monitoring in patients with measurements less than 35° may be useful for early detection of potential secondary neurological dysfunctions. Magnetic resonance imaging provides very precise information on the secondary involvement of the spinal cord and nerve roots in patients with vertebral malformations (fig. 5.28), while computed tomography allows the obtaining of 3D images with excellent anatomical detail, especially of the bone components of the affected segment. These 3D images can also be used to print 3D anatomical models, which can be invaluable in surgical planning for patients requiring surgery. Spondylosis deformans It is a degenerative alteration, characterised by the development of bony growths in the ventral area of the cranial and/or caudal end- plates of the vertebral bodies (fig. 5.29). These growths are considered enthesophytes that form on the vertebral epiphysis. Over

time they tend to increase in size and even to fuse with adjacent vertebrae, forming bony bridges (fig. 5.30). They can also grow on the lateral surface of the end-plates of the vertebral bodies, although this is less common (fig. 5.31). When growth occurs laterally, it rarely causes compression at the exit of the nerve roots, except in the case of lumbosacral instability, where the impingement of the roots is caused by narrowing of the foramen caused by the dorsal extension of the enthesophytes. Dural ossification It is characterised by the formation of bony plaques in the dura mater, which may be visible or not on a plain radiograph. When they are observed, they appear as thin lines of mineral density running parallel to the floor of the spinal canal (fig. 5.32). It is more common in large breed dogs. It is considered an incidental finding of degenerative origin. If it coincides with the presence of an extradural lesion, meningeal deviation can be seen if the lesion is compressing the spinal cord (“automyelogram”). Spondyloarthrosis The degenerative joint disease involving intervertebral joints is called spondyloarthrosis. It causes remodelling of the joint process margins, with osteophyte formation and, occasionally, joint space narrowing (fig. 5.33). It is observed more frequently in the lumbar region and occasionally, in the cervical region. It should not be confused with spondylosis deformans, even if both are of a degenerative origin. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis It is a rare idiopathic condition in dogs and very rare in cats. It mainly affects Boxers and Great Danes. It is characterised by the appearance of abundant new linear bone formations on the ventral and lateral surfaces of the spine (fig. 5.34), which causes ankylosis. It does not usually produce clinical signs apart from stiffness when walking, although it could be a predisposing factor for disc disease in the intervertebral spaces adjacent to the affected segment. The

image is similar to that of advanced spondylosis deformans, but at present they are considered to be different pathologic entities. It is diagnosed when at least four of the following X-ray findings occur at the same time in a patient: Formation of ventrolateral bony bridges in at least three contiguous vertebral bodies. Normal width of the intervertebral spaces in the affected segment with no obvious signs of disc degeneration (disc calcification or sclerosis of the end-plates of the vertebral bodies). Signs of spondyloarthrosis in the joints of the affected segment. Pseudoarthrosis of the spinous process. Appearance of enthesophytes in the axial and appendicular skeleton. Presence of osteophytes, sclerosis and ankylosis of sacroiliac unions. Ankylosis of the pubic symphysis. Inflammation and infection The inflammation of the vertebrae is called spondylitis, and may be accompanied or not by an infection. It usually causes new bone formation in the ventral area of the body of the affected vertebra or vertebrae (fig. 5.35). It is important to remember that the ventral margin of L3 and L4 may appear poorly defined due to the crura of the diaphragm being superimposed. This should not be confused with spondylitis. Vertebral infection is termed osteomyelitis or spondylopyosis. It is characterised by the appearance of an aggressive lesion, which may affect one or several vertebrae, with an osteolytic and osteoproliferative component (fig. 5.36). The infection may extend to the spinal canal, causing meningitis and myelitis. In many cases, it is related to the penetration of foreign bodies (e.g. grass awns), although it may also be associated with penetrating wounds or infections through the haematogenous route.

Vertebral physitis affects young dogs initially causing osteolysis of the physes of the affected vertebrae, with reduction in the size of the epiphyses. With progression, there is collapse of the cranial and caudal aspect of vertebral body and end-plate sclerosis. The most likely cause is a disseminated haematogenous infection. The term discospondylitis is used when an infectious process affects the intervertebral disc and the end-plate of the adjacent vertebral bodies. The infection may extend to the meninges and spinal cord. The radiograhic image varies according to the moment at which the diagnosis is carried out (fig. 5.37): In the early stages, it is possible to observe osteolysis and irregularity of the end-plates of the vertebral bodies adjacent to the affected disc or discs (fig. 5.38), which may cause a widening of the intervertebral disc space. Bone growths form on the ventral and lateral surfaces of the affected vertebrae, which is similar to spondylosis deformans. However, if they are secondary to discospondylitis, they tend to present greater extent and a more aggressive appearance. Over time, bone is produced in the areas where it had been destroyed, resulting in a narrowing of the intervertebral disc space (fig. 5.39). Sclerosis of the end-plates of the affected vertebral bodies is observed and the ventral new bone acquires a more regular and well-defined image (similar to that of spondylosis). Discospondylitis is often caused by the haematogenous spread of genitourinary infections, although it can also be associated with the presence of paraspinal abscesses or foreign body migration. It affects mostly middle-aged dogs and large breeds, and one or more intervertebral spaces may be involved (fig. 5.40). In the early stages of the infection, no obvious abnormalities may appear on the radiograph. A normal image of the vertebrae does not rule out early stage discospondylitis, which can be detected early with magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography and even ultrasound in young animals. A study of 10 dogs under 6 months of age indicated that the radiographic image of discospondylitis in these animals may differ

from that of adults in the initial phase of the process. In these puppies, the initial radiographic finding was a decrease in the width of the affected intervertebral space, with no evidence of osteolysis at this early stage, although it did appear later on follow-up radiographs with an osteolytic pattern similar to that of adults. Some of these animals also presented subluxation of the affected vertebrae at the time of diagnosis or during follow-up. FIGURE 5.27. Fractures and luxations They are generally caused by trauma, although they may also be secondary to other lesions (pathological fractures). The ease with which a vertebral fracture is identified on radiographs depends on the degree of displacement of the fragments (fig. 5.41). In cases of fractures by compression, the image shows an apparent loss of vertebral body height. If a vertebral fracture is suspected, the patient should be handled with extreme care. A lateral projection should be taken first, as positioning the patient in dorsal recumbency for a ventrodorsal projection poses an increased risk of aggravating possible spinal cord damage. When working with X-ray machine that allows the tube to be rotated to deliver the beam horizontally, the X- ray cassette can be positioned adjacent to the spine, perpendicular to the table, while the animal is in lateral recumbency. Emitting the beam horizontally, a ventrodorsal projection is obtained without moving the patient.

During a fracture recovery period, it must be taken into account that the bone callus can produce spinal cord compression. Fractures of spinous or transverse processes are not usually clinically significant (fig. 5.42). Complete luxations are easily identifiable on plain radiographs. The ease with which a vertebral subluxation is identified depends on the degree of displacement of the affected vertebrae (fig. 5.43). In normal conditions, the body of L4 may have a position that is slightly ventral to that of L3, which should not be confused with pathological subluxation. Both in spinal fractures and luxations, a vertebral displacement of more than 2/3 of the diameter of the spinal canal is considered a sign indicating severed spinal cord (fig 5.44). In patients with spinal trauma, computed tomography is considered superior to magnetic resonance imaging to determine the degree of bone injury, although magnetic resonance imaging offers more precise information on secondary spinal cord damage. Tumours Tumours in vertebrae are quite rare. The tumours that usually affect vertebrae are osteosarcomas, chondrosarcomas and mestastases of primary tumours of a different origin. While usually only a single vertebra is involved, it can sometimes spread to adjacent vertebrae in advanced stages. Lesions are usually predominantly osteolytic (fig. 5.45) or have a mixed osteolytic and osteo-proliferative pattern (fig. 5.46). Secondary pathological fractures can occur (fig. 5.47). Given the morphological complexity of the vertebrae, tumours are not usually identified on radiographs until the advanced stages of disease. The spine is a site of predilection for myelomas, which have a radiographic pattern that is characterised by the appearance of numerous small, round osteolytic areas (3–5 mm, although they can be larger in diameter when several lesions converge) in long bones and spine (fig. 5.48). Bone lymphoma may also present a multifocal pattern, with lesions that are predominantly osteolytic. Metastases usually appear as single or multiple aggressive bone lesions located in the spine and other bones. Bone metastases of

some pelvic tumours, especially prostate and transitional cell carcinomas, have a peculiar image, since they affect the surrounding bones (last lumbar vertebrae, sacrum and pelvis), causing lesions that are fundamentally proliferative (fig. 5.49). These lesions are sometimes detected before the primary tumour. Soft tissue tumours adjacent to the spine may also secondarily affect the vertebrae (e.g. post-vaccination sarcomas in cats, retroperitoneal tumours, etc.). They can involve several vertebrae adjacent to the tumour (fig. 5.50). Hypervitaminosis A It usually affects cats from 2 to 4 years old that ingest excessive amounts of liver. It is much less frequent in dogs. The excess of vitamin A causes the growth of subperiosteal bone. In young animals, an asymmetric longitudinal growth of the long bones occurs. In adults, bone exostoses develop essentially in the cervical and thoracic spine, ribs and around the limb joints, and can lead to ankylosis of these joints and of the vertebrae. Mucopolysaccharidosis Mucopolysaccharidosis can cause vertebral lesions in cats similar to those caused by hypervitaminosis A, as well as alterations in vertebral morphology and spondylosis deformans in young animals. Osteopetrosis Osteopetrosis, also known as myelofibrosis, is rare in cats and extremely rare in dogs. It causes generalised increased radiopacity of the skeleton, including the spine (fig. 5.51). It has been associated with feline leukaemia and lymphoma in cats and with pyruvate kinase deficiency in dogs. Other possible causes are excessive intake of dietary calcium, hypervitaminosis D and myelosclerotic neoplasia. Multiple cartilaginous exostoses It is an uncommon anomaly, which is characterised by osteo- proliferative benign lesions in the metaphyses of the long bones, ribs

and vertebrae of young dogs (fig. 5.52). The growth of the lesions generally stops when skeletal maturity is reached. It is not usually clinically significant, unless the lesions invade the spinal canal or the intervertebral foramina, causing compression of the spinal cord or nerve roots. Exceptionally, a late evolution to osteosarcoma or chondrosarcoma has been described. FIGURE 5.41. Images of various vertebral fractures.

Head 6 Normal radiographic anatomy of the head https://goo.by/BOjKw Principles of interpretation The head is an extremely complex anatomical region, formed by approximately 50 bones, numerous teeth and various soft tissues. Furthermore, its morphological characteristics vary greatly among species and, within the canine species, among different breeds. Three basic conformations of the skull have been described: Dolichocephalic: nasal area longer than the cranial cavity. Mesaticephalic: the nasal area has approximately the same length as the cranial cavity. Brachycephalic: nasal area shorter than the cranial cavity. Brachycephalic breeds have a series of anatomical features distinctive from other breeds, including a smaller size of the nasal cavity, the vomer bone may by slightly wavy in the dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections, smaller or absent frontal sinuses, common mandibular prognathism and variations in the dentition. In order to correctly interpret radiographs of the head, it is essential for the animal to be correctly positioned, since the radiological interpretation will often be based on the symmetrical image of the skull. Performing the radiological study under sedation or anaesthesia is recommended to obtain good-quality images. If an endotracheal tube is used, it will sometimes be necessary to remove it at the moment of taking the radiograph, so that it is not superimposed with the anatomical structures that are going to be assessed in the image. In some cases, it

will also be necessary to change the position of the tongue, especially when taking a ventrodorsal open-mouth radiograph. As it is an extremely complex anatomical region, comparing the images obtained with those that are included in atlases of normal radiographic anatomy is very useful. When the lesions affect only one side of the head, the contralateral half may also be used as reference for normality. A wide variety of projections may be used to assess the different clinically important regions of the head. The choice of projections will be made according to the region that is to be examined. Cranial vault: lateral and ventrodorsal projections. Nasal cavity and frontal sinuses: lateral, ventrodorsal open mouth (ventral 20º rostral-dorsocaudal) or dorsoventral intraoral (occlusal) and rostrocaudal tangential (also termed “skyline”) projections of the frontal sinuses. Mandible: lateral, dorsoventral, ventrodorsal intraoral and lateral oblique with open mouth (left 20º dorsal-right ventral to assess the right mandibular arcade and right 20º dorsal-left ventral to assess the left mandibular arcade). Maxilla: lateral, dorsoventral, dorsoventral intraoral and lateral oblique with open mouth (left 20º ventral-right dorsal to assess the right maxillary arcade and right 20º ventral-left-dorsal to assess the left maxillary arcade). Temporomandibular joint: dorsoventral and oblique lateral (with a 20 to 45º inclination of the rostral part of the head). Teeth: lateral oblique open mouth (those indicated above for the mandible and maxilla) and intraoral. Auditory apparatus: dorsoventral, lateral oblique, rostrocaudal with open mouth in dogs and rostral 10º ventral–caudodorsal in cats and brachycephalic dogs. In many cases it will be useful to take radiographs centred on the lesion, which will provide complementary information to that provided by standard projections.

Radiographs provide valuable information of the bone structure of the head, but are usually not very useful to assess soft tissues in this anatomical region. Ultrasonography may help to characterise lesions located in superficial soft tissues and is of great interest for the study of the eyeball and retrobulbar space. However, the diagnostic imaging techniques that offer more comprehensive diagnostic information about the head are computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. Both provide tomographic images of the patient (with no superimposition of structures) with excellent detail of intra- and extracranial anatomical structures. In general, magnetic resonances imaging is more appropriate to assess soft tissues, while computed tomography offers more detailed images of bone structures. Cranial vault Congenital hydrocephalus It is more common in miniature breeds such as Chihuahua, Pomeranian and Yorkshire Terrier, among others. It can be asymptomatic or present with various neurological disorders. The radiological signs that may be associated with this disease are excessive enlargement of the cranial vault, thinning of the bones that form it, persistence of the fontanelles in the adult animal and relatively homogeneous appearance of the intracranial content (fig. 6.1a and b). Ultrasound examination can be very useful to assess the degree of dilation of the ventricular system when the fontanelle is large enough to allow good transducer contact and ultrasound beam penetration (fig. 6.1c), although magnetic resonance imaging is the technique of choice to accurately assess this condition. Occipital dysplasia As with hydrocephalus, this congenital alteration also mainly affects miniature breeds and can have little clinical significance. Rostrodorsal– caudoventral radiographs are particularly useful for its radiological assessment. The main radiological sign is the abnormal dorsal enlargement of the foramen magnum, which acquires a “lock” shape (fig. 6.2). In some cases, this malformation appears associated with other abnormalities such as deformation of the C1 vertebra (shortened and

with prominent dorsal arch), hypoplasia of the occipital condyles or atlantoaxial subluxation. Computed tomography is the preferred advanced imaging technique for its evaluation. Occipital dysplasia is considered a normal morphological variation in brachycephalic breeds. Fractures Fractures located in the cranial vault are generally difficult to visualise on radiographs, since the displacement of the fragments is usually minimal (fig. 6.3). The areas of greater inflammation of the soft tissues are a useful guide and the patient should be positioned so that these areas are centred on the radiograph (fig. 6.4). Computed tomography is an excellent option to assess patients in which a skull fracture is suspected, since in addition to providing detailed information about bone structures, it also allows the evaluation of possible associated intracranial lesions. Infection Infections in the cranial vault are uncommon. They can present with an osteolytic pattern, an osteoproliferative pattern or a combination of both, similar to what is observed in other bone locations (fig. 6.5). Tumours Osteosarcomas are the bone tumours that most frequently appear in the cranial vault (fig. 6.6), followed by chondrosarcomas and multilobular osteochondrosarcomas. These tumours usually have a greater osteoproliferative than osteolytic component. Multilobular osteochondrosarcomas generally appears as well-defined masses, characterised by a pattern of granular ossification with minimal or no associated osteolysis. The most common location is the occipito– temporal region (fig. 6.7), although they have also been described in the orbit, maxilla, mandible, tympanic bulla, zygomatic arch and hard palate. Osteomas are less common and tend to be more sclerotic and delimited than osteosarcomas, and sometimes have a “cauliflower” shape (fig. 6.8).

As in other anatomical regions, aggressive soft-tissue neoplasms (e.g. squamous cell carcinomas, melanomas, fibrosarcomas, etc.) may also secondarily affect the bones of the skull (fig. 6.9). Nasal cavity and sinuses The complete radiological study of the nasal cavity and the sinuses must be carried out under sedation or anaesthesia and should include lateral, ventrodorsal open mouth with oblique orientation of the X-ray beam and rostrocaudal tangential (skyline) projections of the frontal sinuses. Standard dorsoventral and ventrodorsal projections offer very limited information due to the overlapping of the mandible with the rostral and lateral area of both nasal cavities. The main limitation of the lateral projection is that both nasal cavities and the two frontal sinuses overlap on the image. However, it is particularly useful when assessing the integrity of the dorsal nasal bone in patients with advanced-stage nasal neoplasms.

The ventrodorsal view performed with the mouth open and the X-ray beam at a 20º angle (ventral 20º rostral–caudodorsal) circumvents or minimises overlapping of the mandible with the nasal cavity. If it is not possible to tilt the X-ray tube, it will be technically more difficult to obtain this projection. A syringe case (or another object of low radiopacity) placed between the upper and lower canines can be used to keep the mouth open. It is important to remove the tongue and endotracheal tube from the radiographed area, as far as possible, to avoid overlapping with the region of interest. The rostrocaudal tangential view is taken by positioning the long axis of the patient’s head parallel to the direction of the X-ray beam, aligning the centre of the beam with the frontal sinuses. In this way, both sinuses can be visualised in the same image, avoiding their overlapping with each other, as happens in the standard lateral projection.

In radiographic images obtained in dorsoventral or ventrodorsal projection, the nasal cavity appears divided into two halves by the nasal septum, formed by the vomer bone and nasal cartilage. The nasal conchae appear as thin lines of mineral density in the rostral part of the cavity (dorsal and ventral nasal conchae) and as thicker swirls of mineral density in the caudal area of the cavity (ethmoid labyrinth or ethmoid conchae). The morphologic pattern of the nasal conchae is highly symmetrical in dogs but may be slightly asymmetrical in cats with no nasal pathology. In both dogs and cats, the paranasal sinuses include the frontal sinuses, the lateral maxillary sinuses or recesses and the small sphenoid sinuses. The frontal sinuses are the most clearly observed on radiographs and their morphology can vary greatly depending on the patient’s cranial conformation. They appear delimited by a bone wall and contain air. In dolichocephalic breeds, they may be very flattened which limits their evaluation in the tangential rostrocaudal projection, while in brachycephalic breeds, they may be smaller or absent. Fractures Fractures affecting the nasal bone (fig 6.10) or the frontal sinuses (fig. 6.11) may be difficult to diagnose. There is usually depression of the bone fragments, which is accompanied by inflammation of the adjacent soft tissues and, in many cases, subcutaneous emphysema as air escapes to the adjacent tissues.

Rhinitis Rhinitis secondary to bacterial infections and lymphoplasmatic rhinitis usually lead to increased radiographic density of the nasal cavity, accompanied or not by increased density of the frontal sinuses, although the nasal conchae are usually still well-differentiated in the image (fig. 6.12). In acute processes, there may not be any evident alterations of the cavity in the radiographic image. Hyperplastic chronic rhinitis may cause, together with an increase in the radiopacity of the cavity, a loss of differentiation of the nasal conchae due to a thickening of the mucosa and the presence of exudate between them (fig. 6.13). It is more difficult to assess the image of the nasal conchae in cats, since under normal conditions they have a more irregular pattern than in

dogs. It is important to bear this aspect in mind when assessing a possible case of feline chronic rhinitis, since it may cause a disorganisation or destruction of the conchae (fig. 6.14). Fungal rhinitis, especially when caused by Aspergillus, is a destructive or aggressive type rhinitis. It usually presents a mixed radiological pattern in which areas of osteolysis (where there is a loss of differentiation of the conchae) are combined with areas of increased focal opacity (fig. 6.15). In advanced stages of the disease, a deviation or erosion of the vomer bone may appear, as well as lysis of the bones adjacent to the nasal cavity, although these findings are more common in cases of nasal neoplasia than in fungal rhinitis. Foreign bodies Mineral or metallic density foreign bodies located in the nasal cavity are usually easy to identify on radiographs. However, those with a radiographic density similar to that of soft tissues and fluids (radiolucent foreign bodies), such as grass awns, sticks, small plastic objects, etc., usually cannot be visualised in the image, although in many cases the underlying signs of focal rhinitis are identified (fig. 6.16). Intranasal foreign bodies that remain in the cavity for a long time can cause atrophy of the conchae in the affected area, which could be

mistaken for osteolysis. FIGURE 6.16. Enlarged image of the nasal cavity on a ventrodorsal open-mouth radiograph of a dog with focal rhinitis due to penetration of a foreign body. The arrow points to an area of increased soft tissue opacity with a radiolucent centre, located in the middle third of the right nasal cavity, due to focal inflammatory changes

associated with the presence of the foreign body (grass awn, not identifiable in the image). Tumours In small animals, approximately two thirds of nasal tumours are carcinomas and the other third are sarcomas. Nasal lymphoma, which is more common in cats, has also been described. The radiographic image of a nasal neoplasm varies depending on the type of tumour and its stage of development (fig. 6.17). In the early phase, it can cause an increase in soft tissue opacity in the affected nasal cavity, which could be confused with the radiological changes caused by inflammatory rhinitis. As the disease progresses, the tumour may cause displacement or destruction of the nasal septum and osteolysis of the conchae and paranasal bones. In cats, the loss of teeth adjacent to the lesion is also common. Radiographic identification of osteolysis is more indicative of neoplasia than of aggressive rhinitis, but it can occur in both cases. It is usually not possible to establish a differential diagnosis based solely on radiographic findings. Nasal tumours sometimes cause osteolysis of the nasal bone which can spread to the superficial planes leading to the formation of an external soft-tissue mass which in turn can produce facial deformities (fig. 6.18). This is more typical in cases of tumours than in cases of rhinitis. Nasal neoplasms may also invade the cribriform plate and penetrate into the cranial cavity. They may thus affect the brain. The cribriform plate can be identified in the ventrodorsal and dorsoventral radiographs in the caudal area of the nasal cavity as a C or V shape. However, confirmation of possible erosion or destruction of the plate is usually difficult. This type of lesion can be evaluated more precisely with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging. Although extension of the tumour to the frontal sinus is also possible, the increase in density that is often observed in the ipsilateral sinus is usually due to the development of obstructive sinusitis, more than to a neoplastic invasion of the sinus (fig 6.19). Nasal lymphoma in cats may cause an increase in the radiographic density of the nasal cavity, accompanied or not by bone destruction (fig. 6.20).

Regarding advanced imaging diagnostic techniques, computed tomography should be selected to analyse the involvement of the bone structures with greater precision, while magnetic resonance imaging is more appropriate if the animal had neurological signs that would suggest a secondary spreading of the tumour to the brain through the cribriform plate. Tumours affecting the frontal sinuses are not uncommon; the most common is squamous cell carcinoma. They generally cause increased radiopacity in one or both frontal sinuses, which is often accompanied by lysis of the frontal bone as the process progresses. Extensive destruction and/or expansion of the frontal bone and invasion of other adjacent bones and soft tissues may be observed in more advanced stages (fig. 6.21). FIGURE 6.17. Mandible, maxilla and temporomandibular joint Fractures Fractures of the mandible usually appear in the symphysis (especially in cats) (fig. 6.22) or in the body of the mandible (fig. 6.23). They are

identified with greater or lesser difficulty depending on the degree of displacement of the fragments. The lateral oblique and ventrodorsal intraoral projections (fig. 6.24) are the most appropriate to examine these fractures. Fractures may be secondary to marked bone loss due to severe periodontitis or neoplasms. In order to assess fractures of the maxilla, the ventrodorsal open- mouth or dorsoventral intraoral projections are used (fig. 6.25). Fragments of the maxillary bone are often minimally displaced, which makes radiographic identification of this type of fracture difficult. Mandibular and maxillary fractures may be accompanied by tooth injuries, so dentition should also be carefully examined in these patients. The fractures that affect the components of the temporomandibular joint are often difficult to accurately assess using X-rays. Computed tomography offers an excellent alternative for the diagnosis of this type of lesion. Temporomandibular joint luxation In addition to performing the standard views to examine the temporomandibular joint, when a temporomandibular luxation is suspected, it will be useful to compare the image obtained with the closed-mouth and open-mouth lateral and lateral oblique projections. The fracture is better visualised on the oblique radiograph. The luxation of the temporomandibular joint is more frequent in cats than in dogs. It usually appears as a sequela of trauma, may be uni- or bilateral and is often associated with a fracture of the mandible. Clinically, the affected animals cannot close their mouth completely, have poor dental occlusion with lateral displacement of the mandible and suffer from excessive salivation. This problem may be difficult to identify on radiographs. The condyloid or condylar process of the mandible usually appears displaced in rostral and dorsal direction (fig. 6.26). Associated fractures of the condyloid process of the mandible or of the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone may also be observed. Temporomandibular subluxations are difficult to identify on radiographs (fig. 6.27). Computed tomography is an excellent alternative for the diagnosis of this type of lesion.
