Temporomandibular dysplasia This is a rare congenital abnormality that has been described more frequently in the Basset Hound, although it can appear in many other breeds. Radiographs may show alterations in the bone such as flattening of the condyle, shallow fossa and the joints may be angled more obliquely than normal rostromedially (fig. 6.28). Oblique projection both with the mouth closed and open may show subluxation of the mandibular condyle, causing joint space narrowing. The technique of choice to confirm the diagnosis is computed tomography, which can be used for three-dimensional volume rendering that can greatly enhance the surgical planning for these patients. Temporomandibular joint ankylosis Ankylosis involves a reduction in the mobility or complete immobility and consolidation of the joint. It usually occurs as a result of untreated intra- articular (true ankylosis) or extra-articular (false ankylosis) trauma. The latter may be due to untreated mandibular and zygomatic fractures, mandibular or zygomatic masses, marked new bone formation in patients with severe chronic otitis media or craniomandibular osteopathy, or it may be due to the presence of abscesses close to the temporomandibular joint. True ankylosis is more common in cats and is characterised radiographically by the appearance of irregularities in the joint space and contour of the mandibular condyle, with periarticular new bone formation.

FIGURE 6.28. Lateral (a), dorsoventral (enlarged image) (b), right lateral oblique (c) and left lateral oblique (d) radiographs of a 9-year-old Basset Hound with temporomandibular dysplasia. Images (c) and (d) are the most useful to evaluate the degree of deformation of both temporomandibular joints, which show flattening of the condyle and condylar fossa, as well as partial fusion of the left joint (arrow). Degenerative joint disease Degenerative joint disease (arthritis) of the temporomandibular joint may appear as a sequel to trauma, dysplasia or contralateral mandibulectomy. Radiographic signs include joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and periarticular osteophyte formation. Involvement is usually bilateral. Infection

Osteomyelitis of the maxilla and mandible are usually secondary to fractures of these bones or infections that primarily affect the teeth. They usually appear as osteoproliferative reactions in the periphery, with thickening of the cortical bone and medullary lysis, which can give the appearance that the teeth are surrounded by soft tissue instead of bone. Infections of the temporomandibular joint are rare. They usually occur from the spreading of osteomyelitis involving the ipsilateral tympanic bulla or from bites in this region. Hence, they are usually unilateral. The radiographic image may be similar to that of osteoarthritis, with bone- forming alterations, although bone lysis may also be evident. Tumours Primary bone tumours of the maxilla and mandible are rare, with the most common being osteosarcomas (fig. 6.29), multilobular osteochondrosarcomas, fibrosarcomas and undifferentiated sarcomas. Most maxilla and mandible tumours originate in the adjacent soft tissues and are, therefore, identified in the physical examination. A radiograph is then useful to determine possible secondary involvement of the adjacent bones. The most common malignant oral tumours in dogs are melanomas (fig. 6.30), squamous cell carcinomas and fibrosarcomas (fig. 6.31). In cats, the most common are squamous cell carcinomas (fig. 6.32) and fibrosarcomas. They appear on radiographs as masses of soft-tissue opacity which, when infiltrating the adjacent bone, cause the appearance of an aggressive bone lesion with both bone-lytic and bone- forming components. The osteolytic lesions may present a moth-eaten pattern, while bone proliferative lesions usually present a spiculated or sunray pattern. The tumour can cause tooth displacement or loss. When a radiographic image is suggestive of an oral tumour, osteomyelitis should also be included in the differential diagnosis, especially in cats as the periosteal reaction can be proliferative and poorly defined. Craniomandibular osteopathy It is also known as “lion’s jaw”. This disease appears in young dogs, of 3 to 18 months of age, especially in the West Highland White Terrier, although it has also been described in the Boston Terrier, Cairn Terrier, Scottish Terrier and, exceptionally, in the Labrador Retriever and Doberman Pinscher. Clinically, it is possible to observe inflammation of the mandible, difficulty to pick up food, pain when opening the mouth or

when chewing, and fever. On radiographs, a marked bone proliferative reaction is observed in the affected areas, which could involve the mandible (fig. 6.33.), the tympanic bullae and the petrous part of the temporal bone (fig. 6.34). The temporomandibular joint, and therefore its mobility, may also be affected. The changes may be uni- or bilateral. The dorsal area of the cranial vault may also appear enlarged, although its aspect is usually not as irregular as in other regions (fig. 6.35). Bone proliferation usually ceases upon completion of skeletal growth, and occasionally, a remodeling of the lesions occurs. Secondary renal hyperparathyroidism It is also called renal osteodystrophy or “rubber jaw”. The reduction in the degree of glomerular filtration causes retention of phosphorus, which reduces calcium levels in blood. This stimulates the production of parathyroid hormone. This disease seems to affect the mandible and maxilla. It usually appears in older dogs, but can also be detected in young patients with congenital renal dysplasia. Clinically, it may be characterised by the appearance of dental disease, excessive salivation, loss of teeth or respiratory problems due to maxillary collapse. The radiographic signs include demineralisation of the mandible and/or maxilla, loss of the lamina dura and formation of radiolucent halos around the dental roots. At advanced stages, the mineral density of teeth markedly contrasts with the demineralised surrounding bone (fig. 6.36). In chronic processes, there may be demineralisation of the long bones of the limbs.

Teeth The tooth (fig. 6.37) is divided into crown, neck and root or root canal. A distinction is made between the anatomical crown and the clinical crown. The latter is defined as the visible part of the tooth, that is, the part that protrudes above the gum line. The hard tissues of the tooth are dentin, enamel (covering only the crown) and cementum (covering only the root), which are of mineral density. Dental enamel is the most highly mineralised tissue in the body, so it appears slightly more radiopaque than dentin. In contrast, dentin cannot be radiographically distinguished from cementum. The pulp cavity is of soft tissue density, is larger in young animals and diminishes with age. The periodontium, also referred to as periodontal tissues, is the tooth’s connective tissue, that is, it is the supporting structure that surrounds the tooth. It is composed of the cementum (dentists consider the cementum part of the periodontium

rather than a part of the tooth itself), the periodontal ligament, the alveolar bone and the gingiva. The periodontal ligament is made up of collagen fibres that anchor the tooth to the alveolar bone and is of soft tissue opacity. The more radiopaque margin of alveolar bone, which is in contact with the periodontal ligament, is the lamina dura. The socket in the bone where the teeth are inserted is called the alveolus. The gingiva covers the alveolar bone and has soft tissue opacity.The dental formulas of the dog and cat are shown in table 6.1. The Triadan numbering system is used (fig. 6.38) in which each tooth is identified by a three-digit number. The first digit denotes the quadrant of the mouth and indicates whether the tooth is part of the primary or permanent dentition: Permanent teeth: 1. Upper right arcade. 2. Upper left arcade. 3. Lower left arcade. 4. Lower right arcade. Temporary or deciduous teeth: 5. Upper right arcade. 6. Upper left arcade. 7. Lower left arcade. 8. Lower right arcade.

Although some dental abnormalities can be identified using conventional X-ray equipment and standard cassette-film or digital radiography systems, the use of dental X-ray equipment or at least

dental film or intraoral digital radiography systems (direct digital sensors and photostimulable phosphor plates) is preferable. Projections with X-ray equipment and standard digital film, screen or detector systems are open-mouth lateral oblique of maxilla and mandible, open-mouth ventrodorsal (ventral 20º rostral–caudodorsal), intraoral dorsoventral to evaluate the rostral portion of the maxillary arch and the intraoral ventrodorsal to evaluate the rostral portion of the mandibular arch. To perform intraoral projections, a distinction is made between the paralleling and bisecting angle techniques. The paralleling technique (fig. 6.39) is used to examine the mandibular molars and premolars (excluding the first premolar) by positioning the dental digital detector or cassette medially to the body of the mandible, as parallel as possible to the tooth to be examined so that the X-ray beam is oriented perpendicular to the tooth and the film/detector. The bisecting angle technique (fig. 6.40) permits correction of the distortion in the radiographic silhouette of the tooth due to the angle of the X-ray beam (fig. 6.41). It is used to evaluate the maxillary and mandibular incisors and canines, as well as the maxillary premolars. For this, the X-ray beam must be directed perpendicular to the imaginary line that divides the angle formed by the cassette/detector and the long axis of the tooth in two. In this way, the silhouette of the tooth presents less geometric distortion in the image.

FIGURE 6.38. Schematic diagram of the Triadan permanent tooth numbering system in the dog (left) and the cat (right). Periodontal disease This is the most common dental disease in dogs and cats. The incidence is very high in small and miniature breed dogs. Initially, radiographs reveal loss of visualisation of the lamina dura and later progressive lysis (resorption) of the alveolar bone. This creates an image of progressive widening of the periodontal space (fig. 6.42). Two resorption patterns can be distinguished: a horizontal pattern, in which there is a somewhat homogeneous loss of alveolar bone height, which generally affects several teeth (fig. 6.43), and a vertical pattern, in which alveolar bone height loss affects more of a localised area (fig. 6.44). It is very common for both radiological patterns to appear together. As the process progresses, external resorption of the roots may also be observed. Also, periodontal disease can secondarily affect the pulp cavity causing it to widen, and this would indicate pulpitis. In severe cases of periodontal disease, significant bone loss can lead to pathologic fractures. Periapical abscess

These abscesses may appear associated with periodontal disease, caries or fractures of dental roots. They give rise to the formation of a radiolucent halo around the root of the tooth affected by the destruction of the alveolar bone. Reabsorption of the dental root, which appears thinner and with an irregular outline, may also be observed (fig. 6.45). In dogs, infections of the fourth maxillary premolar (carnassial) may lead to the formation of a fistulous tract that usually opens to the outside under the eye. Periapical abscesses sometimes progress to chronic osteomyelitis, which can cause more extensive bone lytic and proliferative lesions that can resemble a tumour. A biopsy would be required for a definitive diagnosis. Tooth resorption Tooth resorption develops progressively and is caused by the activation of odontoclasts. It begins on the surface of the root, from there spreads to the root dentin and then into the crown dentin, where it can cause enamel defects. Two types of dental resorption have been distinguished: inflammatory and idiopathic. Idiopathic tooth resorption is very common in cats (fig. 6.46), although it can also occur in dogs. A complete radiological examination of the mouth is recommended for the evaluation of this pathology in feline patients. The number of lesions increases with the patient’s age. The American Veterinary Dental College has established a classification based on the severity of the lesions (stages 1 to 5) and on their location (types 1 to 3).

Tumours The most common tumours are peripheral odontogenic fibromas (formerly known as fibromatous epulis, arising from the periodontal ligament), odontomas and acanthomatous ameloblastomas. Peripheral odontogenic fibromas are very common oral growths in dogs and can be either fibromatous or ossifying types. They arise from the periodontal ligament and create localised firm swellings. They contain variable amounts of bone and osteoid substances, dentinoid or even cementum-like material. The radiographic image depends on the degree of calcification and can range from the appearance of small lesions starting from the bone margin to single or multiple lesions, as islets of bone, with a trabecular pattern. The teeth may be displaced but there is usually no osteolysis. Odontomas are made up of regular dental tissue that has grown in an irregular fashion (hamartomas). Compound odontomas are hamartomas that contain numerous complete tooth-like structures (fig. 6.47). Complex odontomas contain structures derived from individual dental components: enamel, dentin, cementum and pulp. They can form close to the crown or root of normal teeth so can be confused with a displaced or extra tooth. On radiographs they appear as expansile masses with

regular borders that cause lytic changes to adjacent bone by compression atrophy. They may present mineralised dental elements. Acanthomatous ameloblastomas are locally invasive and generally cause tooth displacement (fig. 6.48). They most often form around the canines and incisors. On radiographs they usually appear as slow- growing, expansive lesions. Auditory system In order to assess the auditory system, it is recommended to take a ventrodorsal radiograph, which allows the examination of the ear canals, a rostrocaudal open-mouth radiograph, in which the two tympanic bullae may be observed, and right and left oblique lateral radiographs, which improve the visualisation of the bulla closest to the chassis. Although the standard open-mouth rostrocaudal view can also be performed in the cat, it is preferable to obtain the rostroventral–oblique caudodorsal at a 10º angle (rostral 10º ventral–caudodorsal) to visualise and compare both tympanic bullae on the image (fig. 6.49).

FIGURE 6.48. Ventrodorsal intraoral radiograph of the mandible of a dog with an acanthomatous ameloblastoma. The tumour produces an osteoproliferative reaction with displacement of the affected incisor (tooth 203) and swelling of the adjacent soft tissues (arrow). The ear canals appear as gas density tracts lateral to the tympanic bullae on ventrodorsal radiographs. On lateral oblique and rostrocaudal open-mouth radiographs, the tympanic bulla appears as an approximately round structure containing air, limited by a thin wall of mineral density (fig. 6.50). The image is slightly different in cats, since they have a bone division that creates two compartments, one internal and the other external (fig. 6.51).

Otitis externa Otitis externa is diagnosed clinically and, in many cases, does not cause any evident alteration of the radiographic image of the patient’s ear canals. Obstruction of the affected canal or canals is sometimes observed and it is common to find calcification of the walls in chronic processes (fig. 6.52). Otitis media It is usually secondary to chronic otitis externa. The left and right lateral oblique views, as well as the rostrocaudal open-mouth view, are the most appropriate to assess this alteration. The radiological signs indicative of otitis media are thickening and/or irregularity of the bone wall of the tympanic bulla, as well as increased radiographic density in its interior (fig. 6.53). The process may be uni- or bilateral (fig. 6.54). If the osteoproliferative reaction is very marked, it may eventually affect the temporal bone and temporomandibular joint. A normal radiographic image of the bullae does not rule out otitis media. Both computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are excellent techniques for the evaluation of this disease. In young cats, inflammatory polyps can form in the middle ear that can extend into the external auditory canal or into the nasopharynx, producing masses of soft tissue opacity that can be identified on the lateral projection with some degree of difficulty depending on their size. Usually, the cranial margin of these nasopharyngeal polyps is masked by the overlapping of other structures, while its caudal margin is more easily identified as it contrasts with the air contained in the nasopharynx.

Primary or secondary

middle ear tumours often cause bulla wall lysis, bone proliferation and soft tissue swelling. An increase in the opacity of the affected bulla is generally observed, either due to accumulation of exudate or to proliferation of tissue it contains. Cholesteatoma Middle ear cholesteatomas are non-neoplastic lesions that can appear similar to aggressive tumours in that they can cause expansion and lysis of the bone components of the ear (fig. 6.56). These are epidermoid cysts that accumulate hyperkeratotic material. As they progressively increase in size, they can cause compression and destruction of the adjacent tissues. Sometimes they break, causing inflammation and in some cases infection of the surrounding tissues. They may be primary acquired associated with Eustachian tube dysfunction and chronic poor ventilation of the ear canal, or secondary

to chronic otitis media, middle ear trauma or previous surgeries of the external auditory canal or middle ear. X-rays may show features similar to those of otitis media. If bulla wall lysis appears, chronic otitis media, cholesteatoma and neoplasia should be considered as differential diagnoses. Enlargement of the bulla suggests a cholesteatoma or tumour since it is not a typical sign of otitis media. The definitive diagnosis between cholesteatoma and neoplasia must be established by histological study, given the similarity of the radiographic findings of these processes, and even of those observed by computed tomography and magnetic resonance. Presentation Explanation

Most common diagnostic errors 7 The main disadvantages of radiography against other diagnostic imaging techniques are the limited differences of opacity in the image (gas, fat, soft tissues and fluids, mineral and metal) and the superimposition of structures, which often causes a loss of diagnostic information as well as optical effects that may lead to errors in the diagnosis. Diagnostic errors are also frequently caused by apparently anomalous images due to a poor position of the patient when the radiograph was taken, the use of incorrect exposure values, an inappropriate administration of the contrast agent, and by a poor knowledge of the normal anatomical variations of certain structures. This chapter reviews the most common diagnostic errors divided by anatomical regions and includes a specific reference to those that are typical of digital radiography in the last section. Many of them have already been mentioned in the corresponding chapters of this book. Note: the text includes references to the figures in this chapter as well as to other figures that have already appeared in previous chapters. Abdomen Lack of abdominal fat, wet hair Very thin (fig. 7.1) or very young (fig. 7.2) animals have very little intra-abdominal fat, which renders identification of abdominal structures more difficult. This image may be mistaken for that caused by ascites, peritonitis or peritoneal carcinomatosis. The image produced by overlying wet hair, for example when a radiograph is

taken after an abdominal ultrasound in which gel was applied to enhance the transmission of ultrasonic waves, should not be confused with that of these diseases either. Underexposure and overexposure A greatly underexposed abdominal radiograph (taken with very low exposure values) may also give a false appearance of increased and more homogeneous radiopacity than normal, which should not be confused with peritoneal disease. On the other hand, on a highly overexposed abdominal radiograph (taken with very high exposure values), the decrease in radiopacity caused by the technical error may be confused with that caused by a pneumoperitoneum. FIGURE 7.1. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a very thin, healthy dog. The abdominal organs appear poorly differentiated due to the lack of intraabdominal fat. This could be confused with ascites, peritonitis or peritoneal carcinomatosis.

In case of doubt, an ultrasound scan will allow us to establish a precise diagnosis. FIGURE 7.2. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a healthy young dog. The abdominal organs appear poorly differentiated due to the lack of intraabdominal fat, which is normal in young animals. We should not confuse this image with that caused by ascites, peritonitis or peritoneal carcinomatosis. In case of doubt, an ultrasound scan will allow us to establish a precise diagnosis. Caudal hepatic border depending on thoracic conformation The caudal hepatic border is usually seen at the level of or slightly beyond the costal arch on lateral radiographs. In order not to give an

incorrect diagnosis of increase or reduction in the size of the liver, it must be borne in mind that, in breeds with a deep and narrow thorax, the whole shadow of the liver may be located in the thoracic cage (false appearance of decrease in size) while, on the other hand, the caudal hepatic border extends beyond the limit of the costal arch to a greater extent in breeds with a wide and shallow thorax (false appearance of increase in size). Physiological organomegaly in young animals It should be remembered that young animals display a certain degree of organomegaly in comparison with adult animals. This should be taken into account in the first months of life so as not to make an incorrect diagnose of increase in the size of the abdominal organs. False impression of splenomegaly It is also important to highlight that splenomegaly is assessed in function of the thickness of the shadow of the spleen, since its length depends on the position of the tail of the spleen when taking the radiograph. A long shadow with no increase in its thickness does not indicate splenomegaly (fig. 2.38). Gestation before foetal mineralisation Before day 45 of pregnancy in the dog and between days 36 and 45 in the cat, the pregnant uterus appears increased in size, but the mineralised foetal structures cannot be differentiated in it (fig. 2.86). We may therefore mistake pregnancy for pathological dilatation of the uterus. Performing an abdominal ultrasound scan will allow us to establish a differential diagnosis.

Superimposition of the prepuce and os penis The shadow of the prepuce on a ventrodorsal radiograph may be mistaken for the shadow of the bladder or for a mass. Especially on rotated radiographs, the shadows of the prepuce and os penis may create optical effects of superimposition on the hip that may be confused with lesions of the latter. “Pseudomasses” Some normal abdominal images may produce a pseudomass effect. Thus, a very distended bladder filled with fluids may be mistaken for masses originated by pathological causes in other organs (fig. 2.64). The fat that accumulates in the falciform ligament of obese cats creates a shadow ventral to the liver that reminds of a mass, although its density, which is lower than that of soft tissues, facilitates its identification as fat (fig. 2.10). The superimposition of the two kidneys on lateral radiographs creates an optical effect since their radiographic densities add up, which may be confused with the presence of a third structure in the area. Another example of pseudomass is the markedly round image that the normal pyloric antrum may have on right lateral radiographs. This is a classical example of a possible diagnostic pitfall, as it may be confused with a mass or with a round foreign body (fig. 7.3). False thickening of the gastric or intestinal wall Although this has already been mentioned in the corresponding section of this book, it is important to highlight that one of the most important errors that may be made when assessing an abdominal X- ray is to diagnose a thickening of the gastric (fig. 2.108) or intestinal

(fig. 2.125) wall. In the image, it is impossible to distinguish a wall that is really thickened from a normal wall with fluid or mucus adjacent to it, which gives a false impression of increase in thickness. The thickness of the walls of the stomach and intestine must be assessed by ultrasonography. Increase in the amount of gastric and intestinal fluid/gas A predominance of fluid (fig. 7.4) or gas (fig. 7.5) content in the small intestine is considered to be indicative of enteritis, but it is important to highlight that these findings alone do not mean there is a disease process. In a similar way, a very dilated stomach filled with gas in a nervous animal may be exclusively due to aerophagia and may not have any pathological significance.

FIGURE 7.5. Lateral radiograph of the abdomen of a healthy dog. In the image, it is possible to observe a marked predominance of gas content in the small intestine, which is not accompanied by alterations of its diameter. This finding alone does not have any pathological significance, although it sometimes appears associated with processes of enteritis. As in the case of a predominance of fluid, it would be a serious error to diagnose enteritis based only on this radiological finding. Anatomical variations of the gastrointestinal tract in cats

The accumulation of loops of the small intestine in the centre of the abdomen in obese cats is due to the tendency shown by these animals to accumulate fat in the peripheral areas of the abdomen (fig. 2.10), and this finding should therefore not be attributed to pathological causes. The radiographs of some cats also show a band of fat density in the gastric wall, which is considered an incidental finding with no clinical significance. Intestinal particularities in dogs The caecum in dogs often appears dilated, with gas content and a C- shape in the right cranial area of the abdomen on ventrodorsal radiographs (fig. 2.142), and superimposed on the descending colon on lateral radiographs. It is important not to confuse it with a segment of abnormally dilated small intestine so as not to make an incorrect diagnosis of intestinal obstruction. Some dogs have a longer colon than normal, which is called redundant colon and is considered a normal anatomical variation. Peristaltic waves A wavy appearance of the wall of the small or large intestine may sometimes be observed. This finding is indicative of an inflammatory or diffuse infiltrative process if it persists on various radiographs taken at different times, but when it is an isolated finding in a radiographic study, it is usually due to the appearance of a peristaltic wave when the radiograph was taken (fig. 7.6). Inappropriate doses of contrast agent With regard to contrast techniques, the most frequent cause of diagnostic errors is the administration of an inappropriate dose of contrast medium. For instance, if positive-contrast gastrography is

used to evaluate gastric emptying and a lower dose than recommended is administered, the rate of emptying will be slower, while if an excessive dose is administered it will be faster. The results of the test will therefore not be objective. Patterns of contrast medium accumulation When carrying out a barium study of the small intestine in small dogs, it is possible to observe out-pouchings in the contrast column as this goes through the duodenum. These are called pseudoulcers (fig. 7.7), and are due to the focal accumulation of the contrast medium in areas with lymphatic tissue. In approximately 30 % of cats, it is also possible to observe a peculiar image of the duodenum when administering barium, which is referred to as the “string of pearls” sign (fig. 7.8), and is due to strong segmental contractions of the duodenal wall with no pathological significance. This image is similar to the one that the presence of a linear foreign body may cause in any intestinal segment. Presence of gas bubbles When retrograde urethrography or positive-contrast cystography are used, it is easy to confuse the image created by the gas bubbles that were introduced when the patient was catheterised with real filling defects caused by calculi or clots (fig. 2.69). These gas bubbles usually have a round morphology, while calculi and clots usually have a more irregular shape and distribution. Contrast diffusion Finally, on retrograde urethrograms in males, it is possible to observe the passage of a small amount of contrast medium to the prostatic

ducts. This finding does not have any pathological significance, unless it is accompanied by a focal accumulation of contrast material in cavities or cystic areas. FIGURE 7.6. Enlarged image of the abdomen on a lateral radiograph of a healthy dog. The wavy appearance of the large intestinal wall may be due to an inflammatory process, but it may also be due to normal peristalsis. The persistence of this image on serial radiographs is considered indicative of a disease.

FIGURE 7.7. Enlarged image of the duodenum 20 minutes after administering barium by oral route to a healthy dog. The out-pouchings that appear on the lateral aspect of the contrast column are due to the presence of normal lymphatic tissue in the duodenal wall. This image may be confused with ulcers, which is why it is referred to as pseudoulcers.

FIGURE 7.8. Enlarged image of the duodenum 30 minutes after administering barium by oral route to a healthy cat. The wavy appearance of the duodenal wall is due to normal peristaltic contractions and is termed “string of pearls” sign. It may be confused with the image of a linear foreign body. Neck and thorax

Confusion of the hyoid apparatus with foreign bodies When the presence of a foreign body in the neck is suspected, the bones that form the hyoid apparatus should not be confused with foreign bodies in the pharynx. If a real foreign body is detected on a lateral radiograph, its exact location should always be confirmed by taking a ventrodorsal radiograph. Cricopharyngeal sphincter When administering a contrast agent by oral route and evaluating its passage from the orophraynx to the oesophagus, it is important not to confuse the image of the cranial oesophageal sphincter (cricopharyngeal sphincter) with a filling defect or “mass effect” due to pathological causes. Cutaneous nodules and nipples Cutaneous nodules may have a similar image to nodular lesions in the lung. The same may sometimes occur when nipples are superimposed (fig. 7.9) on rotated radiographs. In case of doubt, the thoracic wall should be examined thoroughly and a small amount of barium should be applied on the cutaneous lesion or nipple to repeat the radiograph. Calcification associated with age Calcification of the costochondral junctions associated with age, which has no clinical significance, should not be confused with aggressive bone lesions (fig. 3.10). On ventrodorsal radiographs, these calcifications may create a false effect of calcified nodular lesions in the lung (fig. 7.10).

FIGURE 7.9. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of a healthy dog. The arrow indicates a hyperplastic nipple, which, due to the rotated position of the thorax, is superimposed on the ventral area of the shadow of the liver and may be mistaken for a calculus in the gallbladder or for a nodular lesion in the lung.

FIGURE 7.10. Ventrodorsal radiograph of the thorax of a healthy dog. The arrows show calcifications of the right costochondral junctions. These should not be confused with aggressive bone lesions or calcified nodular lesions in the lung. Folds of skin The folds of skin that form when the patient is placed on the cassette may create well-defined shadows of soft-tissue density surrounded by gas, which should not be confused with diseases (fig. 3.1c).

Rib curvature and costal cartilage calcification Chondrodystrophic breeds sometimes show a peculiar curvature of the ribs and costal cartilages towards the inside of the cavity, in the area proximal to the costochondral junction. This creates shadows of soft-tissue density that may be similar to a pleural or pulmonary lesion (fig. 3.7). Costal cartilages may appear partially calcified in cats, which may produce a false impression of a fracture (fig. 3.66).

FIGURE 7.11. Left lateral radiograph of the thorax of a healthy dog. It is possible to observe a band of soft-tissue density in the caudodorsal area of the thorax, between the aorta (Ao) and the caudal vena cava (CVC). This shadow is due to the retention of fluid or mucus in the caudal area of the thoracic oesophagus (Oe), and is not considered pathological unless it persists on serial radiographs. False alterations of the trachea

Minimal variations in the diameter of the trachea between inspiration and expiration are physiological. The rotation of the thorax at the moment when a lateral radiograph is taken may cause the oesophagus and/or muscles and the trachea to be superimposed, thus creating a false image of tracheal collapse. This type of image may also be caused by the so-called redundancy of the dorsal tracheal membrane, or by contraction or invagination of the membrane (fig. 3.24). The thoracic trachea may have a slightly wavy course if the radiograph is taken with the patient’s head or neck in an incorrect position. In addition, a false dorsal displacement of the trachea may appear when the radiograph is taken with the median plane of the thoracic cavity inclined on the cassette (fig. 3.4) (this is corrected by placing a positioning block that elevates the sternum). In obese animals, it is possible to observe a right displacement of the trachea on ventrodorsal radiographs, caused by the excessive accumulation of fat in the mediastinum, not by pathological causes. In order not to make an incorrect diagnosis of tracheal hypoplasia, it is important to remember that the diameter of the trachea is proportionally smaller in brachycephalic breeds, especially in the Bulldog (fig. 3.26). False alterations of the oesophagus The presence of minimal accumulations of gas in the oesophageal lumen is not considered pathological (fig. 3.28), unless it persists over time. The accumulation of a small amount of fluid/mucus in the distal area of the thoracic oesophagus (fig. 7.11), just before going through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm, is also considered physiological. This finding is more frequent on left lateral radiographs than on the right lateral ones. When barium is administered, the temporary retention of a small amount of contrast medium between the folds of the oesophageal wall is not considered significant, but if it persists over time it would be considered indicative of oesophagitis. We should also remember that the oesophagus may appear moderately dilated in anaesthetised animals (fig. 3.30), so as not to make an incorrect diagnosis of pathological dilatation in these cases.

Mediastinum in brachycephalic breeds and obese animals In brachycephalic breeds, the shadow of the mediastinum is wider compared with other breeds. In obese animals the mediastinum may also appear enlarged, which could be similar to the image of a mediastinal mass or effusion, especially on ventrodorsal and dorsoventral radiographs. On lateral radiographs, fat may cause a more or less noticeable elevation of the cardiac silhouette (fig.3.61). False impression of cardiomegaly A false impression of cardiomegaly may be given by rotated radiographs (they show evident increased cardiosternal contact —fig. 3.4—) and expiratory radiographs (the small volume of the lung gives a false impression of increased cardiac size —fig. 7.12—). We should also remember that in old cats, the heart tends to be in greater contact with the sternum due to the progressive elongation of the aorta. This could be confused with an increase in the width of the cardiac silhouette (fig. 3.76). The cardiac silhouette should not be assessed on ventrodorsal and dorsoventral radiographs when the thorax is in rotated position, since it may result in incorrect diagnoses of increased right or left heart size, depending on the side to which the patient has been rotated (fig. 3.5). The accumulation of fat in the pericardial space that may appear in obese animals may also create a false image of increased cardiac size. The organomegaly observed in young animals also affects the heart. Thymus The thymus is observed until approximately 6 months of age and should not be confused with pleural or pulmonary lesions (fig. 3.62).

Coronary vessels A serious diagnostic error is to mistake the pulmonary vessels that overlap the heart for coronary vessels (fig. 7.13). These latter have the same radiopacity as the myocardium, so they cannot be differentiated on a radiograph with no contrast. False pleural effusion Various normal structures may be mistaken for a pleural effusion on a radiograph. In cats, it is normal to observe a minimal retraction of the dorsocaudal border of the caudal pulmonary lobes (fig. 3.6), while the same finding would be indicative of a mild pleural effusion in dogs. Thickening or calcification of the pleura with no pathological significance may also be mistaken for mild pleural effusion (fig. 3.56). False pulmonary alterations The costal cartilages may have the appearance of interlobar fissures, although they can be differentiated since the cartilage is straighter and its junction with the rib can be identified. Folds of skin may cause an artefact known as pseudopneumothorax, which is termed this way because it produces a marked difference of radiopacity between the areas lateral and medial to the fold of skin, resulting in a very dark lateral area (fig. 3.52). This may be mistaken for a pulmonary retraction due to the presence of gas in the pleural space.

FIGURE 7.12. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of a healthy dog. The radiograph was taken in expiration, which causes a false appearance of cardiomegaly due to the smaller volume of the lung and superimposed shadow of the diaphragm and cardiac silhouette.

FIGURE 7.13. Enlarged image of a lateral radiograph of the thorax of a healthy dog. Mistaking the pulmonary vessels (arrow), which appear superimposed on the cardiac silhouette, for coronary vessels is a serious diagnostic error. Coronary vessels have the same radiopacity as the cardiac wall and therefore cannot be identified on a plain radiograph. The radiopacity of the lung may appear falsely increased in obese animals (because of the summation with the density of the subcutaneous fat and limitation of the degree of pulmonary expansion due to the presence of fat in the mediastinum) on underexposed or expiratory radiographs (fig. 1.46b), which should not be confused with a real interstitial pattern due to pathological causes. If a conventional radiograph is overexposed (fig. 1.46a), a false reduction of pulmonary radiopacity is observed, which should not be confused with emphysema or pulmonary hypovascularisation.

The appearance of signs of atelectasis in the lower part of the lung is a usual finding in animals that have remained in lateral recumbency for a long period of time, especially if they have been anaesthetised. The alveolar pattern caused by atelectasis can be differentiated from that caused by oedema, pneumonia or haemorrhage, because a displacement of the mediastinal structures to the side where the atelectasic lung is located will appear on ventrodorsal and dorsoventral radiographs (fig. 3.131). The superimposed pulmonary vessels and ribs may create shadows of greater radiopacity that are similar to nodular lesions in the lung. It is also possible to confuse the transversal shadows of those vessels that run parallel to the X-ray beam with nodules, in which case we should evaluate the adjacent vascular structures to determine whether the diameter of the shadows corresponds or not with that of the vessels in the area (fig. 7.14). Pleural and pulmonary calcifications (fig 3.56) are usually small and it is difficult to mistake them for pulmonary metastases, as these are very rarely calcified. The presence of calcified sludge in the gallbladder may be confused with areas of pleural or pulmonary calcification, or with pulmonary nodules (fig. 7.15). The location of the gallbladder on the two projections allows differentiation and in case of doubt, an abdominal ultrasound examination may be performed. The shadow of the gastric fundus on left lateral radiographs may also be mistaken for a lesion in the dorsocaudal area of the thorax (fig. 7.16).

FIGURE 7.14. Enlarged image of a lateral radiograph of the thorax of a healthy dog. The arrow indicates the transverse image of a normal pulmonary vessel, which could be confused with a pulmonary nodular lesion. In order not to make an incorrect diagnosis, we must check whether other vessels in the area have a similar diameter. In case of doubt, a more precise diagnosis may be established with the help of computed tomography.
FIGURE 7.15. Lateral radiograph of the thorax of a healthy dog. The arrow shows a calculus/gallbladder sludge, which may be mistaken for a calcified nodular lesion in the lung.

FIGURE 7.16. Left lateral radiograph of the thorax of a healthy dog. The arrow indicates the image of the normal gastric fundus (with gas and food content), which shows an apparently more cranial position on the left lateral view than on the right lateral view. This image may be mistaken for a pulmonary lesion. Appendicular skeleton Radiographic technique An error that is often made when evaluating the appendicular skeleton is not to take two orthogonal projections, since some lesions are evident in only one of them (e.g. fractures with little displacement, joint subluxations) (fig. 7.17).

Overexposure of the radiograph may lead to an incorrect diagnosis of osteopaenia, as the bone appears less radiopaque in the image. Age and breed Growth lines in young animals should not be mistaken for fractures (fig. 7.18) and it is therefore recommended to use an atlas with radiographic images of animals throughout their development in case of doubt. It should be remembered that large-breed dogs may have slightly irregular metaphyseal margins, which may be confused with a periosteal reaction or with osteolysis. It is also important to be familiar with the peculiar morphology of bones in chondrodystrophic breeds (e.g. Basset Hound). Incorrect positioning of the patient The most frequent cause of diagnostic errors in the assessment of the appendicular skeleton is the incorrect positioning of the patient when taking the radiograph. This is especially significant in the examination of some joints such as the coxofemoral joint, as its image is greatly altered by minimal rotations of the pelvis. When this joint is rotated to one side, it is possible to see it in the image because the obturator foramen of the same side appears smaller and the shadow of the wing of the contralateral ilium appears narrower. In these conditions, reduced acetabular coverage (false increase of the joint space) on the side to which the pelvis is rotated, and greater acetabular coverage (false reduction of the joint space) in the contralateral joint will be observed (fig. 7.19). The position of the femurs will also affect the width of the joint space, which means that for a proper assessment of the joint, the femurs must remain parallel, with the patellas aligned with the trochlear groove.

FIGURE 7.17. Enlarged images in mediolateral (a) and craniocaudal (b) projection of the radius and ulna of a dog with a fracture of both bones. The fracture of the ulna (arrow) is not visible on the mediolateral view and would therefore not be diagnosed if this radiograph alone were taken.

FIGURE 7.18. Mediolateral radiograph of the tibia of an 11-week- old, healthy dog. The growth plate of the tibial tuberosity (arrow) appears separated from the metaphysis until 6-8 months of age, which could be confused with an avulsion fracture of the tuberosity. The integrity of the sacroiliac joints is not assessed properly when the pelvis is rotated, since one of the joints will appear falsely enlarged, which could be confused with a luxation or subluxation. Clavicle and sesamoid bones

Two important anatomical variations among those that may lead to diagnostic errors are vestigial clavicles (fig. 7.20) and some sesamoid bones that do not appear in a constant manner in dogs. Vestigial clavicles appear as small structures with mineral opacity medial to the head of the humerus. The sesamoid bone in the tendon of origin of the supinator muscle sometimes appears on radiographs of the elbow joint (fig. 4.72), craniolateral to the head of the radius. A sesamoid bone may also be observed in some cases on the lateral plantar aspect of the tarsometatarsal joint or in it. Sesamoid bones may also appear in the iliopubic ligament, and these are located cranial to the pubic eminence of the pelvis on lateral radiographs.

FIGURE 7.19. Ventrodorsal radiograph of the hip of a dog with a mild degree of hip luxation due to dysplasia. We can detect that the pelvis is rotated to the right side because the obturator foramen appears smaller and the shadow of the wing of the ilium is narrower. Due to this rotation, the right hip joint space (arrow) appears falsely increased, while in the left hip joint, the acetabular coverage is falsely increased.

FIGURE 7.20. Caudocranial radiograph of the scapulohumeral joint of a healthy dog. The arrow shows the vestigial clavicle, which is sometimes observed in dogs. It is bilateral and should not be mistaken for a pathological calcification of the soft tissues of the area.

Spine Incorrect positioning of the patient The main source of diagnostic errors in the assessment of the spine is the incorrect positioning of the patient when taking a radiograph. If no radiolucent positioning blocks are used to elevate the cervical and lumbar spines, these remain curved towards the cassette/X-ray table, causing an evident narrowing of the intervertebral disc spaces (fig. 7.21). Even if the position of the spine is correct, only the intervertebral disc spaces that are most centred in the image should be evaluated, since the X-ray beam penetrates through them more obliquely as these spaces are farther away from its centre, thus creating a false narrowing in the image. In order for the median plane of the spine to be parallel to the cassette, it is necessary to place radiolucent positioning blocks between the limbs or under them. If this is not done, the spine remains rotated and the transverse processes of each side appear separated in the image (fig. 5.2a). The most ventral ones may easily be confused with spondylosis deformans. Overexposure and underexposure Overexposure or underexposure of the radiograph may cause a false alteration of the radiopacity of the vertebrae, which we may be confused with osteopaenia o sclerosis. Superimposed structures The superimposition of the large bowel containing gas or faeces on the sacrum or pelvis may create an image similar to that of lines of fracture in these structures.

FIGURE 7.21. Enlarged image of the lumbar spine on a lateral radiograph of a healthy dog. When an area of the spine (cervical or lumbar) is curved towards the cassette/X-ray table, a false narrowing of the intervertebral disc spaces (arrows) will be observed on the radiograph. This defect is corrected by placing a radiolucent positioning block under the spine to ensure its axis is parallel to the cassette. In this image, the transverse processes of each vertebra appear at a different height, which indicates that the spine is rotated on its longitudinal axis (this can be corrected by placing a radiolucent positioning block between the limbs). The most ventral transverse processes may be confused with spondylosis deformans.

FIGURE 7.22. Lateral radiograph of the lumbar spine of a healthy dog. The ventral margin of the vertebral body of L3 and L4 (arrows) appears less defined due to the insertion of the crura of the diaphragm. This finding is more evident in large breed dogs. FIGURE 7.23. Enlarged image of the thoracic spine on a lateral radiograph of a healthy dog. A mild narrowing of the T10-T11 intervertebral disc space (arrow) can be seen when compared with the others. This is considered a normal anatomical variation. FIGURE 7.24. Enlarged image of the thoracolumbar area of the spine on a lateral radiograph of a dog that has received an injection of an iodinated contrast agent

in the subarachnoid space for a myelogram, and in the extradural space by mistake, which creates irregularities in the margin of the contrast columns. Normal anatomical variations Some normal anatomical variations that may be mistaken for diseases are: the lack of definition of the ventral margin of the body of L3 and L4, due to the insertion of the crura of the diaphragm (fig 7.22) (more evident in large breed dogs); the narrowing of the T10-T11 intervertebral disc space, as it is an anticlinal space (fig 7.23); and the presence of haemal processes at the ends of the coccygeal vertebrae, which may be confused with spondylosis deformans. Contrast medium in extradural space If the contrast medium is introduced by mistake in the epidural space instead of in the subarachnoid space when performing a myelogram, the contrast columns will have a very irregular morphology (fig. 7.24) and making a precise diagnosis will thus be more difficult. Head Incorrect positioning of the patient Most of the interpretation errors made when evaluating radiographs of a patient’s head are due to a poor positioning of the patient. In this region, it is essential not to rotate the skull, especially on dorsoventral and ventrodorsal radiographs (fig. 7.25), since the symmetry or lack of symmetry of the structures is a key element on which the diagnosis of many diseases of this anatomical region is based. On ventrodorsal open-mouth radiographs, the superimposition of the tongue should be avoided, since it may create a false image of

mass in the nasal cavity (fig. 7.26). Rostrocaudal tangential radiographs may provide images of a false increase in radiopacity of the frontal sinuses due to a poor positioning of the patient, or to the actual morphology of the sinuses and nasal bone depending on the breed (fig. 7.27). FIGURE 7.25. Dorsoventral radiograph of the head of a healthy young dog (superimposed deciduous and permanent teeth are observed). The rotation of the head increases the summation effect of the right mandibular body and nasal

cavity of the same side, which hinders the correct assessment of this region of the skull. FIGURE 7.26. Ventrodorsal open-mouth radiograph of a healthy dog. The superimposition of the tongue (arrow) creates a false image of mass in the caudal area of the left nasal cavity.

FIGURE 7.27. Rostrocaudal tangential radiograph of the frontal sinuses of a healthy dog. The incorrect positioning of the patient results in the X-ray beam penetrating through the cranial vault and frontal sinuses. The images of both structures add up, which results in a false image of increased radiopacity of the sinuses. Digital imaging One of the great advantages of digital radiology is that it has a high contrast resolution compared with conventional radiology. The veterinary surgeon who acquires digital radiology equipment for the first time therefore has to get used to “a new way of observing radiographs”. Some diagnostic errors can be made during this transition period. Greater definition of the elements of the lung In digital radiography, the blood vessels of the lung are very well- defined, which may lead to an incorrect diagnosis of vascular

congestion. In some healthy animals, the bronchial walls may also be identified in the medial area of the lung, a finding that would be considered as indicative of a thickening of the bronchial walls, the presence of peribronchial infiltrates or calcification on a conventional radiograph. Higher pulmonary radiopacity The lung generally appears less transparent on a digital radiograph (fig. 1.29), which could be confused with a pathological interstitial pattern. In addition, on a digital radiograph, minimal degrees of lung displacement caused by mediastinal fat or by being in a lateral recumbent position may become more evident and may be similar to a pleural or mediastinal effusion. Higher tissue contrast The higher contrast between soft tissues and fat may lead to this latter being mistaken for free peritoneal gas on a digital radiograph of the abdomen. An incor-rect diagnosis of pneumoperitoneum may thus be established. The trabeculae of bones may also appear better defined, which should not be interpreted as a pathological change in the bone marrow. Overexposure On highly overexposed digital radiographs, black areas with a loss of image information may appear in the affected area, and are not possible to recover with post-processing tools (fig. 7.28). When these areas appear in the lung, we may mistake them for pulmonary bullae while if they appear in the bone, they may be similar to areas of osteolysis.

Metallic implants The appearance of an artefact around metallic implants placed in the bone has already been described. It is observed as radiolucent bands around these implants, and may be confused with a sign of mobility or rejection of the material (fig. 7.29). This artefact has already been corrected in many of the current machines and is caused by an excessive use of the edge-enhancement tool. Excessive post-processing In general, post-processing tools allow the improvement of the image quality, but when overused they may worsen it and lead to errors (fig. 7.30), in many cases due to an overdiagnosis (we see more than what is actually there). Excessive zooming A significant advantage of digital radiography is that we can use the zoom tool to greatly enlarge small areas of the image. However, we should not overuse this tool as we run the risk of losing the global view of the image, which in many cases is essential to establish a correct diagnosis.

FIGURE 7.28. Enlarged image of the cranioventral area of the thorax of a healthy dog. The arrows indicate an overexposed area of the image (digital), which could be mistaken for an area of hypovascularisation or a pulmonary bulla.

FIGURE 7.29. Enlarged image of the tibia on a mediolateral radiograph of a dog after the placement of pins and a cerclage wire. When the edge-enhancement tool is overused in digital radiography, radiolucent halos may appear around metal implants, which could be mistaken for a sign of rejection or mobility of the material.

FIGURE 7.30. Enlarged images of the caudodorsal area of a healthy dog. One of them shows the properly processed digital radiograph (a), while the other shows the same image after overuse of the edge enhancement tool (b), which highlights the image of the vessels, bronchial walls and even the lung parenchyma excessively.
